Chapter Two Hundred Sixty-Five

Romans 8:1–11 — Introduction to the New Life; Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 8:1 “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: Therefore there is no judgment to those who are in Christ Jesus.

Romans 8:2 “For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: For the principle of the Spirit — that is, the ministry of the Holy Spirit of salvation, who is the source of eternal life — has set you free in Christ Jesus from the principle of the sin nature and the resultant spiritual death.

Romans 8:3 “For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,” (ESV)

Corrected translation: For what was impossible from the law — because it was weak through the flesh — God, by having sent His own Son in the likeness of the flesh of sin and as a sin offering, judged the sin nature in the flesh,

Romans 8:4 “in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: in order that the legal requirement of the law might be filled up in us who keep walking not according to the old sin nature but according to the Spirit.

Romans 8:5–8 “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace. For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: For those believers who are according to the flesh — that is, those dominated by the old sin nature — keep thinking about the things of the flesh, the trends toward sin, good, and evil. But those believers who are according to the Spirit, that is, dominated by the Holy Spirit, keep thinking about those doctrines from the Spirit. Consequently, the thought pattern of the flesh, the old sin nature, is death — maximum discipline of the sin unto death. But the thought pattern of the Spirit, Bible doctrine resident in the soul, is life and prosperity. Because the thought pattern of the flesh, the old sin nature, is hostile to God — for it is not subordinate to the law of God, because it is not able to be subordinate to Bible doctrine. Moreover, those who are under the authority of the old sin nature — whether unbeliever or reversionistic believer — are not able to please God.

Romans 8:9–11 “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness. If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: In fact, you are not in the flesh — the believer is divorced from the old sin nature. But in the Spirit, assuming that the Spirit of God indwells you. In fact, if anyone does not have the Spirit from Christ — the Holy Spirit — he does not belong to God. In fact, if Christ is in you, on the one hand the body is dead because of sin, the old sin nature. But on the other hand, the Holy Spirit is new life because of imputed righteousness. Now if the Holy Spirit — from God the Father, doctrine of procession — who raised up Jesus from deaths, both spiritual and physical, indwells you, and He does (first-class condition), He who raised Christ Jesus from deaths will also make alive your mortal bodies by His Spirit who indwells you.

Romans 8 stands as the great exposition of the new life — the life of the believer operating within the Protocol Plan of God. The title for this chapter is drawn from Romans 6:4: 'Therefore we have been buried together with Him through the baptism of the Spirit into His death, in order that as Christ has been raised up from deaths, spiritual and physical, through the glory of the Father, so also we might walk in newness of life.' The principle is straightforward: the plan of God is greater than any condemnation, any sin, any failure, any personal suffering or adversity, any historical disaster, any problem of life. The new life, sustained by the daily intake of Bible doctrine, places the believer above the circumstances of life so that life never finally destroys him. We may bend, but we do not break.

The plan of God for the believer's life divides into three phases. Phase one is salvation, accomplished by the Lord Jesus Christ on the cross and communicated to the individual through the ministry of God the Holy Spirit in common grace and efficacious grace. Phase two finds the believer alive after salvation — the believer in time — accomplished through the filling of the Spirit plus the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), designed to reach the objective of maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Phase three finds the believer in eternity, accomplished by all three persons of the Godhead, with the Holy Spirit as the agent of resurrection.

The chapter divides into three paragraphs: (1) the new life and sanctification, verses 1–17; (2) the new life and suffering, verses 18–30; (3) the new life and its challenges, verses 31–39. Before the exegesis of any verse can have its full impact, the doctrine of sanctification must be clearly in view, for sanctification is the theological framework within which the entire chapter operates.

I. The Doctrine of Sanctification

A. Definition and Description

Sanctification is a technical biblical term describing the plan of God in the language of divine objectives in each of the three phases: salvation, time, and eternity. It is therefore not a single event but a comprehensive category covering the entire arc of the believer's existence. Sanctification as a word means 'set apart as sacred' or 'set apart as consecrated,' but that surface definition must be filled with its full theological content: God has a plan for the believer's life in three phases, and sanctification is the technical description of that plan.

Sanctification is further defined as a priestly and royal family term, tying the church-age believer to the grace contract of God forever. The royal family of God is the church-age believer only — from Pentecost AD 30 to the rapture of the church. The dispensation of the church is an intercalation into the age of Israel, interrupting it seven years short of its completion, in order to call out the royal family of God. The differentiation between the church-age believer and every Old Testament believer is the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which did not occur in Old Testament times and will not occur in the Tribulation or the Millennium. It is the means by which believers are entered into permanent union with Christ and the royal family of God is constituted.

The resurrection, ascension, and session of the Lord Jesus Christ abrogated the old contract of the Mosaic Law and simultaneously interrupted the Jewish age. The interruption was caused by the battlefield royalty given to the Lord at the Father's right hand — 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet' (Psalm 110:1). Having received this third category of royalty — King of kings, Lord of lords — with no royal family yet in existence, the age of Israel was interrupted so that the age of the church might be inserted to call out that royal family. Every church-age believer therefore occupies a unique position in history, with greater opportunity and greater accountability than any Old Testament, Tribulation, or Millennial believer.

Because church-age believers are royal family, divine discipline for apostasy and reversionism is proportionally greater than that received by any believer in the Old Testament for similar failure. Every believer has a life of meaning, purpose, and definition — and this is what sanctification describes.

B. Etymology of Sanctification

The key text for the etymology is John 6:69, where the disciples confess: 'We have believed, in fact we have come to know, that you are ho hagios tou theou — the holy one from God.' The word hagios (ἅγιος) in the nominative singular is applied to the Lord Jesus Christ before it is ever applied to the believer. The genitive tou theou (τοῦ θεοῦ) should be read as an ablative of source: 'the sanctified one from God,' 'the aristocrat from God.' The title points to the unique royalty and aristocracy of the Lord Jesus Christ — the supreme aristocracy in the entire human race.

Jesus Christ bears three categories of royalty. First, as God — His title is Son of God, the title of divine aristocracy, with His royal family being the Father and the Holy Spirit. Second, in the Davidic line — His title is Son of David, Jewish royalty. He is descended through both royal lines of David: the senior line through Solomon (through Joseph, His legal father) and the junior line through Nathan (through the Virgin Mary, His real mother). Third, battlefield royalty received at the right hand of the Father — King of kings and Lord of lords — the title earned through resolution of the angelic conflict.

Since believers are in union with Christ, the term hagios applies to them as well — not by their own merit but derivatively, through union with the one who is ho hagios tou theou. This is the meaning of the title 'saint' wherever it appears in the New Testament. It is not a designation earned by religious achievement; it is a declaration of aristocracy by divine patent. The Magna Carta of this aristocracy is the Word of God; the instrument of investiture is the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

C. The Greek Word Group for Sanctification

The root is hagio- (ἁγιο-). From this root come four related forms, each covering a distinct aspect of the believer's aristocracy in Christ.

1. hagios (ἅγιος) — adjective, translated 'holy' or 'saint.' It designates the status of the believer as spiritual aristocracy, one class only, without distinction of race, sex, or social standing (Galatians 3:28). The translation 'saint' in English has been heavily distorted by ecclesiastical tradition; its biblical meaning is simply 'aristocrat by divine appointment.'

2. hagiotēs (ἁγιότης) — noun, translated 'holiness.' It designates the status quo of the royal family of God — the state in which all believers exist by virtue of their union with Christ, describing the principle by which believers are related to the integrity and aristocracy of God.

3. hagiōsynē (ἁγιωσύνη) — noun, translated 'sanctification.' It emphasizes the categorical stages of the believer's aristocracy across all three phases of the plan of God: phase one sanctification (salvation), phase two sanctification (time), phase three sanctification (eternity and resurrection body).

4. hagiasmos (ἁγιασμός) — noun, translated 'holiness,' 'consecration,' or 'sanctification' in various versions. It refers to the investiture of aristocracy — the state of being made an aristocrat permanently. God the Holy Spirit in regeneration and the baptism of the Spirit provides a permanent aristocracy. It also emphasizes the believer's relationship to the integrity of God.

5. hagiazō (ἁγιάζω) — verb, 'to make holy, to consecrate, to sanctify.' It means appointed by the justice of God as aristocracy forever. The appointment carries with it an aristocratic function: maturity adjustment to the justice of God. All historical aristocracies began as working aristocracies; the same is true of the royal family of God. The aristocratic function to which believers are appointed is the consistent intake of Bible doctrine leading to maturity.

D. The Three Phases of Sanctification

Phase one sanctification is positional and instantaneous. At the moment of salvation, the believer is entered into permanent union with Christ through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. This is the foundation of all that follows. The justice of God is permanently satisfied with respect to the penalty of sin; no subsequent failure can remove the believer from this status.

Phase two sanctification is experiential and progressive. The believer in time functions as royal aristocracy — some advancing to maturity through consistent doctrine intake, others falling into reversionism and receiving discipline proportional to their royal status. Throughout life, from the day of salvation, the believer is aristocracy. The objective of phase two is maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Phase three sanctification is ultimate and eternal. In eternity, the believer receives the aristocratic decoration of a resurrection body — minus the old sin nature, minus human good. The Holy Spirit is identified in Romans 8:11 as the agent of resurrection, completing the work begun at regeneration.

II. Orientation to Romans 8

Romans 8 is the great chapter of the new life — the exposition of what it means to function as royal aristocracy in the Protocol Plan of God. The chapter does not stand alone; it is the culmination of the argument that has run from Romans 1:17 through chapters 5, 6, and 7. The justice of God, which condemned sin and judged the old sin nature at the cross, is the same justice that now provides life, freedom, and blessing to the believer who walks according to the Spirit.

The three paragraphs of the chapter address three dimensions of the new life. In verses 1–17, the new life is set in contrast to the old life under the old sin nature and the Mosaic Law: the Spirit sets the believer free from the principle of sin and death. In verses 18–30, the new life is set against the background of suffering: present suffering is not the final measure of anything, for the Spirit intercedes and the purpose of God stands. In verses 31–39, the new life is defended against every conceivable challenge: nothing in all creation can separate the believer from the love of God in Christ Jesus.

The connective tissue across all three paragraphs is sanctification — the three-phase plan of God for royal aristocracy. The chapter cannot be properly understood without the doctrine of sanctification clearly in view. What God declares the believer to be in phase one, He progressively manifests in phase two through the ministry of the Spirit and the intake of doctrine, and He will consummate in phase three at resurrection.

Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Sixty-Five

1. Romans 8 is the chapter of the new life. The title is drawn from Romans 6:4: the believer who has been buried with Christ through the baptism of the Spirit is to walk in newness of life. The plan of God is greater than any sin, failure, adversity, or historical disaster the believer will face.

2. The plan of God for the believer operates in three phases: phase one — salvation adjustment, instantaneous; phase two — experiential life in time, accomplished through the filling of the Spirit and the daily intake of Bible doctrine via the Grace Apparatus for Perception; phase three — eternity, with the Holy Spirit as the agent of resurrection.

3. Sanctification is the technical theological term for the plan of God described in the language of divine objectives across all three phases. It is not reducible to 'set apart unto God' as a static description; it is the dynamic three-phase aristocratic appointment of the believer by the justice of God.

4. Sanctification is a priestly and royal family term. It belongs specifically to the church-age believer, who is royal family of God by virtue of the baptism of the Holy Spirit. No Old Testament believer, Tribulation believer, or Millennial believer shares this precise status.

5. The Greek term hagios (ἅγιος) designates the believer as spiritual aristocracy. It is applied first to the Lord Jesus Christ in John 6:69 — 'the sanctified one from God' — and derivatively to every believer in union with Christ. The translation 'saint' in English has been distorted by ecclesiastical tradition; its biblical meaning is aristocrat by divine patent.

6. The aristocracy of the believer is the most secure aristocracy in history. Every human aristocracy is temporary — contingent on the survival of the patron who granted the title. The believer's aristocracy rests on the eternal person and battlefield royalty of the Lord Jesus Christ. It will never be abrogated.

7. Sanctification carries an aristocratic function. All productive aristocracies begin as working aristocracies. The believer's aristocratic function is maturity adjustment to the justice of God — consistent intake of Bible doctrine leading to the maturity barrier and beyond to supergrace and ultra-supergrace.

8. Divine discipline for reversionism is proportionally greater for the royal family. Because church-age believers hold a uniquely high position before God, departure from that position through sustained carnality or reversionism draws proportionally greater corrective action from the justice of God than was applied to believers of any previous dispensation.

9. Romans 8 divides into three paragraphs: (1) the new life and sanctification, verses 1–17; (2) the new life and suffering, verses 18–30; (3) the new life and its challenges, verses 31–39. The doctrine of sanctification is the prerequisite for understanding all three.

10. The Holy Spirit is the agent of resurrection (Romans 8:11). The same Spirit who indwells the believer in phase two will make alive the mortal body in phase three. The indwelling of the Spirit is thus the earnest of the resurrection — phase two sanctification guarantees phase three sanctification.

Chapter Two Hundred Sixty-Six

Romans 8 Introduction — The Doctrine of Sanctification: Agents, Phases, and the Royal Family of God

Romans 6:4 “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: Therefore we have been buried together with Him through baptism into His death, in order that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so also we might walk in newness of life.

Hebrews 10:10 “And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: By means of which will we have been sanctified in the past, with the result that we remain consecrated to God forever, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

Hebrews 10:14 “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: For by means of one offering He has perfected for all time the ones being sanctified.

Romans 8 divides into three paragraphs: (1) the new life and sanctification, verses 1–17; (2) the new life and suffering, verses 18–30; and (3) the new life and its challenge, verses 31–39. The title of the chapter is drawn from Romans 6:4 — 'so also we might walk in newness of life.' Before engaging verse 1, this chapter continues the doctrinal foundation established in the previous session, working through the full structure of the doctrine of sanctification. That doctrine, properly understood, is the doctrine of the royal family of God, and it provides the framework within which Romans 8 must be read.

I. Point 3 — The Agents of Sanctification

Every imputation has a home — a divinely prepared target. The soul was created by God as the home for human life. The old sin nature, formed genetically through the male line, was the target for the imputation of Adam's original sin, producing spiritual death. The imputation of eternal life finds its home in regeneration, prepared by the Holy Spirit. The imputation of divine righteousness finds its home in the human spirit at salvation. In each case, the agent of imputation determines the character of what is received. Imputations in which God is the agent are a source of blessing; the imputation whose agent is the old sin nature produces only death.

Sanctification likewise has agents. The identity of the agent at each phase is both theologically significant and practically decisive. Understanding the agents is the key to understanding what sanctification requires — and what it does not require — of the believer.

Agent of Phase 1 Sanctification: The Lord Jesus Christ

At salvation, the agent of sanctification is the Lord Jesus Christ. He provided eternal salvation through His impeccable humanity and undiminished deity across the entire thirty-three years of the incarnation, culminating in the cross. What the righteousness of God demands, the justice of God executes: at the cross, every personal sin of every human being was judicially imputed to Christ and judged to exhaustion. The work was complete before His physical death — as our Lord Himself declared, 'It is finished.'

Hebrews 10:9 states that at the moment of His arrival — the incarnation — Christ declared: 'Behold, I have arrived to accomplish Your plan, Your purpose, Your design.' The commentary that follows in the text indicates that He thereby abrogated the Mosaic covenant in order to establish the new. The result, stated in verse 10, is that believers 'have been sanctified' — the Greek perfect tense — hēgiasmenoi (ἡγιασμένοι), a perfect passive participle: sanctified in the past with the result that we remain consecrated to God forever. The agent is Christ; the basis is His one offering on the cross.

Hebrews 10:14 extends this: 'By means of one offering He has perfected for all time the ones being sanctified.' The perfection is the imputation of divine righteousness — the foundational act that opens the grace pipeline. This is phase 1 sanctification, and its agent is Christ alone. No human work, no meritorious act, no addition of any kind is possible or necessary.

Agents of Phase 2 Sanctification: The Holy Spirit and Bible Doctrine

After salvation begins phase 2 — the believer in time. Two agents operate in this phase: God the Holy Spirit and Bible doctrine resident in the soul. These two cannot be separated. The Spirit provides the enabling, and doctrine provides the content. Together they constitute the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), the only means of spiritual advance available to the church age believer.

Romans 15:16 describes Paul's ministry as that of a priest 'ministering the gospel of God, that the offering of the Gentiles might become acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit' — hagiazō (ἁγιάζω), the verb of sanctification, here with the Holy Spirit as agent. Second Thessalonians 2:13 joins the two agents explicitly: God chose believers 'for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and faith in the doctrine.' John 17:17 supplies the doctrinal side: 'Sanctify them by means of the doctrine — Your word is doctrine.' Ephesians 5:26 states that Christ gave Himself for the church 'that He might sanctify her by the washing of the water with the word.' The word for 'sanctify' is again hagiazō. Sanctification in phase 2 is not accomplished by production, service, sacrifice, or works. It is accomplished by the Word of God received into the soul under the filling of the Spirit.

The soul is the battleground of the Christian life. The body is the base of operations for the old sin nature; it is also the dwelling place of the indwelling Holy Spirit and the indwelling Christ. The question is which controls the soul: the Holy Spirit through resident doctrine, or the old sin nature through the vacuum and blackout produced by negative volition. Experiential sanctification therefore combines the filling of the Spirit with the daily function of the GAP to attain maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Agents of Phase 3 Sanctification: The Entire Trinity

Ultimate sanctification — the resurrection body — involves all three members of the Trinity. God the Holy Spirit is the agent of resurrection for the believer's body, as Romans 8 will establish. God the Son presides at the judgment seat of Christ, where all human good accumulated in the believer's life is removed and destroyed. God the Father is the source of eternal blessing dispensed to the believer in eternity. Phase 3 sanctification is thus the cooperative work of the full Trinity, culminating in a resurrection body minus the old sin nature and minus human good — the permanent foundation for all blessing in eternity.

II. Point 4 — Phase 1 Sanctification: The Mechanics

Two Imputations at Salvation

At the moment of faith in Christ, the justice of God executes two imputations — one judicial, one real.

The judicial imputation is the imputation of divine righteousness. We do not earn or deserve this righteousness; it is not antecedently our own. God's righteousness is imputed to us without merit on our part, strictly on the basis of Christ's work on the cross. This act of justification constructs the grace pipeline — a channel running from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. This pipeline is indestructible: nothing can sabotage, interrupt, or compromise it. The integrity of God is its encasing structure.

The real imputation is the imputation of eternal life to its divinely prepared home, regeneration. The Holy Spirit creates the human spirit as the target for this imputation. Eternal life is imputed to regeneration; it cannot be lost. This is the challenge for the future: the blessings of eternity are real and infinite, but they require a foundation laid in time through doctrine.

Thirty-four additional things flow through the grace pipeline at salvation, and then the valve closes. It does not reopen until the believer cracks the maturity barrier. Between salvation and maturity, the believer is sustained by logistical grace: a right pastor, the teaching of Bible doctrine, the filling of the Holy Spirit, provision of physical necessities, adversity designed as tests of existing doctrine, and incremental blessings commensurate with the level of advance. These are genuine provisions, but they are not the same as the supergrace blessings that flow when the maturity barrier is breached.

The logic is a fortiori: if God accomplished the greater at salvation — the judicial imputation of divine righteousness — then it follows a fortiori that He will not withhold the lesser, which is blessing in time. This is the argument of Romans 5 and will recur in Romans 8:32. Justification is not merely a legal declaration; it is the foundation and challenge to advance to maturity, because maturity is the only point at which the grace pipeline reopens and the blessings of supergrace begin to flow.

The Baptism of the Holy Spirit and Positional Truth

Among the thirty-four things that flow through the grace pipeline at salvation, the baptism of the Holy Spirit is of particular importance for understanding phase 1 sanctification. The baptism of the Spirit accomplishes two things simultaneously: retroactive positional truth and current positional truth.

Retroactive positional truth is identification with Christ in His spiritual death, physical death, and burial. At the cross, in His spiritual death, all personal sins were judicially imputed to Christ — but good and evil, the operational system of the old sin nature, were not imputed. Identification with Christ in His spiritual death is therefore tantamount to rejection of good and evil, which is the first stage of divorce from the old sin nature. Identification with Christ in His physical death is separation from the old sin nature — the second stage of divorce. Identification with Christ in His burial is the completion of the divorce: as the Mosaic law established, divorce is death between the two parties — they are dead to each other. Romans 7 uses exactly this language. The old sin nature is the first husband; at physical birth the unbeliever is bound to it; at salvation the believer dies to that first husband through union with Christ and is thus free.

Current positional truth is identification with Christ in His resurrection, ascension, and session at the right hand of God the Father. This constitutes the second marriage: Christ is the new husband, the believer is the wife, and the Holy Spirit is the marriage counselor. This is the basis of the command in Romans 6:4 — 'walk in newness of life.' The believer has a new life because he is in union with the risen, ascended, enthroned Christ.

Because of both retroactive and current positional truth, even the most carnal believers are said to be sanctified at the point of salvation. First Corinthians 1:2 addresses 'those who have been sanctified in Christ Jesus' — a congregation that included every category of carnal failure documented in the epistle. The ground of their sanctification is not their conduct but their union with Christ: 'in Christ Jesus.' Phase 1 sanctification is universal among believers; it is not a second work of grace nor an attainment. It is positional, permanent, and entirely the work of Christ.

III. The Royal Family of God and the Double Portion

The term 'sanctification' — and its cognate 'sanctified' — functions in the church age as a technical title for the royal family of God. It emphasizes the uniqueness of the believer in this dispensation. Throughout all of human history, from the fall of Adam through the end of the Old Testament period, there existed no royal family of God among human beings. Old Testament believers, including the greatest among them, were family of God — but not royal family. Even David and Solomon, who held earthly royal titles, were simply family of God in the plan of God.

The church age began when the Lord Jesus Christ, having completed His earthly ministry, died, rose, ascended, and was seated at the right hand of the Father. At that point He held the title of battlefield royalty — King of kings and Lord of lords — acquired through victory in the angelic conflict. But He was without a royal family to complement His title. Beginning on the Day of Pentecost, AD 30, God began calling out that royal family. Every church age believer is royal family of God, entered into that status at the moment of faith through the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

This royalty carries with it a double portion unlike anything received by any Old Testament believer. Old Testament believers received the imputation of eternal life and the imputation of divine righteousness — both genuine, both permanent. But the church age believer receives these and more. Because the believer is in union with Christ, and because Christ is Himself eternal life (1 John 5:11–12), the believer possesses eternal life both by imputation from the Father and by participation through union with the Son. Similarly, 2 Corinthians 5:21 establishes that the church age believer possesses both the righteousness of the Father, imputed at salvation, and the righteousness of the Son, shared through union with Christ. These double portions — double eternal life, double divine righteousness — define the aristocratic status of the royal family of God.

The practical implication is that the blessings designed under the supergrace paragraphs for the church age believer are of a different magnitude than those designed for even the greatest Old Testament believer. The prosperity of Solomon was the prosperity of family of God; the prosperity designed for the mature church age believer is royal family prosperity — a double portion. God never provides blessing without first providing capacity for it, and He never provides the capacity apart from doctrine. The double portion is not automatic; it requires the advance to maturity through the daily intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Spirit.

IV. The Three Phases Summarized

The three phases of sanctification provide the structural framework for Romans 8 and for the believer's entire existence.

Phase 1 — salvation sanctification: The agent is the Lord Jesus Christ. The basis is the judicial imputation of divine righteousness and the real imputation of eternal life. The mechanism includes the baptism of the Holy Spirit, retroactive positional truth (identification with Christ in spiritual death, physical death, and burial), and current positional truth (identification with Christ in resurrection, ascension, and session). The result is that every believer, regardless of conduct, is sanctified in Christ Jesus. This phase is universal, instantaneous, and permanent.

Phase 2 — experiential sanctification: The agents are the Holy Spirit and Bible doctrine. The mechanism is the daily function of the GAP under the filling of the Spirit. The objective is maturity adjustment to the justice of God — cracking the maturity barrier and entering supergrace. This phase is progressive, volitional, and the subject of the entire first paragraph of Romans 8. Production is not the means; it is a by-product of advance. God provides legitimate production when the believer has the capacity for it.

Phase 3 — ultimate sanctification: The agents are all three members of the Trinity. The mechanism is resurrection — the provision of a resurrection body minus the old sin nature, minus human good. This body is the foundation for all eternal blessing. The blessings built above that foundation in eternity correspond to the doctrine received and the maturity attained in time. There will be no equality in eternity: some believers will have supergrace blessings parlayed into phase 3 blessings of staggering magnitude; others will have the resurrection body alone. What will not exist in eternity is regret, because the resurrection body itself is the permanent removal of all capacity for regret. But the absence of regret in eternity is no argument for neglect of doctrine in time.

V. The Grace Pipeline and the Integrity of God

The grace pipeline runs from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. Justice is the point of contact; righteousness is the home. What the righteousness demands, the justice executes. The integrity of God — the inseparable combination of His perfect righteousness and His perfect justice — is both the source and the encasement of this pipeline. It cannot be destroyed, interrupted, or compromised from outside. The only variable is on the human side: whether the believer advances to the point where the valve reopens at maturity.

At salvation, thirty-four things flow through the pipeline and then the valve closes. During the interim — the entire period between salvation and the cracking of the maturity barrier — the believer is under logistical grace. Logistical grace sustains life; it provides a right pastor, the Word of God, the filling of the Spirit, physical provisions, adversity as doctrine-testing, and incremental blessing above subsistence. These are genuine blessings, but they are not the supergrace blessings for which the double portion was designed. The opening of the valve at maturity depends entirely on Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

This is the theological reason why every distraction from the intake of doctrine is, in the precise sense, an interference with the plan of God. Service organizations, production-oriented Christianity, and any system that substitutes human activity for doctrine intake does not merely fail to advance the believer — it actively retards the advance by substituting a counterfeit objective. God provides production when He provides the capacity for it. Production is the output of maturity, not the path to it.

Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Sixty-Six

1. Sanctification is a technical title for the royal family of God. It does not refer primarily to moral improvement or experiential holiness in the popular sense, but to the unique status of church age believers as royal family of God — distinguished from all believers in all previous dispensations.

2. The agent of phase 1 sanctification is exclusively the Lord Jesus Christ. His judicial imputation of divine righteousness and His real imputation of eternal life through the grace pipeline constitute the entire basis of salvation sanctification. No human work supplements or initiates this.

3. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is the mechanism of phase 1 sanctification. Through retroactive positional truth the believer is identified with Christ in spiritual death, physical death, and burial — a three-stage divorce from the old sin nature. Through current positional truth the believer is entered into union with the risen, ascended, and enthroned Christ — the second marriage.

4. The church age believer holds a double portion of both eternal life and divine righteousness. Eternal life by imputation from the Father plus eternal life by union with the Son. Righteousness of the Father imputed at justification plus righteousness of the Son shared through union with Christ. No Old Testament believer possessed this double portion.

5. Phase 2 sanctification has two agents: the Holy Spirit and Bible doctrine. These two are inseparable. The Spirit provides enabling; doctrine provides content. Together they constitute the GAP. Production, works, service, and sacrifice are excluded as agents. They are at most by-products of mature advance, never the cause of it.

6. The objective of phase 2 sanctification is maturity adjustment to the justice of God. This is the point at which the grace pipeline reopens, supergrace begins, and the blessings designed for the royal family of God begin to flow. The maturity barrier is cracked through sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine, not through any amount of Christian service or emotional experience.

7. The grace pipeline is constructed of divine integrity and is indestructible. It runs from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. Nothing external can sabotage it. The only variable is whether the believer advances sufficiently to reopen the valve at maturity.

8. Phase 3 sanctification — ultimate sanctification — provides the resurrection body as foundation. This foundation is the platform for all eternal blessing. Blessings above the foundation in eternity correspond directly to the doctrine accumulated and the maturity attained in time. There will be no equality in eternity: differentiation of reward is permanent. The absence of regret in eternity does not nullify the urgency of doctrine intake in time.

9. Even the most carnal believers are phase 1 sanctified. First Corinthians 1:2 addresses the most carnal congregation on record as 'those who have been sanctified in Christ Jesus.' The ground is their union with Christ, not their conduct. Phase 1 sanctification is universal among believers, positional, and permanent.

10. The a fortiori argument governs all blessing from God. If at salvation the justice of God provided the greater — the judicial imputation of divine righteousness — then it follows a fortiori that He will not withhold the lesser, which is blessing in time at maturity. This argument will recur at Romans 8:32 and is the logical backbone of the entire chapter.

sanctification ἁγιασμός hagiasmos — sanctification, consecration From hagiazō (to set apart, to consecrate). In Romans and the Pauline corpus, a technical title for the royal family of God in the church age. The perfect passive participle hēgiasmenoi in Hebrews 10:10 indicates a completed past action with permanent present result: sanctified in the past, remaining consecrated forever.
hēgiasmenoi ἡγιασμένοι hēgiasmenoi — having been sanctified (perfect passive participle) Perfect passive participle of hagiazō. Hebrews 10:10: 'we have been sanctified in the past with the result that we remain consecrated to God forever.' The perfect tense in Greek emphasizes a completed action whose results are permanent. Used to establish the eternal finality of phase 1 sanctification.
baptism of the Holy Spirit βάπτισμα πνεύματος baptisma pneumatos — baptism of the Spirit The ministry of the Holy Spirit at salvation by which the believer is entered into union with Christ. Accomplishes both retroactive positional truth (identification with Christ in spiritual death, physical death, and burial, resulting in divorce from the old sin nature) and current positional truth (identification with Christ in resurrection, ascension, and session). Unique to the church age; not experienced by Old Testament believers.
retroactive positional truth The aspect of the baptism of the Holy Spirit that identifies the believer with Christ's spiritual death, physical death, and burial. Constitutes a three-stage divorce from the old sin nature: (1) identification with spiritual death = rejection of good and evil; (2) identification with physical death = separation from the old sin nature; (3) identification with burial = actual divorce. The positional power of the old sin nature is broken.
current positional truth The aspect of the baptism of the Holy Spirit that identifies the believer with Christ's resurrection, ascension, and session at the right hand of the Father. Constitutes the second marriage: Christ is the husband, the believer is the wife, the Holy Spirit is the marriage counselor. The basis of the command to 'walk in newness of life' in Romans 6:4.
double portion The unique endowment of the church age believer in contrast to Old Testament believers. At salvation the church age believer receives (1) eternal life by imputation from the Father and eternal life by union with the Son (1 John 5:11–12), and (2) the righteousness of the Father by imputation and the righteousness of the Son by union (2 Corinthians 5:21). This double portion constitutes the basis for supergrace blessings that exceed those designed for any Old Testament believer.
grace pipeline The channel of divine blessing that runs from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. Opened at salvation when thirty-four blessings flow through it; closed until the believer cracks the maturity barrier, at which point it reopens for supergrace blessing. The pipeline is encased in the integrity of God and cannot be destroyed or compromised.
logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and spiritual sustenance during the period between salvation and the cracking of the maturity barrier. Includes a right pastor, Bible doctrine, the filling of the Holy Spirit, food, shelter, transportation, adversity designed as doctrine-testing, and incremental blessings above subsistence. Genuine provisions, but not the same as supergrace blessings.
maturity adjustment to the justice of God δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The objective of phase 2 sanctification. The point at which sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit results in the cracking of the maturity barrier. At this point the grace pipeline reopens, supergrace A begins, and the blessings designed for the royal family of God begin to flow. Distinguished from salvation adjustment (phase 1) and ultimate sanctification (phase 3).
a fortiori a fortiori — from the stronger (Latin logical term) The logical argument that if the greater has been accomplished, the lesser will not be withheld. Applied throughout Romans to the justice of God: if God provided the greater (judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation), it follows a fortiori that He will provide the lesser (blessing in time at maturity). The argument appears in Romans 5 and recurs in Romans 8:32.
royal family of God The category of church age believers as distinct from Old Testament and future dispensational believers. Church age believers are entered into this status at salvation through the baptism of the Holy Spirit and union with Christ, who holds the title of battlefield royalty. The royal family is being called out from Pentecost AD 30 to the Rapture. 'Sanctification' is the technical title for this royal family.

Chapter Two Hundred Sixty-Seven

Romans 8:1–17 — Sanctification: Definition, Phases, and the Angelic Conflict

Romans 8:1 “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: There is therefore now no judgment to those who are in Christ Jesus.

Romans 8:2 “For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: For the principle of the Spirit — that is, the ministry of the Spirit of salvation, who is the source of eternal life — has set you free in Christ Jesus from the principle of the sin nature and its result in spiritual death.

Romans 8:4 “in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: In order that the legal requirement of the law might be filled up in us who keep not walking according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.

Romans 8 opens the third major division of the epistle, beginning the extended treatment of Phase 2 of the divine plan — the believer in time. This chapter is organized around three paragraphs: verses 1–17 on the new life and sanctification, verses 18–30 on the new life and suffering, and verses 31–39 on the new life and its challenges. The present chapter provides necessary introductory material on the doctrine of sanctification before the verse-by-verse exposition of Romans 8:1 begins. The command to 'walk in newness of life' in Romans 6:4 supplies the title and controlling principle for all that follows.

I. The Doctrine of Sanctification — Review and Continuation

The doctrine of sanctification has been under study across several sessions. The first four points — definition and description, etymology, agents of sanctification, and Phase 1 (salvation) sanctification — have been covered previously. The present chapter resumes at Point 5.

Point 5 — Phase 2 Sanctification: Experiential Sanctification

The purpose of Phase 2 sanctification is the maximum flow of divine blessings through the grace pipeline. The grace pipeline is established at the moment of salvation through a judicial imputation: the justice of God imputes divine righteousness to the believer. Because this righteousness is not inherently the believer's own, the imputation is judicial in character. Simultaneously, eternal life is imputed as a real imputation to regeneration — the regenerate human spirit provided by God the Holy Spirit serves as the target or home for eternal life.

At the moment of salvation, thirty-four distinct things flow through this grace pipeline from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is one of these thirty-four. Once they have flowed through, the pipeline valve closes. No further flow of special blessing occurs until the believer cracks the maturity barrier, at which point the valve opens again and the justice of God begins to provide blessings for Supergrace A, Supergrace B, and ultimately ultra-supergrace status. These blessings fall into five categories, designated the SG2 paragraph.

The objective of Phase 2 is therefore this: that the justice of God, operating through the grace pipeline, imputes to the righteousness of God resident in the believer those blessings which balance the believer's portfolio in time and provide a new portfolio for eternity. These blessings glorify the Lord Jesus Christ and resolve the angelic conflict.

The believer is kept alive in Phase 2 so that the justice of God can complete what was begun at salvation. The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation was judicial — it did not establish a balanced state. What is missing between that initial imputation and the blessings of maturity is capacity, and capacity is maximum doctrine resident in the soul. The justice of God cannot act unfairly: it would be unjust to provide blessings for which the believer has no capacity, since without capacity, what would be a blessing becomes a curse. Prosperity, success, promotion, and every other category of divine benefit becomes destructive apart from the capacity that comes only from doctrine resident in the soul. Capacity must precede blessing, not follow it.

Phase 2 sanctification may therefore be defined as maturity adjustment to the justice of God through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. The conversion of gnosis (γνῶσις) in the left lobe into epignosis (ἐπίγνωσις) — full, exact perception — in the right lobe is the mechanism by which capacity is built. The formula: primary potential plus capacity equals the reality of blessing in time. Primary potential is the imputation of divine righteousness; capacity is maximum doctrine resident in the soul; and the reality of blessing in time is the SG2 paragraph in its five categories.

A secondary potential is also in view: the baptism of the Spirit plus the same capacity equals the reality of an encapsulated environment for those blessings — an encapsulation far greater than the environment Adam and Eve possessed in the Garden. What the mature believer possesses in experiential sanctification cannot be lost, whereas the original parents lost their blessings under perfect environment. This encapsulated environment of blessing is permanent.

The tactical objective of the royal family of God — described in the King James idiom as 'godliness' — is identical to Phase 2 sanctification. These terms will be fully clarified in the course of Romans 8. Experiential sanctification is the subject of this entire chapter.

Point 6 — Phase 3 Sanctification: Ultimate Sanctification

Phase 3 sanctification is designated ultimate sanctification because it refers to the eternal state. It is the eternal status of all Church Age believers as members of the royal family of God.

In Phase 2, the foundation for blessing from the justice of God is the imputed divine righteousness possessed by every believer at the moment of salvation. In Phase 3, the foundation for eternal blessing is the resurrection body — minus the old sin nature. Every believer already possesses the Phase 2 foundation. The Phase 3 foundation will be received at the rapture of the Church.

It is what is built or constructed on each foundation that determines the extent of blessing. The blessings of time are constructed on the foundation of imputed righteousness. The blessings and rewards of eternity are constructed on the resurrection body. No believer ever loses the imputed righteousness in time; no believer in eternity ever loses the resurrection body. The question in both phases is what has been built upon that foundation.

Phase 3 sanctification occurs at the termination of the Church Age — specifically at the rapture of the Church, the moment at which the resurrection body is received. Ultimate sanctification therefore consists of two elements: possession of the resurrection body at the rapture, and the burning of all human good at the judgment seat of Christ. There is no human good in heaven. Human good is, in fact, one of the principal distractions from the divine objectives for the Christian way of life in Phase 2.

The basic concept of ultimate sanctification is possession of the resurrection body minus human good and minus the lake of fire. Romans 8:1 introduces this chapter with the declaration that there is no judgment — no condemnation, no lake of fire — for those who are in Christ Jesus. Once a person has believed in Christ, the lake of fire is a matter of doctrine but never a future reality. Whether the believer receives rewards and blessings above and beyond the resurrection body depends entirely on his or her attitude toward Bible doctrine in Phase 2.

Ultimate sanctification converts the body of Christ into the bride of Christ. The Church, as resurrected aristocracy, is distinguished from all other resurrection categories by its rank and by the priority of its resurrection.

Excursus: The Echelons of the First Resurrection

The first resurrection is structured in 1 Corinthians 15 according to a military analogy — a battalion review. Four companies pass in review before God in distinct sequence:

Alpha Company: the Lord Jesus Christ, already resurrected and seated at the right hand of the Father. This company has already passed the reviewing stand.

Bravo Company: Church Age believers exclusively. The technical expression 'the dead in Christ' (1 Thessalonians 4:16) is a precise term referring to those who died within the Church Age dispensation. This company receives resurrection bodies at the rapture — at minimum seven years before the next company. The Church Age is a dispensation of intercalation: the royal family is resurrected first because rank has its privileges.

Charlie Company: Old Testament believers. These are not resurrected at the rapture but at the second advent of Christ. They are not needed during the Tribulation period and they do not receive resurrection bodies until Christ returns.

Delta Company: Tribulational martyrs and millennial believers, who receive resurrection bodies at the end of the Millennium.

The priority of the Church in the resurrection sequence is not incidental. It reflects the unique status of Church Age believers as royalty — members of the royal family of God, in union with the King of kings. The bride must be prepared and present for the coronation. To whom much is given, much is expected: the elevated status of the Church Age believer is itself the strongest motivation for cracking the maturity barrier.

Points 7–9 — Further Features of Ultimate Sanctification

All of Phase 3 sanctification is described as being 'conformed to the image of His Son' — a concept that will receive full treatment when the commentary reaches Romans 8:29.

In Phase 3, the believer is described as blameless — ἄμεμπτος (amemptos) — as stated in 1 Corinthians 1:8: "who shall also confirm you to the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." In the present life, no believer can be classified as blameless. But at the rapture, the entirety of the royal family is made permanently blameless through reception of the resurrection body and the removal of the old sin nature. There will be no future fall, no new corruption, no possibility of regression. Blamelessness is permanent and complete.

Philippians 3:21 describes this transformation: 'who shall change the form of the body of our humiliation to conform to the body of His glory.' The body of humiliation is the present body — not necessarily humble by human standards, but classified as such by the divine standard because it is the vehicle of the old sin nature and its attendant lusts. The body of glory is the perfect resurrection body of the Lord Jesus Christ.

1 Thessalonians 5:23 provides a summary benediction for all phases of sanctification: 'Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely, and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.' Similarly, 1 John 3:2 states: 'Beloved, right now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when He shall appear, we shall be exactly like Him, because we shall see Him just as He is.'

II. Sanctification and the Angelic Conflict

Each phase of sanctification is directly related to the angelic conflict.

Phase 1 sanctification — union with Christ through the baptism of the Holy Spirit — places the believer positionally higher than all angelic creatures. Hebrews 1 establishes that the risen, seated Christ is higher than all angels. In union with Christ, the believer shares that positional superiority. Salvation sanctification is therefore immediately a factor in the angelic conflict.

Phase 2 sanctification — the mature believer having cracked the maturity barrier and made the maturity adjustment to the justice of God with maximum doctrine resident in the soul — constitutes a tactical victory in the angelic conflict. When the grace pipeline is opened for direct blessing from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God in the mature believer, a tactical victory has been scored. The mature believer, occupied with Christ, sharing the happiness of God, and receiving maximum blessings from the justice of God, glorifies the Lord Jesus Christ in time. This demonstrates that the grace of God is greater and can provide something better than what Adam and Eve possessed in the Garden of Eden — under perfect environment they lost everything, whereas what the mature believer possesses in experiential sanctification cannot be lost either as a blessing in time or as a basis for reward and blessing in eternity.

What Satan took from our first parents has been reproduced in the devil's own world as something immeasurably greater. The status of Supergrace or ultra-supergrace provides something far superior to what mankind possessed in the Garden under perfect environment.

Phase 3 sanctification — the resurrection body — renders the royal family of God physically superior to all angelic creatures. Power, authority, blessing, and prosperity corrupt creatures who retain an old sin nature, but in the resurrection body these are permanently incorruptible. No corruption will ever attach to the resurrection body. Through the three phases of sanctification, the justice of God wins a decisive and permanent victory over Satan, demonstrating the principle of 1 John 4:4: 'Greater is He that is in us than he that is in the world.'

III. Sanctification and the Purpose of Life After Salvation

Between salvation and eternity, the believer spends a designated amount of time on earth — time allotted by the plan of God specifically to each individual. This time is dispensed one day at a time. In any given day, two things are required for advance in the plan of God: first, rebound when necessary (naming known sins to God per 1 John 1:9, restoring the filling of the Spirit); second, a portion of that day devoted to the perception of Bible doctrine through the function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). Beyond these two requirements, the day belongs to the believer for whatever legitimate activities are necessary — work, recreation, personal responsibilities.

The objective for time spent on earth after salvation is the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ. Glorification of the Lord is not an abstract concept but a precisely defined one: it is the use of one day at a time, fulfilling the purpose of that day through rebound and the function of GAP, and assembling those days cumulatively into maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Romans 8 will define and develop this concept in detail.

The attainment of spiritual maturity is the tactical victory of the angelic conflict. This is the concept described in 1 Timothy 6:3–6 and 2 Peter 1:3 by the term 'godliness' — an older English word that functions as a synonym for experiential sanctification.

The means of attainment is the filling of the Holy Spirit plus the daily function of GAP. The capital available for the spiritual life is not monetary but temporal: God assigns time, and the believer invests that time. The investment consists of rebound for the recovery of the filling of the Spirit and a portion of time set aside for the intake of Bible doctrine. Failure to reach maturity constitutes maladjustment to the justice of God, which brings maximum saturation of divine discipline and can eventuate in the sin unto death.

Either the believer adjusts to the justice of God, or the justice of God will adjust to the believer. Adjustment in time is experiential sanctification. Maladjustment is reversionism and the influence of evil.

Production in the Christian life is the result of spiritual advance, never the means. Experiential sanctification has nothing directly to do with working for God in the external sense. Witnessing, sacrifice, and visible Christian service are not the means of attaining maturity. Production is incidental to experiential sanctification — it follows from it but is not the mechanism of it. The means of attainment is grace. The hindrances to attainment occupy two poles: legalism on one side and antinomianism on the other. Both are distractions from the grace objective.

Experiential sanctification — the subject of Romans 8 — keeps priorities aligned and maintains constant focus on the objective: the divine plan for the believer in Phase 2. With this doctrinal framework established, the verse-by-verse exposition of Romans 8:1 begins in the following chapter.

Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Sixty-Seven

1. Romans 8 addresses Phase 2 of the divine plan — the believer in time. Its three paragraphs cover sanctification (vv. 1–17), suffering (vv. 18–30), and the challenges of the new life (vv. 31–39). The title 'new life' derives from the command to 'walk in newness of life' in Romans 6:4.

2. Phase 2 sanctification is maturity adjustment to the justice of God through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Its purpose is the maximum flow of divine blessings through the grace pipeline — from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God possessed by the mature believer.

3. The grace pipeline is established at salvation by two imputations: the judicial imputation of divine righteousness, and the real imputation of eternal life to regeneration. Thirty-four salvation blessings flow through the pipeline at the moment of faith. The pipeline closes until the maturity barrier is cracked.

4. Capacity must precede blessing. God's justice cannot impute blessings for which the believer has no capacity. Without capacity, what would be blessing becomes cursing. Capacity is maximum doctrine resident in the soul — the product of the daily function of GAP under the filling of the Holy Spirit.

5. Phase 3 (ultimate) sanctification is the possession of the resurrection body minus the old sin nature and minus human good. It occurs at the rapture of the Church. It renders every member of the royal family permanently blameless and physically superior to all angelic creatures.

6. The Church Age believer is resurrected before all other categories of believers because the royal family holds the highest rank in the first resurrection. The technical expression 'the dead in Christ' (1 Thess. 4:16) refers exclusively to Church Age believers, not to Old Testament saints.

7. All three phases of sanctification are directly related to the angelic conflict. Phase 1 places the believer positionally higher than angels. Phase 2 constitutes a tactical victory over Satan by reproducing in the devil's world something greater than was possessed in the Garden of Eden. Phase 3 renders the royal family permanently incorruptible and physically superior to all angelic creatures.

8. The purpose of Phase 2 is glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ, accomplished by using one day at a time for rebound and the intake of Bible doctrine, cumulatively advancing to maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

9. Production is incidental to experiential sanctification — it is the result, not the means. Neither legalism nor antinomianism produces maturity. The means of attainment is grace, operating through the filling of the Holy Spirit and the daily function of GAP.

10. Either the believer adjusts to the justice of God or the justice of God adjusts to the believer. Maladjustment to the justice of God is reversionism. Maximum maladjustment eventuates in the sin unto death — physical death as the terminal expression of divine discipline for sustained reversionism.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
sanctification ἁγιασμός hagiasmos — sanctification, holiness The process and state of being set apart to God. In systematic theology, three phases are distinguished: Phase 1 (positional/salvation sanctification — union with Christ at the moment of faith); Phase 2 (experiential sanctification — maturity adjustment to the justice of God through doctrine resident in the soul); Phase 3 (ultimate sanctification — the resurrection body received at the rapture, permanent and blameless).
epignosis ἐπίγνωσις epignosis — full, exact knowledge The category of knowledge required for spiritual growth. Distinguished from gnosis (academic or surface knowledge in the left lobe) by its residence in the right lobe as metabolized, applied doctrine. The function of GAP converts gnosis into epignosis under the enabling ministry of the Holy Spirit.
gnosis γνῶσις gnosis — knowledge Academic or surface knowledge residing in the left lobe. Gnosis becomes epignosis when the Holy Spirit metabolizes it into the right lobe through the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Gnosis alone produces no spiritual capacity.
amemptos ἄμεμπτος amemptos — blameless, without blame Used in 1 Corinthians 1:8 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23 of the ultimate sanctification of the royal family at the rapture.
