neged נגד neged — in the sight of, over against, in the presence of Hebrew preposition indicating spatial opposition or direct visibility. In Psalm 23:5 it emphasizes that the enemies are not distant — they are arrayed in full view, surrounding the psalmist — while the table is still fully prepared.
tzar צר tzar — enemy, adversary, one who confines Hebrew noun from a root meaning to bind or confine. Used in the plural with the first-person singular suffix in Psalm 23:5 (tzoreray — my enemies) to denote those who surround and press in upon the psalmist from all sides.
Judicial imputation An imputation having only one factor — the thing being imputed — which is always imputed to something not antecedently its own. Two judicial imputations govern the plan of God: (1) the imputation of all personal sins to Christ at the cross; (2) the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation. Both are non-meritorious and non-antecedent.
Real imputation An imputation having two factors — the thing imputed (factor one) and its divinely prepared residence (factor two) — between which there is affinity, antecedence, or divinely prepared suitability. Examples: human life imputed to the human soul; Adam's sin to the old sin nature; divine blessing to the righteousness of God resident in the mature believer; eternal life to regeneration.
SG2 — Paragraph Supergrace Blessings The six-category structure of divine blessing imputed to the mature believer through the justice of God. Category 1: spiritual blessings and occupation with Christ. Category 2: material, social, and temporal prosperity. Category 3: blessing by association. Category 4: historical impact through the pivot. Category 5: dying blessing. Category 6: historical adversity and personal catastrophe producing phenomenal blessing.
Maturity adjustment The third and progressive category of adjustment to the justice of God. Achieved through consistent daily intake of Bible doctrine via the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), culminating in the cracking of the maturity barrier. At that threshold, the righteousness of God demands that the justice of God execute the real imputation of divine blessing in time.
GAP — Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which the believer receives, metabolizes, and internalizes Bible doctrine. Doctrine received through GAP moves from gnosis (academic knowledge) to epignosis (full, exact perception resident in the soul), which constitutes the capacity basis for divine blessing.
Old sin nature (OSN) The sin capacity inherited at birth through the male genetic line, antecedently prepared to receive the real imputation of Adam's original sin. The OSN is the source of the sin trend, the lust pattern, and the area of weakness and strength that characterize each individual's fallen humanity.

Chapter Two Hundred Ninety-One

Psalm 23:5b–6 — The Overflowing Cup, the Pursuit of Grace, and the A Fortiori of Eternal Blessing

Psalm 23:5b–6 “You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: You have anointed with oil my head; my cup is overflowing. Only prosperity and grace shall pursue me all the days of my life, and I will dwell prosperously in the house of the LORD forever.

This chapter concludes the exegesis of Psalm 23:5–6, which was introduced as a sustained illustration of the phrase 'capacity for life and prosperity' at the end of Romans 8:6. The psalm, written by David during the Absalom revolution while he was fleeing through the Judean wilderness, provides three analogies in verse 5 — the soldier's table, the king's anointing, and the guest's overflowing cup — and then resolves in verse 6 with the a fortiori logic that governs both temporal and eternal blessing. The whole passage develops the theological content that underlies the adjustment to the justice of God at maturity.

I. Review of the Three Imputations Underlying Prosperity

Before the three analogies of verse 5 can be understood, the imputation structure that makes prosperity possible must be in view. Three imputations are involved: one non-imputation and two judicial imputations.

The non-imputation is the Christmas event itself. When the eternal Son of God entered human history, human life was imputed to his divinely prepared soul — a real imputation with genuine affinity between the two factors. But Adam's original sin was not imputed to an old sin nature, because Christ had no old sin nature. He was born as Adam was created: perfect. Living thirty-three years in that perfection, he was qualified to go to the cross.

The first judicial imputation occurred at the cross. Every personal sin of every human being was imputed to Christ and judged. This imputation is judicial — there is only one factor, the sins being imputed; they were not inherently his own. He was impeccable. The judicial character of the transaction is the basis of its sufficiency.

The second judicial imputation occurs at the moment of salvation. God's perfect righteousness — one half of divine integrity — is imputed to the believer. This righteousness is also not inherently the believer's own; there is no natural affinity between fallen humanity and divine righteousness. The imputation is entirely judicial. But the moment that righteousness is possessed, the believer has the divinely prepared home — the target — for the real imputation of blessing in time.

The logical structure is: judicial imputation one (sins imputed to Christ at the cross) + judicial imputation two (divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation) = the basis for real imputation of blessing in time at maturity. This is the controlling logic of Romans 8:28–30 and is the same a fortiori framework Paul employs throughout Romans 8. The psalm uses the Hebrew term kal wa-ḥomer (the argument from greater to lesser) where Paul uses the Greek a fortiori: if justice accomplished the greater (imputing divine righteousness at salvation), it will certainly accomplish the less (imputing blessing in time at maturity).

II. The Three Analogies of Psalm 23:5

A. The Soldier's Table — Real Imputation of Blessing at Maturity

The first analogy is military. David is in the Judean wilderness, having fled Jerusalem ahead of the Absalom revolution. He has abandoned his castles, his crown, and most of his possessions. Yet he writes: 'You have prepared before me a table in the presence of my enemies.' The table is not a wish or an anticipation — it is a completed reality. The pre-battle tension that builds in any soldier is met by complete relaxation in the face of the prepared table.

The table represents David's material and spiritual prosperity as a mature believer — all of it received as real imputation from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. He was the greatest general of his age, the wealthiest king in the world, and a man of extraordinary social and relational blessing. None of it was earned. All of it was imputed. Factor one is the blessing itself; factor two is the divinely prepared home of God's righteousness resident in David. The affinity between the blessing and that righteousness is what makes the real imputation possible.

Because these blessings are a real imputation, they cannot be taken away by any historical reversal. David temporarily lacks the visible expression of his blessings — the throne, the palace, the army, the wealth — but the imputation itself is secure. The table is still prepared, even in the wilderness.

B. The King's Anointing — Security of Blessing in Catastrophe

The second analogy concerns the anointing of the king. The Hebrew reads: 'You have anointed with oil my head.' The verbal form is the Piel perfect of the root

The verbal form is the Piel perfect of the root dāšen (דשן), which in the Qal stem means 'to become fat' or 'to become prosperous, to provide abundance.' In the Piel stem it means 'to be made rich, to be appointed to high office' — and therefore 'to anoint' in the sense not of hairdressing but of royal appointment. The preposition bĕ plus the noun šemen (שמן) designates the special oil used in royal consecration. The first-person suffix on the noun rōš (ראש) specifies that this anointing belongs to David alone.

The reference is first historical: the Prophet Samuel anointed David king over Israel in 1 Samuel 16:1–13. It then refers to the spiritual reality: David cracked the maturity barrier, developed the capacity through doctrine to hold the highest office, and was confirmed as ruler of all Israel. Psalm 78:70 states: 'He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfold to make him king over all Israel.'

Absalom's revolution was a challenge to legitimate authority confirmed by God. David would lose Absalom in the ensuing battle — his most beloved son — yet even this undeserved suffering could not remove David from his kingship. The anointing represents the security of all maturity blessings. No revolution, no failure, no conspiracy, no historical catastrophe can destroy a real imputation. The blessing imputed to divine righteousness is as secure as the righteousness itself, and divine righteousness is eternal and immutable.

Just as the table is the content of maturity blessing, the anointing is the security of that blessing. These are two distinct theological points communicated through two distinct images within the same verse.

C. The Guest's Overflowing Cup — Capacity for Blessing Through Doctrine

The third analogy is that of the banquet guest. The Hebrew word translated 'cup' is

The Hebrew word translated 'cup' is kôs (כוס), which designates not an ordinary drinking vessel but a banquet cup — a golden or silver goblet used for the finest wines. The cup represents capacity. At the moment of salvation, the cup is empty. It holds divine righteousness, but the capacity for blessing has not yet been developed. As doctrine accumulates in the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), the cup fills. At maturity, it overflows.

There is no verb in the Hebrew at this point; the construction is elliptical. This ellipsis conveys David's intensity — the sentence breaks off because the reality exceeds what syntax can contain. What follows is a predicate nominative:

What follows is a predicate nominative: rĕwāyāh (רויה), meaning 'overflowing.' My cup — overflowing. The first-person suffix sets David apart not as king but as a mature believer who has filled his soul with maximum doctrine.

The justice of God is incorruptible and entirely fair. It will never impute to the righteousness of God those blessings — wealth, promotion, social prosperity, or any other category — for which the believer has no capacity. Capacity must precede the imputation. Without capacity, the same blessings that would constitute prosperity for the mature believer would constitute misery for the immature one. Great wealth given to a believer without the doctrinal capacity to handle it becomes a source of arrogance, instability, and unhappiness. This is not divine injustice — it is divine integrity operating in the believer's true interest.

Capacity comes from maximum doctrine resident in the soul. With that capacity, the believer has all four factors simultaneously: the justice of God as the source; the divine righteousness as the divinely prepared target; the security of those blessings through the immutability of that righteousness; and the capacity to receive, hold, and enjoy them. The overflowing cup depicts all four factors in their proper relationship.

III. Psalm 23:6 — The A Fortiori of Temporal and Eternal Blessing

A. The Conjunction of Affirmation

Verse 6 opens with the Hebrew particle ʾak (אך), a strong adverb of affirmation and restriction. It is best translated not as 'surely' but as 'only.' This single word expresses the confidence of the mature believer who has understood the meaning of the table, the anointing, and the cup. He narrows his entire perspective to one reality: only this matters, only this is certain, only this is the proper object of his attention.

B. Prosperity and Grace — The Two Pursuers

David says that ṭôb (טוב) and ḥesed (חסד) shall pursue him. Both words are standardly mistranslated in this verse. Ṭôb is an adjective also used as a substantive equivalent to the Greek agathos (αγαθός), meaning intrinsic good, divine good, or here: prosperity — the real imputation of divine blessing from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. Ḥesed does not mean 'mercy' in this context. It means grace — the policy of the justice of God in blessing the mature believer. Together, 'only prosperity and grace' encapsulates the entire grace pipeline: justice of God on one end, righteousness of God on the other, with all human ability, merit, and production screened out.

The verb translated 'follow' is the Qal perfect of rādap (רדף), which means 'to pursue' — active, relentless, intentional pursuit. David does not see grace and prosperity walking behind him at a distance; he sees them in active pursuit. This is the theological reality of the mature believer's life: the justice of God is not passive but actively seeks the target of divine righteousness in the mature believer's soul for the purpose of imputing blessing.

At this moment, David is surrounded. Three armies are closing in from multiple directions. He has his sword, his fatigues, a mule, and the doctrine resident in his soul. He looks not outward at the armies of Absalom but upward at the pursuing grace of God. The direction of attention is itself a theological decision — and it is the only decision that produces stability in disaster.

'Only prosperity and grace shall pursue me all the days of my life.' David makes no exceptions. He does not say 'all the days of my life except this present catastrophe.' The present catastrophe is included. The overflowing cup overflows in the wilderness just as much as it overflows in the palace. The real imputation is not contingent on external circumstances, because it is imputed to divine righteousness, which does not change with external circumstances.

C. Dwelling Prosperously — The Second A Fortiori

The final clause uses the Qal perfect of yāšab (ישב), which does not simply mean 'to dwell' but often carries the extended meaning 'to dwell in prosperity, to live prosperously.' The corrected translation is: 'I will dwell prosperously in the house of the LORD forever.' This introduces the second a fortiori argument in the verse.

If the justice of God at maturity accomplishes the greater — the real imputation of divine blessing in time to divine righteousness — it follows a fortiori that the justice of God will accomplish the less: the real imputation of divine blessing in eternity, imputed to the divinely prepared home of the resurrection body, which carries no old sin nature and no human good. Blessing in time is imputed to the righteousness received at salvation. Blessing in eternity is imputed to the resurrection body. Both are real imputations with genuine affinity between the blessing and its prepared home.

David therefore sees not only the security of his present blessings and the reality of their continuation through the present disaster, but also the parlaying of those temporal blessings into greater reward in eternity. The suffering he is enduring — undeserved suffering, the sixth category within the framework of paragraph SG2 — does not diminish what he has; it amplifies what he will receive. The undeserved suffering of the mature believer is God's instrument for producing greater blessing, not a sign of divine abandonment.

IV. The Host and the Guest — The Hospitality Principle

The fourth element in this verse is implicit in the banquet imagery: where there is a cup, there is a host. The host in the analogy is the Lord Jesus Christ — the Good Shepherd of verse 1 who provides the pasture of doctrine; the Great Shepherd who accomplishes the real imputation of divine blessing in time; and the Chief Shepherd who dispenses blessing and reward in eternity.

Under the ancient laws of hospitality, what mattered was never the identity of the guest but the character of the host. Genuine hospitality does not depend on whether the guest is admirable, well-known, or socially desirable. It depends entirely on the nature of the host and the host's commitment to excellence in provision. The host is God the Father. The guest is the believer. The imputation of blessing does not depend on the merit, production, sacrifice, or devotion of the guest. It depends exclusively on the integrity of the host.

This is why believers are left on earth after salvation. They are the guests of the Lord Jesus Christ — here temporarily, functioning as ambassadors while the Host is in heaven. Nothing about the ambassador's personal qualities qualifies the blessing. The blessing qualifies itself through the integrity of the One who provides it, flowing from divine justice through the grace pipeline to divine righteousness.

V. Psalm 23 and Romans 8:6 — The Governing Connection

The entire excursus through Psalm 23 has been in service of the last two words of Romans 8:6: capacity for life and prosperity. The psalm demonstrates through three analogies — table, anointing, cup — and through the a fortiori argument of verse 6 exactly what that capacity consists of and how it is produced. Capacity is not emotional intensity, not moral performance, not religious devotion. It is the accumulation of Bible doctrine in the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception over time.

When doctrine fills the cup, the justice of God imputes the corresponding blessings to the target of divine righteousness. The believer in the midst of undeserved suffering, like David in the wilderness, does not lose the table, the anointing, or the cup. He is still the king. The real imputation stands. The grace pipeline continues to deliver. And the direction of attention — upward rather than outward — is the practical expression of that theological reality in daily experience.

Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Ninety-One

1. Three imputations underlie all prosperity. One non-imputation (Adam's original sin not imputed to Christ at the virgin birth) and two judicial imputations (sins imputed to Christ at the cross; divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation) together establish the basis for the real imputation of divine blessing at maturity.

2. The table of Psalm 23:5a depicts the content of maturity blessing. All categories of prosperity — spiritual, material, relational, vocational — are received as real imputations from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. They are not earned, deserved, or produced by the believer.

3. The anointing of Psalm 23:5b depicts the security of maturity blessing. No historical reversal, catastrophe, or undeserved suffering can remove a real imputation. The blessing is as secure as the divine righteousness to which it is imputed, which is eternal and immutable.

4. The overflowing cup of Psalm 23:5c depicts capacity for blessing. The justice of God never imputes blessing for which the believer lacks capacity. Capacity is produced by maximum doctrine resident in the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Without capacity, the same blessings that constitute prosperity for the mature believer would produce misery for the immature one.

5. Ṭôb and ḥesed in Psalm 23:6 are correctly rendered 'prosperity and grace,' not 'goodness and mercy.' Ṭôb as a substantive is equivalent to the Greek agathos — divine good, intrinsic good, prosperity. Ḥesed in this context means grace — the policy of divine justice in blessing the mature believer — not mercy in the sense of compassion toward the undeserving.

6. Rādap means 'to pursue,' not merely 'to follow.' The justice of God actively and relentlessly pursues the target of divine righteousness in the mature believer for the purpose of imputing blessing. The grace pipeline is not passive. It is directed and intentional.

7. David makes no exceptions in Psalm 23:6. 'All the days of my life' includes the present catastrophe of the Absalom revolution. The overflowing cup overflows in disaster exactly as much as it does in prosperity. The reality of the real imputation is not contingent on external circumstances.

8. Two a fortiori arguments structure Psalm 23:6. First: if the justice of God accomplished the greater (imputing divine righteousness at salvation), it will accomplish the less (imputing blessing at maturity). Second: if the justice of God accomplished the greater (imputing blessing in time at maturity), it will accomplish the less (imputing blessing in eternity in reward). Both use the Hebrew kal wa-ḥomer / Greek a fortiori structure that Paul employs in Romans 8.

9. Yāšab in Psalm 23:6c means 'to dwell prosperously.' The final statement is not merely a declaration of perpetual residence in God's presence but of prosperous residence — blessing in eternity imputed to the divinely prepared home of the resurrection body, which carries no old sin nature and no human good.

10. Blessing depends on the host, not the guest. The hospitality framework of the banquet imagery makes explicit what the entire psalm assumes: the imputation of blessing is determined by the integrity of God as host, not by any quality, achievement, or devotion of the believer as guest. This eliminates all legalism from the doctrine of blessing and grounds everything in the justice and grace of God.

11. Undeserved suffering in maturity amplifies rather than diminishes blessing. The sixth category within the framework of mature believer testing uses disaster as the instrument by which the justice of God produces greater blessing — in time and parlayed into eternity. The mature believer who looks upward rather than outward in catastrophe sees not the armies closing in but the pursuing grace of God.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
tôb טוב ṭôb — good, prosperity, divine good Hebrew adjective also used as a substantive. Equivalent to the Greek agathos (intrinsic good, divine good). In Psalm 23:6, used substantively to denote prosperity — specifically the real imputation of divine blessing from the justice of God to the righteousness of God at maturity.
ḥesed חסד ḥesed — grace, loyal love, covenant faithfulness Hebrew noun widely translated 'mercy' or 'lovingkindness.' In Psalm 23:6 the contextual meaning is grace — the policy of divine justice in blessing the mature believer. Paired with ṭôb to describe the two characteristics of the divine pursuit of the mature believer.
rādap רדף rādap — to pursue, to chase, to follow relentlessly Hebrew verb meaning active, purposeful pursuit. Used in Psalm 23:6 of prosperity and grace pursuing the mature believer. Conveys the active, intentional character of the grace pipeline — the justice of God directing blessing toward the target of divine righteousness.
rĕwāyāh רויה rĕwāyāh — overflowing, saturation, abundance Hebrew substantive used predicatively in Psalm 23:5c: 'my cup — overflowing.' Denotes the condition of full capacity for blessing. Used elliptically, conveying the intensity of David's confidence that his cup of capacity is completely filled.
kôs כוס kôs — cup, goblet Hebrew noun designating a banquet goblet, typically of gold or silver, used for the finest wines at formal meals. In Psalm 23:5 it represents the believer's capacity for blessing — empty at salvation, filling through doctrine, overflowing at maturity.
dāšen (Piel) דשן dāšen — to anoint, to appoint to high office Hebrew verb, Qal stem: to become fat, to become prosperous, to provide abundance. Piel stem: to be made rich, to be appointed to high office, to anoint in the sense of royal consecration. In Psalm 23:5b the Piel perfect refers both to the historical anointing of David by Samuel (1 Samuel 16:1–13) and to the security of divine appointment to the highest office.
šemen שמן šemen — oil, consecration oil Hebrew noun referring to the special oil used for royal and priestly anointing. In Psalm 23:5b it designates the oil of royal appointment, not cosmetic anointing.
rōš ראש rōš — head Hebrew noun. In Psalm 23:5b it carries a first-person singular suffix ('my head'), indicating that this royal anointing belongs specifically to David as a mature believer who has been divinely appointed to the highest office.
ʾak אך ʾak — only, surely (adverb of restriction) Hebrew adverb functioning here as a strong adverb of affirmation and restriction. Best translated 'only' in Psalm 23:6. Expresses the mature believer's focused confidence: nothing else matters, nothing else is certain, only the pursuit of God's prosperity and grace.
yāšab ישב yāšab — to dwell, to dwell prosperously Hebrew verb meaning to sit, to dwell, to settle. In Psalm 23:6 the extended meaning is 'to dwell in prosperity, to live prosperously.' The final clause of the psalm anticipates not merely residence in God's presence but prosperous residence — blessing in eternity imputed to the resurrection body.
agathos αγαθός agathos — intrinsically good, divine good Greek adjective denoting that which is good in its essential nature — intrinsic good, divine good. Distinguished from kalos (aesthetically good) and chrestos (practically useful). The Hebrew ṭôb used substantively in Psalm 23:6 is the functional equivalent.
a fortiori a fortiori — from the greater to the lesser Latin logical term for the argument from greater to lesser: if something is true in the more difficult case, it is certainly true in the easier case. The Hebrew equivalent is kal wa-ḥomer. Paul employs this structure throughout Romans 8 (cf. 8:32); David employs it in Psalm 23:6. The argument: if justice accomplished the greater (imputing divine righteousness at salvation), it will accomplish the less (imputing blessing at maturity and in eternity).

Chapter Two Hundred Ninety-Two

Romans 8:7 — The Thought Pattern of the Flesh: Hostility Toward God

Romans 8:7 “For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: Because the thought pattern of the flesh — the old sin nature — is hostile toward God; for it does not subordinate itself to the law of God, for neither is it able to do so.

Romans 8 continues its exposition of the two competing thought patterns available to the believer: the thought pattern dominated by the old sin nature, and the thought pattern dominated by the Holy Spirit. Verse 6 established that the thought pattern of the Spirit is life and prosperity; verse 7 now diagnoses the alternative — the carnal mind — as a state of active hostility toward God. This chapter examines the grammatical structure of verse 7 through the first phrase, identifies the three categories of thinking that constitute such hostility, and draws out the doctrinal implications for both the individual believer and the nation.

I. Review of the Context: Romans 8:1–6

The opening verses of Romans 8 establish the legal and experiential freedom available to the believer in Christ. Verse 1 announces no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus; verse 2 grounds that freedom in the ministry of the Holy Spirit, who liberates the believer from the principle of the sin nature and the spiritual death it produces. Verses 3–4 explain how what the law could not accomplish — because human flesh was too weak to meet its demands — God accomplished by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, judging the sin nature in the flesh, so that the legal requirement of the law might be fulfilled in believers who walk according to the Spirit.

Verse 5 draws the contrast: those dominated by the old sin nature think about the things of the flesh; those dominated by the Holy Spirit think about the things of the Spirit. Verse 6 assigns the outcome: the thought pattern of the flesh is death; the thought pattern of the Spirit is life and prosperity. Verse 7 now explains why the carnal thought pattern produces death — it is constitutionally hostile toward God.

II. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 8:7a

The Causal Conjunction

The verse opens with the causal conjunction dioti (διότι), meaning because or for the reason that. This conjunction links verse 7 to the death-verdict of verse 6: the thought pattern of the flesh is death because it is hostile toward God. The causal relationship is logical and necessary, not incidental.

The Subject: Phronēma

The nominative singular subject is phronēma (φρόνημα), meaning thought pattern, mind-set, mentality. This is not a reference to a single sinful act or isolated thought, but to the governing orientation and operational framework of the mind. It is the characteristic cast of the mind when it is dominated by a particular principle.

The Possessive Genitive: Sarkos

Modifying the subject is the possessive genitive sarkos (σαρκός), the genitive singular of sarx (σάρξ), the flesh — here used as a technical designation for the old sin nature. In the Pauline epistles, sarx in this theological context does not refer simply to physical tissue but to the sin capacity inherited at physical birth through the male genetic line. It is the principle of corruption resident in fallen human nature. The full subject phrase therefore reads: the thought pattern of the flesh — the old sin nature.

The Predicate: Echthra

The predicate is the nominative noun echthra (ἔχθρα), meaning enmity, hostility, active opposition. The verb of being is elliptical — Paul omits it for rhetorical force. The construction is a predicate nominative without a copula, making the identification stark and unqualified: the thought pattern of the old sin nature is hostility. It does not merely tend toward antagonism; it is enmity in its essential character.

The Prepositional Phrase: Eis Theon

The hostility is directed eis theon (εἰς θεόν), literally toward God or against God. The absence of the definite article before theon emphasizes the qualitative character of the object: the hostility is directed toward the very nature and essence of God — toward all that God is. The corrected translation of the first phrase of verse 7 reads: Because the thought pattern of the flesh — the old sin nature — is hostile toward God.

III. The Carnal Believer Defined

A common misunderstanding identifies the carnal believer as any believer who sins. This is imprecise. The carnal believer, in precise Pauline usage, is not simply the sinning believer but the sinning believer who rejects or neglects the rebound technique — the naming of known sins to God the Father as defined in 1 John 1:9.

The critical distinction is recovery. Every believer sins; the question is whether the believer returns to fellowship through rebound. The carnal believer never rebounds and therefore never recovers the filling of the Spirit. Without the filling of the Spirit, spirituality is impossible, the thought pattern of the flesh reasserts itself, and the governing orientation of the soul becomes one of hostility toward God — not necessarily conscious or articulate hostility, but the functional hostility of a life organized apart from divine authority and divine thinking.

The filling of the Spirit — plērōsis pneumatos (πλήρωσις πνεύματος) — is the non-negotiable operational basis for the metal attitude of spiritual winners. Without it, the believer's thought pattern, however sincere, is structurally aligned with the old sin nature rather than with the Holy Spirit.

IV. Three Categories of Thinking Hostile to God

The hostility expressed by the thought pattern of the old sin nature is not limited to overt rebellion or moral depravity. Paul's diagnosis encompasses three distinct categories of thinking, each of which is constitutionally antagonistic to the character and purposes of God.

Category One: Mental Attitude Sins

The first category is the category of sin — specifically, mental attitude sins. These are the thought-level expressions of the old sin nature operating in the soul: arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, hatred, fear, worry, implacability, vindictiveness, and guilt complex. Each of these represents the soul oriented away from God and toward the autonomy of the self or the tyranny of circumstances. Mental attitude sins are not passive failures; they are active orientations of the mind that constitute hostility toward the character of God.

Arrogance, for example, is not merely excessive self-confidence; it is the assertion of the self in the place properly occupied by God. Guilt complex is not humility; it is a refusal to accept the provision God has already made through rebound and the completed work of Christ. Fear and worry are functional denials of the faithfulness and sovereignty of God. Each mental attitude sin is, in its structure, a form of practical atheism.

Category Two: Human Good

The second category of thinking hostile to God is human good — the thought pattern that attempts to solve spiritual, social, and historical problems through human initiative, organization, legislation, and moral reform apart from the Word of God.

Human good thinking operates on the premise that man can improve his condition, achieve justice, and produce blessing through the application of human wisdom and collective effort. This is hostile toward God not because it produces obviously evil outcomes in every case, but because it displaces divine provision with human achievement, which is structurally incompatible with grace. Grace operates on the principle that God does the work and man receives the benefit through faith and adjustment. Human good reverses this — man does the work and attempts to generate blessing through effort.

The clearest diagnostic marker of human good thinking is the belief that external structural changes — new laws, new administrations, new social arrangements — can accomplish what only a change of thinking at the individual level can achieve. Legislation cannot produce mental attitude transformation. Transferring material resources cannot build the capacity for life that comes only through sustained intake of Bible doctrine. Human good, however well-intentioned, undermines the principle of individual responsibility, destroys the mental attitude of self-reliance and authority orientation, and ultimately works against the divine design for human freedom and capacity.

Category Three: Evil

The third category is evil — the thought pattern that combines with human good to form the policy of Satan as the ruler of this world and the operational agenda of the old sin nature as the governing principle of life. Evil in this technical sense is not simply gross immorality. It is the systematic substitution of Satan's policy for divine principle across every domain of human life: personal, social, political, economic, and religious.

Evil operates most effectively not through obvious depravity but through the appearance of beneficence. It presents itself as compassion, progress, and social improvement — the very register of human good — while systematically dismantling the structures through which God has ordained that blessing should flow: authority, freedom, individual accountability, and the intake of divine viewpoint through the Word of God.

V. The Individual, the Nation, and the Pivot

The hostility of the carnal thought pattern is not merely a private spiritual problem. What a nation thinks collectively is its policy. Foreign policy and domestic policy are the aggregated expression of the mental attitude of the individual citizens who constitute that nation. When the predominant thought pattern of a citizenry is hostile toward God — organized around mental attitude sins, human good, and evil rather than around divine viewpoint — the nation's policy will reflect that hostility in its treatment of divine institutions: the family, legitimate government, free enterprise, and the military.

The five cycles of divine discipline represent the progressive judicial response of God to a client nation whose collective thought pattern has turned away from Him. The process is not arbitrary; it follows from the structural principle that the thought pattern of the flesh is enmity toward God, and that sustained institutional expression of that enmity inevitably draws divine discipline at the national level.

The counterforce to national discipline is the pivot — the body of mature believers whose daily adjustment to the justice of God through maximum doctrine resident in the soul creates a basis on which divine blessing can continue to flow to the nation. Jesus Christ controls history. He has never failed to preserve a nation that maintains a large pivot of believers who have cracked the maturity barrier and advanced into supergrace. The individual believer's daily intake of Bible doctrine and consistent adjustment to the justice of God is therefore not a private spiritual exercise but a historically significant act.

The solution to national decline does not begin with political action, constitutional reform, or collective moral campaigns. It begins with the individual reversal of hostility toward God in the believer's own soul — the replacement of the thought pattern of the old sin nature with the thought pattern dominated by the Holy Spirit, through the daily, systematic intake of Bible doctrine via the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

VI. Metal Attitude and the Thought Pattern of the Spirit

The contrast between verses 6 and 7 is not merely between death and life in an abstract theological sense. It is a contrast between two operational orientations of the mind under combat conditions. The thought pattern dominated by the Holy Spirit produces what the text of verse 6 calls life and prosperity — the capacity to function effectively under pressure, to maintain orientation to divine authority, and to advance rather than retreat in the face of adversity.

This is the spiritual counterpart of what military history recognizes as metal attitude — the disciplined, authority-oriented, professionally competent mindset that enables sustained effective function under the most demanding conditions. The soldier who maintains metal attitude under fire does not function on the basis of emotion, resentment, or the path of least resistance. He functions on the basis of training, discipline, and subordination to a chain of command that he trusts. The spiritually advancing believer functions on the same structural principle: doctrine in the right lobe, filling of the Spirit, orientation to divine authority, and consistent forward movement in the plan of God regardless of external circumstances.

The thought pattern of the old sin nature is structurally incapable of this kind of function. It is, by definition, hostile toward the authority structure that makes effective operation possible. It cannot subordinate itself to the law of God — not merely will not, but cannot, as the second half of verse 7 will establish — because its operational orientation is self-referential rather than God-referential.

Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Ninety-Two

1. The causal conjunction dioti links verse 7 to the death-verdict of verse 6: the thought pattern of the flesh is death because it is constitutionally hostile toward God. The hostility is not incidental but essential to what the carnal mind-set is.

2. Phronēma designates not an isolated thought but a governing mind-set — the characteristic operational orientation of the soul when dominated by a controlling principle. The carnal phronēma is organized around the old sin nature; the spiritual phronēma is organized around the Holy Spirit.

3. The predicate echthra (enmity, hostility) is a nominative noun, not a verb or adjective, making the identification definitive: the thought pattern of the flesh does not merely tend toward hostility — it is hostility in its essential character.

4. The carnal believer is not the sinning believer as such, but the sinning believer who rejects or neglects rebound. The critical variable is recovery of the filling of the Spirit, not the presence or absence of sin. Every believer sins; the carnal believer is the one who does not return to fellowship.

5. Three categories of thinking constitute hostility toward God: mental attitude sins (arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, hatred, fear, worry, implacability, vindictiveness, guilt complex); human good (the attempt to solve man's problems through legislation, collective moral reform, and human initiative apart from doctrine); and evil (Satan's policy combining with human good to systematically displace divine principle across all domains of life).

6. Human good is hostile toward God not because it produces obviously immoral outcomes, but because it displaces grace with human achievement. Grace requires that God does the work and man receives through faith and adjustment; human good reverses this, making man the agent of blessing and thereby structurally excluding divine provision.

7. What a nation thinks collectively is its policy. The foreign and domestic policy of any nation is the aggregated mental attitude of its individual citizens. When the predominant thought pattern is hostile toward God, national policy will reflect that hostility in its treatment of divine institutions and will attract progressive cycles of divine discipline.

8. The pivot of mature believers is the historical counterforce to national discipline. Jesus Christ controls history and has never failed to sustain a client nation with a sufficient pivot of believers at supergrace. The individual believer's daily intake of doctrine and adjustment to the justice of God is therefore a historically significant act, not a private religious exercise.

9. The thought pattern dominated by the Holy Spirit produces the spiritual equivalent of metal attitude — the disciplined, authority-oriented, doctrine-filled operational orientation that enables sustained effective function under pressure. The thought pattern of the old sin nature, being constitutionally hostile toward divine authority, is incapable of this kind of function. Verse 7b will establish that its inability is not merely volitional but ontological: it neither subordinates itself to the law of God, nor is it able to do so.

10. The only solution to individual carnality and its national consequences is maximum Bible doctrine resident in the soul — accumulated daily through the Grace Apparatus for Perception under the filling of the Holy Spirit. No political program, social reform, or collective human effort can accomplish what only the replacement of the carnal thought pattern with the spiritual thought pattern can achieve.

Chapter Two Hundred Ninety-Three

Romans 8:7b — Insubordination to the Policy of God; the Grace Pipeline; Imputation and Divine Blessing

Romans 8:7 “For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: Because the thought pattern of the old sin nature is hostile toward God, for it is not subordinate — under orders — to the policy of God, because it is not able to subordinate to Bible doctrine.

Romans 8 continues the exposition of the ministry of the Holy Spirit and the contrast between life dominated by the old sin nature and life governed by the Spirit. The preceding verses established that the thought pattern of the old sin nature is death, while the thought pattern of the Spirit is capacity for life and prosperity. Verse 7 now provides the explanatory ground for that contrast: the old sin nature's thought pattern is hostile toward God because it is structurally incapable of subordination to divine policy. This chapter examines that incapacity in detail, together with the divine policy — the grace pipeline from the justice of God to the righteousness of God — to which the old sin nature cannot submit.

I. The Grammar of Insubordination (Romans 8:7b)

The conjunction introducing the clause is the post-positive explanatory particle γάρ (gar), used here to explain the ground of the hostility just stated. The explanation has two elements: a statement of fact regarding insubordination, followed by a causal clause establishing that the insubordination is not merely habitual but constitutionally impossible.

The Verb hupotassō — Subordination as Military Order

The central verb is the present passive indicative of hupotassō (ὑποτάσσω), negated by ou (οὔ). Hupotassō is a military compound: hupo (under) + tassō (to arrange, to post in order of battle). It denotes being placed under orders, subordinated to a command structure. The negative construction therefore means: it is not under orders to, it is not subordinate to.

The tense is a retroactive progressive present, denoting a condition begun in the past — whether through carnality or reversionism — and continuing into the present. The indicative mood is declarative, representing the verbal action from the standpoint of reality. This is not a hypothetical or potential insubordination; it is the actual, ongoing condition of the believer whose soul is not loaded with Bible doctrine.

The object of this subordination is stated as the policy of God. The dative singular indirect object is drawn from the noun

nomos (νόμος), which can mean law, principle, or policy. In this context it refers to divine policy — the entire system by which God dispenses blessing through the grace pipeline. The possessive genitive Theou (θεοῦ) establishes that this policy belongs exclusively to God. It cannot be modified, supplemented, or circumvented by human effort.

The Causal Clause — Constitutional Incapacity

The second half of the verse adds the causal conjunction gar (γάρ) combined with the negative conjunction oude (οὐδέ), yielding a compound negative causal: because not even. With this is the present passive indicative of dunamai (δύναμαι), to be able. The present tense here is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results. The thought pattern of the old sin nature is not merely failing to subordinate itself — it is constitutionally incapable of doing so.

This is a deponent verb: passive in form, active in meaning. The thought pattern of carnality or reversionism produces the action of the verb. The indicative mood is declarative. The principle is structural: apart from Bible doctrine resident in the soul, the believer cannot be guided by God, cannot advance to spiritual maturity, and cannot receive the divine blessings that flow through the grace pipeline.

The corrected translation of the full verse therefore reads: Because the thought pattern of the old sin nature is hostile toward God, for it is not subordinate — under orders — to the policy of God, because it is not able to subordinate to Bible doctrine.

II. The Policy of God: The Grace Pipeline

The 'policy of God' referenced in verse 7 is not an abstract moral code. It is the specific operational system by which the justice of God dispenses blessing to believers who have acquired the capacity to receive it. Understanding this system requires tracing the chain of imputations from physical birth through spiritual maturity.

The Two Real Imputations at Birth

The policy of God begins at the moment of birth. There is no human life in the womb; the first occurrence of human life is when the fetus emerges and the justice of God executes a real imputation. A real imputation requires two factors: what is being imputed, and the home or target to which it is imputed — with antecedent affinity between the two.

Real imputation number one: human life is imputed to its antecedently prepared home, the human soul. Human life is antecedently the soul's, because the soul is designed as its residence. That imputation is permanent; death is the human soul departing the body, but the soul retains human life beyond the grave.

Simultaneously, real imputation number two occurs: Adam's original sin is imputed to its antecedently prepared home, the old sin nature. When Adam sinned, he generated the old sin nature. Therefore affinity exists between Adam's original sin and the old sin nature. The result is that every human being enters life physically alive but spiritually dead. Condemnation at birth is not based on personal sins but on Adam's original sin alone — a crucial distinction, because it means that the justice of God can only condemn through what has antecedent affinity with its target.

This is the foundational principle of the grace pipeline: the justice of God can only condemn before it can bless. Condemnation precedes blessing. The two real imputations at birth establish the condition from which all subsequent judicial imputations proceed.

The Two Judicial Imputations

A judicial imputation has only one factor. There is no antecedent affinity between what is imputed and the one to whom it is imputed. The absence of affinity is precisely what makes these imputations judicial rather than real — they are acts of the court of divine justice, not of natural correspondence.

Judicial imputation number one: at the cross, all personal sins of the entire human race — past, present, and future — were imputed to the Lord Jesus Christ. These sins were not antecedently His; there was no affinity between the perfect Son of God and human sinfulness. Nevertheless, they were imputed to Him judicially and judged there. This is the work of salvation. The moment a person believes in the Lord Jesus Christ, that work is credited to him.

Judicial imputation number two: at the moment of faith in Christ, the divine righteousness of God is imputed to the believing sinner. This righteousness is not antecedently the believer's — there is no affinity between sinful humanity and God's perfect righteousness. Nevertheless, it is given as a judicial act in order to prepare a home, a target, for the future dispensing of divine blessing. Simultaneously, eternal life is imputed as a real imputation to its divinely prepared home, regeneration.

All imputations are permanent. The imputation of divine righteousness to the believer cannot be revoked. This is the basis for eternal security: the justice of God cannot cancel its own judicial acts.

The Grace Pipeline Defined

The grace pipeline operates on a single axis: from the justice of God on the originating end to the righteousness of God on the receiving end. The justice of God is both the source of all condemnation and the source of all blessing. The righteousness of God imputed to the believer at salvation is the home into which all blessings are deposited.

Because the righteousness of God is the receiving end, and because that righteousness was given as a judicial act — not earned — the believer can never take credit for any blessing received. Blessings do not flow because the believer is morally good, because he has made sacrifices, because he gives money, because he engages in Christian service, or because he prays in a particular manner. None of these function as conduits through the grace pipeline. The pipeline has only one operational channel: the daily intake and accumulation of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception until the maturity barrier is cracked.

Production from the Christian way of life is not excluded, but it is the result of doctrine resident in the soul, not the means of blessing. When a believer has sufficient doctrine resident in the soul, that doctrine will express itself in some form of production — in vocation, in service, in military excellence, in professional competence, in whatever sphere of life the believer occupies. But the production is the expression of capacity, not its cause.

III. The A Fortiori Structure of Divine Policy

The policy of God described in this passage is further structured by the logical principle of a fortiori — argument from the greater to the less. This principle appears first in Romans 5 and recurs in Romans 8:32. It is a system of logic that operates not on quantity or quality but on degree of effort: if the greater effort has been accomplished, the lesser follows necessarily.

First A Fortiori: From Imputation to Temporal Blessing

The greater: the justice of God accomplished the judicial imputation of divine righteousness to the believing sinner at salvation. This was the greater act — crediting perfect divine righteousness to the account of a fallen human being with no natural affinity for it.

The lesser: if the justice of God could accomplish that greater act, it follows by a fortiori that the justice of God can accomplish the lesser act, which is the imputation of temporal blessings to the home of divine righteousness already prepared in the believer. These blessings are categorized under the six components of paragraph SG2: spiritual blessings including occupation with Christ and capacity for happiness; material prosperity; sexual and social prosperity; establishment prosperity; blessing by association; and historical impact.

The believer who does not crack the maturity barrier — who remains insubordinate to the policy of God — possesses the home of divine righteousness (the base of imputed righteousness), but accumulates no temporal blessings over it. At the end of his life, the account stands: righteousness imputed, blessings absent.

Second A Fortiori: From Temporal Blessing to Eternal Blessing

The greater: if the justice of God can accomplish the imputation of temporal blessings to the divinely prepared home of righteousness in time, it follows a fortiori that the justice of God can accomplish the lesser, which is the imputation of eternal blessings to the divinely prepared home of the resurrection body minus the old sin nature.

The temporal blessings accumulated through maturity become the basis for eternal blessings above and beyond the resurrection body itself. Those who finish life with maximum doctrine resident in the soul — who crack the maturity barrier, advance to supergrace, and die the dying blessing of phase two to phase three — carry forward the escrow account of those blessings into eternity. Those who do not remain believers with resurrection bodies but without the additional eternal decorations and blessings that derive from mature adjustment to the justice of God in time.

Everywhere the policy operates, the directive is the same: advance through doctrine. The daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception — doctrine received, metabolized, and accumulated in the soul — is the singular mechanism by which capacity is developed and through which the justice of God dispenses all that was designed for each believer in eternity past.

IV. Authority, Insubordination, and the Old Sin Nature

The verb hupotassō, drawn from the military sphere, connects the doctrinal principle directly to the concept of authority. Subordination to divine policy is not optional or situational; it is the structural prerequisite for the operation of the grace pipeline. The old sin nature is by constitution anti-authoritarian. Its thought pattern — encompassing the mental attitude of arrogance, pride, bitterness, vindictiveness, implacability, and guilt complex, as well as the thought patterns of human good and evil — is organized around the rejection of authority at every level.

The present tense of the verb with the negative is a retroactive progressive present: the insubordination began at some past point — whether at the onset of carnality through unconfessed sin, or through the progressive drift into reversionism — and continues. The carnal believer and the reversinistic believer share this condition: they are not subordinate to divine policy, and by the perfective present of dunamai with the negative, they are constitutionally unable to be so as long as they remain in that state.

Insubordination in one area of life overflows into other areas. The believer who rejects the authority of Bible doctrine as taught in the local church will manifest the same pattern of rejection in personal life, in professional life, and in his relationship to civil authority. Authority structures — parental authority, institutional authority, chain of command in military or professional settings, the authority of Scripture itself — all reflect the ultimate authority of the justice of God. Rejection of any legitimate authority node is an expression of arrogance toward the ultimate authority.

The Two Marriages and Retroactive Positional Truth

Romans 6 and 7 established the doctrine of the two marriages as the framework for understanding the believer's relationship to the old sin nature. The unbeliever is the wife of the first husband, the old sin nature, with the Mosaic Law as marriage counselor. The believer is the wife of the second husband, the Lord Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit as marriage counselor.

Retroactive positional truth — the believer's identification with Christ in His spiritual death, physical death, burial, and resurrection through the baptism of the Spirit — constitutes the legal separation from the first husband. Identification with Christ in His spiritual death means rejection of the old sin nature. Identification with Christ in His physical death means separation from the old sin nature. Identification with Christ in His burial is the equivalent of divorce: the believer is legally dead to the old sin nature, and the old sin nature is legally dead to the believer.

Carnality and reversionism represent the carnal believer responding to the old sin nature's renewed solicitation — returning to the first husband after the divorce. This is why the thought pattern of the old sin nature is described as hostile toward God: it is the thought pattern of the former spouse, operating under the authority of the first marriage, in opposition to the new marriage's policy.

The corrective mechanism is rebound — the naming of known sins to God, which instantly restores fellowship with the indwelling Holy Spirit (1 John 1:9). Without rebound, the carnal believer remains in a condition of temporal spiritual death, unable to metabolize doctrine, unable to advance, and unable to receive temporal blessing through the grace pipeline. Rebound does not restore lost time or lost blessing, but it does restore the operational capacity for subordination to divine policy and resume the advance.

V. The Progressive Discipline of Insubordination

The perfective present of dunamai with the negative describes not merely a momentary inability but a hardened condition producing continuing results. The carnal or reversinistic believer who persists in insubordination to divine policy moves through a sequence of divine disciplines.

Stage one: warning discipline — initial corrective pressure from the justice of God designed to arrest the drift and return the believer to the policy. Stage two: intensive discipline — sustained pressure, increasingly severe, corresponding to sustained rejection of doctrine and authority. Stage three: the sin unto death — maximum discipline, which is physical death as the terminal expression of the justice of God toward the believer who has exhausted all corrective disciplines without response.

The sin unto death does not terminate the believer's salvation. The judicial imputation of divine righteousness is permanent; eternal life is permanent. The believer who dies the sin unto death is absent from the body and face to face with the Lord. But the manner of death — and the condition of the soul's escrow account at death — contrasts sharply with dying blessing. The mature believer who crosses from phase two to phase three over the golden bridge of dying blessing does so with maximum accumulated doctrine, maximum capacity, and maximum eternal blessings prepared. The reversinistic believer who dies the sin unto death carries none of that capacity into eternity.

The choice presented by verse 7b is therefore not between salvation and damnation — that question was settled at the moment of faith in Christ. The choice is between subordination to the policy of God through daily doctrine intake, with all the temporal and eternal blessings that flow from it, and insubordination to that policy, with the corresponding temporal misery, divine discipline, and eternal deficit above the resurrection body.

Conclusions from Chapter Two Hundred Ninety-Three

1. The verb hupotassō is a military term: it denotes placement under orders within a command structure. The thought pattern of the old sin nature is constitutionally anti-authoritarian — it cannot be subordinate to divine policy because it is organized around the rejection of authority at every level.

2. Insubordination to divine policy is not primarily a behavioral failure: it is a thought pattern. The hostility of the old sin nature toward God is expressed first in the mental attitude of arrogance, pride, bitterness, and implacability, and then in the thought patterns of human good and evil that flow from that mental attitude.

3. The 'policy of God' (nomos tou Theou) in verse 7 is not the Mosaic Law: it is the entire operational system of divine blessing — the grace pipeline from the justice of God on the originating end to the righteousness of God on the receiving end. Submission to this policy means daily intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

4. The grace pipeline operates on one axis only — justice to righteousness: all blessing flows from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God in the believer. No human effort, sacrifice, giving, prayer technique, or religious activity functions as a conduit through this pipeline. Capacity developed through doctrine intake is the sole qualification for the dispensing of blessing.

5. The two real imputations at birth establish the condition for all subsequent judicial imputations: human life to the soul, and Adam's original sin to the old sin nature. The two judicial imputations at salvation — all personal sins to Christ on the cross, and divine righteousness to the believer — form the basis for the imputation of temporal and eternal blessings. All imputations are permanent.

6. The a fortiori structure governs the entire sequence of divine blessing: if the justice of God accomplished the greater (judicial imputation of righteousness at salvation), it follows necessarily that the justice of God can accomplish the lesser (temporal blessing at maturity). And if the justice of God can accomplish temporal blessing, it follows that eternal blessing above the resurrection body is equally secured for the mature believer.

7. The perfective present of dunamai with the negative denotes the continuation of existing results: the carnal or reversinistic believer is not merely failing to subordinate — the accumulated condition of carnality or reversionism makes subordination constitutionally impossible as long as that condition persists. Rebound terminates the condition instantly; sustained doctrine intake prevents its recurrence.

8. Insubordination in one area of authority overflows to all areas: the believer who rejects the authority of Bible doctrine will manifest the same pattern of rejection toward parental, institutional, civil, and professional authority. Authority at every level reflects the ultimate authority of the justice of God; resistance to any node of legitimate authority is ultimately resistance to the source.

9. The retroactive positional truth of the two marriages establishes the legal framework: the believer is divorced from the old sin nature through identification with Christ in His death and burial. Carnality and reversionism represent the believer responding to the old sin nature's renewed solicitation — returning to the first husband. The policy of the new marriage is the policy of God, administered by God the Holy Spirit.

10. The progressive discipline sequence for insubordination — warning, intensive, sin unto death — terminates in physical death but never in the loss of salvation. The permanent judicial imputations of divine righteousness and eternal life cannot be revoked. What is at stake is not eternal destiny but the condition of the escrow account at death and the resulting difference in eternity between resurrection body alone and resurrection body plus eternal blessing.
