It encompasses human good, legalism, emotional substitutes for doctrine, and reversionism — all forms of apparently spiritual activity that divert from consistent doctrinal intake. The devil's triangle is the mechanism by which believers remain perpetually immature, unable to receive the categorical imputations of divine blessing.

Chapter Three Hundred Nine

Romans 8:17 — Heirship, Positional Truth, and the Transition to Suffering as Blessing

Romans 8:17 “and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: and if children, then also heirs — on the one hand, heirs of God, and on the other hand, fellow heirs with Christ — if indeed we suffer together with Him, in order that we might also be glorified together with Him.

Romans 8:17 is a transitional verse standing between two major paragraphs. The first paragraph (8:1–16) has established the believer's standing in the Spirit, the indwelling of God the Holy Spirit, adoption into the royal family of God, and the double witness of the Spirit and the regenerate human spirit to the fact that we are children of God. Verse 17 now gathers those themes into a single sentence of relationship and then pivots, through its second sentence, toward the great doctrinal paragraph on suffering and glory that extends through verse 30. The present chapter treats the first sentence of verse 17 — the relationship sentence — and introduces the transitional sentence that will open the exposition of undeserved suffering as a divine blessing to the mature believer.

I. The Post-Positive Conjunction and the Method of Pauline Genius

The verse opens with a post-positive conjunctive particle, the Greek

The verse opens with a post-positive conjunctive particle, the Greek δέ (de), which connects the thought now being introduced with everything that has preceded in the chapter. This small two-letter particle is the signature of Paul's method as a theological writer of the highest order. Paul does not present one doctrinal principle, pause, and then begin an unrelated principle. He relates every field of thought to every other field of thought, using the connective particles of Koine Greek as the structural tissue. The result is that the Pauline epistles cannot be correctly interpreted apart from a sustained attention to these particles, which carry the logical weight that in English prose would require an entire sentence of transition.

Koine Greek was selected by God the Holy Spirit as the language of the New Testament precisely because its grammatical resources — including its system of conditional particles, its case distinctions, and its wealth of connective particles — are capable of conveying theological precision and dramatic nuance that no translation can fully replicate. The choice of Koine rather than classical Greek reflects the universal accessibility of the first-century common dialect, while retaining the structural precision required for the inspired text.

II. The First-Class Condition: Assumption from Reality

The conditional sentence is introduced by the particle εἰ (ei), which marks a first-class condition. A conditional clause has two structural components: the protasis (the clause containing the supposition) and the apodosis (the clause stating the result or fulfillment). The first-class condition is recognized by the particle εἰ followed by a verb in the indicative mood and is properly defined as a supposition from the viewpoint of reality — the speaker assumes the premise to be true for the purpose of drawing a conclusion from it.

Four categories of conditional supposition exist in Greek:

First class: supposition from reality — the premise is assumed to be true. Second class: supposition from unreality — the premise is stated as though false. Third class: supposition from probability — the premise may or may not be true. Fourth class: supposition from remote possibility — the premise is wished for but currently unrealized.

Here, the first-class condition is appropriate because the premise — that believers are children of God — has already been established in verses 14–16. The assumption is not tentative; it is stated as certain reality. The logical structure is: given that we are children (established fact), we are therefore also heirs (necessary consequence).

III. Ellipsis and Its Theological Function

The first sentence of verse 17 is entirely elliptical. No verb appears in the Greek text. The present active indicative of εἰμί (eimi, to be) is implied but not expressed. This grammatical feature — ellipsis — is the omission of a grammatically necessary element that is self-evident from context. In Koine Greek, ellipsis is not a deficiency of expression; it is a deliberate device that communicates either emotional or intellectual intensity. The drama of the sentence must be conveyed through grammar rather than through tone of voice or theatrical staging. When both emotional and intellectual stimulation are present simultaneously, ellipsis concentrates that force at the very point where the reader must supply the missing element. Here the reader must pause and consciously insert the verb 'to be,' and in that pause, the full weight of the claim — that every believer is an heir of God — is felt.

IV. The Two Categories of Sonship: Teknon and Huios

The predicate nominative that follows the implied verb is the plural of τέκνον (teknon), meaning a child under authority, a child still in the period of learning and formation. This stands in deliberate contrast to the word used in the adoption passages of this chapter, υἱός (huios), which designates an adult son who possesses the full power of attorney of his father. The two terms are not synonyms and their distinction is exegetically significant.

The use of teknon here does not diminish the standing of the believer; it establishes the context of dependence and learning within which the doctrine of heirship is to be understood. We are children in the sense that we remain under the authority of divine instruction, that we have much yet to receive and to learn. At the same time, by virtue of adoption (expressed by huios in the preceding context), we already possess the power of attorney — the full authority and resources — of God the Father. Both categories apply simultaneously to the believer in the Church Age.

V. Heirs of God the Father: The Noun Klēronomos

The conjunction καί (kai), here used adjunctively and translated 'also,' introduces the natural consequence of being a child under parental authority while simultaneously holding the status of adopted son. The predicate nominative plural that follows is κληρονόμοι (klēronomoi), the plural of κληρονόμος (klēronomos), heir. The noun is a compound: κλῆρος (klēros, lot, portion, inheritance) + νέμω (nemō, to distribute, to apportion). An heir is one to whom an inheritance is distributed — one for whom a portion has been set aside and will be delivered at the appointed time.

The genitive singular of relationship that follows indicates the source and owner of the inheritance: God the Father. All believers without exception are heirs of God the Father. The inheritance is not earned by production, sacrificial living, works, giving, or any other form of human effort. It is a function of relationship — specifically, the relationship established at the moment of salvation through the new birth and adoption.

VI. Fellow Heirs with Christ: The Compound Noun Sugklēronomos

The second member of the paired construction employs a compound noun: συγκληρονόμοι (sugklēronomoi), fellow heirs, joint heirs. The prefix σύν (sun, with, together with) is added to klēronomos to produce the compound: one who inherits jointly with another. The dative singular Χριστῷ (Christō) governs the relationship. The dative case here functions not simply as an instrumental of means but as an expression of source: Christ is both the means and the source of our joint heirship. This is inseparable from the doctrine of the baptism of the Holy Spirit and union with Christ.

On the one hand, we are heirs of God the Father — this is our inheritance by virtue of the new birth and adoption. On the other hand, we are fellow heirs with Christ — this is our inheritance by virtue of union with Christ, established through the baptism of the Holy Spirit at the moment of salvation. Both dimensions of heirship are real, simultaneous, and permanent.

VII. The Baptism of the Holy Spirit and Positional Truth

The compound noun 'fellow heirs with Christ' calls for a restatement of the doctrine it presupposes: the baptism of the Holy Spirit and current positional truth. These are the doctrinal foundations without which the concept of joint heirship with Christ cannot be correctly understood.

Retroactive positional truth identifies the believer with Christ in His spiritual death, His physical death, and His burial. Identification with Christ in His spiritual death means that our personal sins were imputed to Him and judged, and that the entire system of the old sin nature as the governing 'first husband' was rejected. Identification with Christ in His physical death means separation from that first husband. Identification with Christ in His burial means divorce from the old sin nature — not the elimination of the nature, which remains biologically present throughout the believer's earthly life, but a legal death to its authority.

Current positional truth is union with Christ in His resurrection, ascension, and session at the right hand of the Father. This union is the basis of the believer's aristocracy in the royal family of God. The Church Age believer is not simply a redeemed sinner; he is a member of the royal family being formed for this unique dispensation. Adoption, studied in the preceding paragraph, places the full power of attorney of God the Father at the believer's disposal — all of the authority, all of the divine power, and all of the divine resources necessary to glorify Christ in the angelic conflict.

VIII. The Doctrine of Heirship and the Cluster of Imputations

Heirship demands blessing. To be the heir of the God of the universe requires that corresponding blessing be provided — blessing of a quality and magnitude commensurate with the character of the One from whom it comes. The only reason any blessing from the justice of God does not flow to a given believer at a given moment is the absence of capacity. Capacity is not produced by works, moral living, giving, witnessing, prayer, or any form of religious production. Capacity comes from one source only: Bible doctrine resident in the human spirit and right lobe of the soul, received through the Grace Apparatus for Perception under the ministry of God the Holy Spirit.

The mechanics of divine blessing flow through a series of imputations — real and judicial — that form interconnected clusters. A real imputation occurs when there is a divinely prepared home, an antecedent affinity, for what is being imputed. A judicial imputation has no such antecedent affinity but is imposed by divine justice for a judicial purpose.

At birth, two real imputations are made: human life is imputed to the soul, and the Adam's original sin is imputed to the old sin nature. These two imputations at birth constitute the grace basis for two judicial imputations that provide the platform for all subsequent blessing. Judicial imputation number one: personal sins are imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. Judicial imputation number two: at the moment of saving faith — the first adjustment to the justice of God — divine righteousness is imputed to the believer. This imputed divine righteousness becomes the permanent, divinely prepared home to which all subsequent blessing from the justice of God is directed. Divine blessing has an affinity for divine righteousness. It has no affinity for moral living, sacrificial service, or any form of human achievement.

The principle known as the argument from the greater to the lesser (Latin: a fortiori) governs the entire sequence of blessing. If the justice of God provided the greater at salvation — namely, the judicial imputation of divine righteousness, which is the basis for all blessing — it follows necessarily that the justice of God will provide the less at spiritual maturity, namely the real imputation of divine blessing in time. And if the justice of God provides blessing in time as a real imputation at maturity, it follows that the justice of God will provide the corresponding blessing in eternity — the real imputation of eternal reward to the divinely prepared home of the resurrection body.

This means that blessing in time at maturity is the sole source of blessing in eternity above and beyond the resurrection body itself. All of the religious production, sacrificial giving, and good deeds performed in the believer's life — however sincere — produce no eternal reward because they do not function through the integrity of God. They do not pass from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. Only what the justice of God imputes can be credited as eternal reward.

IX. The Transitional Sentence: From Relationship to Suffering

The first sentence of Romans 8:17 is complete with the statement of joint heirship. The second sentence of the verse is transitional. It connects the doctrine of heirship — and the blessing that heirship demands — with the paragraph on suffering that extends from verse 18 through verse 30. The connection is not arbitrary. Paul is preparing to demonstrate that suffering, far from being incompatible with the blessings of heirship, is itself the context within which some of the highest forms of divine blessing are delivered to the mature believer.

The second sentence introduces the conditional element 'if indeed we suffer together with Him.' The verb form here is a first-class condition: the supposition is from reality. For the believer advancing toward maturity in the Protocol Plan of God, suffering is not a remote contingency — it is a reality of the experiential life. The question is not whether suffering will come but what category of suffering it is and what the believer's orientation to it is. Punitive suffering, the result of carnality or reversionism, is divine discipline. Providential suffering, designed by the justice of God for the mature believer, is an imputation of blessing in a form that the immature believer cannot receive and would not recognize.

The purpose clause that closes the verse — 'in order that we might also be glorified together with Him' — establishes the telos: glory. Suffering is not the terminus; it is the corridor. The entire paragraph from verse 18 through verse 30 will develop this trajectory: creation's suffering resolved in the millennium; the Holy Spirit's intercessory groaning resolved in perfectly answered prayer; and the mature believer's providential suffering resolved in the highest blessing available to a human being in time and in eternity. The exposition of that paragraph begins in the following chapter.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Nine

1. Romans 8:17 is a transitional verse with two distinct sentences. The first sentence deals with the believer's relationship to God as heir; the second sentence transitions to the theme of suffering as the pathway to glory.

2. The post-positive conjunction de connects verse 17 to everything in 8:1–16. Paul's method as a theological writer is to connect every field of thought to every adjacent field through the precise connective particles of Koine Greek. No doctrinal section stands in isolation.

3. The first-class condition assumes the reality of our status as children of God. The conditional particle ei with the indicative mood introduces a supposition from reality. The premise — that all believers are children of God — has been established in verses 14–16 and is here treated as settled fact.

4. Ellipsis in the first sentence signals both emotional and intellectual intensity. The absence of the verb 'to be' forces the reader to supply it consciously. In Koine Greek, ellipsis is a deliberate grammatical device for concentrating dramatic and theological force at a critical point of the text.

5. Two Greek words for 'son' carry distinct theological freight. Teknon designates a child under authority, still in formation. Huios designates an adult son with full power of attorney. Both apply to the believer simultaneously: we are children under divine instruction, and we are adopted sons with full access to divine authority and resources.

6. Heirship is the natural consequence of the new birth and adoption. The noun klēronomos (heir) denotes one to whom an apportioned inheritance will be delivered. Every believer without exception is an heir of God the Father and a fellow heir with Christ. This status is conferred by relationship, not earned by performance.

7. Fellow heirship with Christ is grounded in the baptism of the Holy Spirit. The compound sugklēronomos (fellow heir) with the dative Christō points to union with Christ established at salvation through the baptism of the Spirit. Retroactive positional truth identifies the believer with Christ's death and burial; current positional truth places the believer in union with the risen, ascended Christ.

8. Heirship demands blessing, but blessing demands capacity. Capacity for divine blessing is not produced by moral effort, religious production, or sacrificial giving. It comes from Bible doctrine resident in the human spirit and right lobe, received through the Grace Apparatus for Perception under the ministry of the Holy Spirit.

9. All divine blessing flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. The imputed divine righteousness received at salvation is the only target for which divine blessing has affinity. Nothing the believer produces can attract blessing from divine justice. The integrity of God is the sole guardian of all divine attributes, and no blessing is ever imputed in any way that compromises those attributes.

10. The cluster of imputations at salvation establishes the platform for all subsequent blessing. Judicial imputation of personal sins to Christ on the cross plus judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation equals the basis for real imputation of blessing in time at maturity, which in turn is the basis for real imputation of eternal reward at the judgment seat of Christ.

11. Blessing in time is the exclusive source of blessing in eternity above the resurrection body. The a fortiori argument governs the entire sequence: if the justice of God provided the greater (divine righteousness) at salvation, it will certainly provide the lesser (temporal and eternal blessing) at maturity and beyond.

12. The second sentence of verse 17 pivots from heirship to providential suffering. The conditional clause 'if indeed we suffer together with Him' is a first-class condition — it assumes the reality of suffering in the mature believer's experience. The purpose clause 'in order that we might be glorified together with Him' establishes suffering as a corridor to glory, not a terminus. The development of this transition occupies Romans 8:18–30.

de δέ de — post-positive conjunctive particle A small connective particle placed second in its clause (post-positive). Used by Paul to link successive doctrinal units, it signals that what follows is both distinct from and continuous with what precedes.
ei εἰ ei — conditional particle, first-class condition The conditional particle introducing a first-class condition: a supposition from the viewpoint of reality. Used with the indicative mood. The premise is assumed to be true for the purpose of drawing a logical conclusion.
teknon τέκνον teknon — child, child under authority Designates a child in the period of formation and learning, under the authority of parents or tutors. Contrasted with huios, which designates an adult son with full power of attorney. In Romans 8:17, teknon emphasizes the believer's dependence on divine instruction.
huios υἱός huios — adult son, son with power of attorney Designates a son who has received the full rights, authority, and power of attorney of his father. In the Roman adoption context of Romans 8, huios signifies the adopted son who possesses all the legal standing and resources of the adopting father.
klēronomos κληρονόμος klēronomos — heir Compound noun: klēros (lot, portion, inheritance) + nemō (to distribute). One to whom an inheritance is apportioned and will be delivered at the appointed time. In Romans 8:17, all believers are designated as heirs of God the Father.
sugklēronomos συγκληρονόμος sugklēronomos — fellow heir, joint heir Compound noun: sun (with, together with) + klēronomos (heir). One who inherits jointly with another. In Romans 8:17, believers are designated as fellow heirs with Christ, grounding their heirship in union with Christ established through the baptism of the Holy Spirit.
eimi εἰμί eimi — to be The Greek verb 'to be.' In Romans 8:17a, the present active indicative of eimi is omitted (ellipsis), requiring the reader to supply it. The ellipsis concentrates dramatic and theological force at the critical statement of heirship.
ellipsis ἔλλειψις elleipsis — omission, ellipsis A grammatical figure in which a necessary element — usually the verb to be — is omitted and left for the reader to supply. In Koine Greek, ellipsis signals emotional or intellectual intensity and is a deliberate rhetorical and theological device.
klēronomia κληρονομία klēronomia — inheritance The estate, portion, or inheritance that an heir receives. Related to klēronomos (heir). In the doctrinal framework of Romans, the believer's inheritance from God the Father encompasses both the real imputation of blessing in time at maturity and the real imputation of eternal reward at the judgment seat of Christ.
epignosis ἐπίγνωσις epignōsis — full, exact knowledge The category of Bible doctrine that has been received through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) and transferred from the left lobe to the human spirit and right lobe. Epignōsis is doctrine that is available for application and constitutes the capacity for divine blessing. Distinguished from gnōsis, which is academic knowledge without spiritual appropriation.

Chapter Three Hundred Ten

Romans 8:17b — Suffering with Maturity Status and Glorification with Christ

Romans 8:17b “...if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: ...if indeed we suffer with maturity status, that also we might be glorified with Christ.

Romans 8:17 consists of two sentences. The first sentence, covered in the preceding chapter, establishes the believer's status as heir of God the Father and fellow heir with Christ. The second sentence is transitional: it introduces the paragraph spanning verses 18 through 30, which traces the arc from undeserved suffering in time to glorification in eternity. Both suffering and glorification are mentioned in this transitional clause, and both terms govern the exposition that follows.

I. The Compound Conditional Conjunction — εἴπερ

The sentence opens with the compound conditional conjunction εἴπερ (eiper), a particle of significant grammatical force. It is composed of εἰ (ei), which introduces a first-class condition with the indicative, and περ (per), an intensive particle conveying the force of 'as is supposed' or 'indeed.' The resulting phrase is best rendered: 'if indeed' or 'if as is the case.' This is not a hypothetical condition but a condition grounded in reality, presupposing the state of affairs it describes.

The conjunction εἴπερ (eiper) thus makes two simultaneous presuppositions: first, that maturity adjustment to the justice of God is attainable and real; and second, that such maturity brings with it the imputation of undeserved suffering. The use of eiper rather than the simple εἰ (ei) signals that the author regards the condition as already obtaining for those who have advanced to maturity.

II. The Compound Verb συμπάσχω — To Suffer with Maturity Status

The verb rendered 'suffer with' in standard translations is the compound συμπάσχω (sumpascho), formed from the preposition σύν (sun, 'with' or 'together with') and πάσχω (pascho, 'to suffer'). Plato used this verb to mean 'to suffer at the same time' or 'to suffer the same as,' but with no implication of identical degree or content. The classical background of the term is indispensable for accurate exegesis here.

The standard translations render this phrase 'if we suffer with him,' and print him in italics — indicating that the pronoun is a translatorial supplement, not present in the Greek text. Neither the noun Χριστός (Christos) nor the intensive pronoun αὐτός (autos), which serves as the third person personal pronoun in Koine Greek, appears in this clause. The insertion of 'him' by translators, while intuitively appealing, produces a theological distortion by suggesting a parallelism between the believer's suffering and the sufferings of Christ on the cross — a parallelism the text does not support and sound exegesis must reject.

A. The Uniqueness of Christ's Suffering

The sufferings of Christ on the cross were absolutely unique — unique as the person who endured them. The Lord Jesus Christ, in the status of impeccability, bore the imputed sins of the entire human race and sustained the judgment of divine justice on those sins. No human being participates in that work, replicates it, or extends it. Ascetic traditions and certain strands of mystical theology have read into συμπάσχω a common participation of Christ and the believer in a shared suffering — this reading has no grammatical or theological basis.

The sufferings of the mature believer cannot be compared with the sufferings of the unique God-man in any degree, category, or content. The believer does not complete what is lacking in Christ's suffering; the believer does not co-redeem; the believer does not enter into the atoning work of the cross through voluntary suffering. Philippians 1:29 draws the correct distinction: 'because it has been granted to you, for Christ's sake, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for his sake.' Suffering for the sake of Christ is categorically different from suffering with Christ in the sense of shared atoning work.

B. The Correct Referent — Maturity Status

If the pronoun 'him' is not in the text and the context is not the cross, what does συμπάσχω denote? The compound verb, read in its Platonic and Koine context, denotes suffering in the same status or at the same time as another who suffers — but not to the same degree or with the same content. The referent is the status of maturity itself. The mature believer suffers in the status of maturity, just as Christ suffered in the status of impeccability. The parallel is one of structural analogy, not ontological identity.

The corrected translation of this phrase is therefore: if indeed we suffer with maturity status. The preposition σύν (sun) points not to a person but to a condition — the condition of maximum doctrine resident in the soul, producing capacity for life, capacity for blessing, and capacity for suffering.

C. Morphological Analysis of συμπάσχω

The verb appears in the present active indicative. The present tense is a retroactive progressive present, denoting attainment of maturity in the past and the continuation of that maturity in the present. Maturity is not a momentary state; it is a status sustained by ongoing intake of Bible doctrine. The active voice indicates that mature believers produce the action of the verb — they suffer as the outworking of their maturity. The indicative mood is the declarative indicative of supposition from the viewpoint of reality: the condition is presumed actual from the standpoint of those who have made maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

III. Deserved and Undeserved Suffering

The justice of God is the common source of both blessing and cursing in the believer's life. All divine blessing is imputed through the justice of God to its divinely prepared home — the divine righteousness imputed at salvation. All divine discipline is likewise administered through the justice of God. This means that suffering, too, has two categories: deserved and undeserved.

Deserved suffering is the expected consequence of sin, negative volition, reversionism, and sustained rejection of Bible doctrine. It is the punitive expression of divine justice — divine discipline in its various stages, culminating in the sin unto death. The reversionist goes from deserved suffering under divine discipline to ultimate sanctification in a resurrection body, but his eternal inheritance is diminished by the years he spent outside the fellowship and advance of the spiritual life.

Undeserved suffering is categorically different. It is not punishment. It is not the consequence of failure. It is an imputation from the justice of God to the mature believer — an imputation just as real as the imputation of blessing. The mature believer who receives undeserved suffering has not brought it upon himself by sin or moral failure; he receives it precisely because he has capacity to handle it without succumbing to mental attitude sins such as bitterness, jealousy, self-pity, vindictiveness, or implacability.

A. Undeserved Suffering as Divine Imputation

Along with the imputation of blessing, the justice of God imputes undeserved suffering to the mature believer. This is not incidental; it is structural. Undeserved suffering is God's down payment on greater eternal blessing. It is the justice of God communicating in time what is reserved in eternity — reward and blessing beyond all of ultimate sanctification, reserved for those who advanced to maturity and endured suffering without complaint, self-pity, or the loss of inner happiness.

The mature believer, when confronted with a category of suffering that would ordinarily produce shock, horror, or collapse in the immature believer, responds with a relaxed mental attitude, undisturbed inner happiness, and the capacity to think clearly under maximum pressure. This is not stoicism; it is the fruit of doctrine resident in the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Where the immature believer falls into mental attitude sins, the mature believer replaces those sins with the perfect tranquility that comes from occupation with Christ.

B. The Implication for Romans 8:18–36

This transitional clause — 'if indeed we suffer with maturity status' — sets the scope for the entire paragraph of Romans 8:18–30 and for the climactic statement of Romans 8:36. The paragraph is addressed to mature believers. Romans 8:28, Romans 8:32, Romans 8:36, and Romans 8:38–39 are not promises for the immature or for believers in general — they are the inheritance of those who have cracked the maturity barrier and receive undeserved suffering as a category of blessing from the justice of God.

Romans 8:36 quotes Psalm 44:22: 'For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.' The verb rendered 'regarded' or 'accounted' is the Greek λογίζομαι (logizomai), the standard term for imputation. The correct rendering is 'we have been imputed as sheep for slaughter.' This is the high-water mark of the paragraph — the imputation of martyrdom from the justice of God to a mature believer whose undeserved suffering has been elevated to its maximum expression. This imputation does not occur frequently in history; it is reserved for those whose capacity for life and suffering has been fully developed through sustained doctrine intake and maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

IV. The Final Clause — συνδοξάζω

The second half of the transitional sentence introduces the purpose clause: 'that also we might be glorified with Christ.' The conjunction ἵνα (hina) with the subjunctive introduces a final clause denoting objective, purpose, aim, or goal. The adjunctive use of καί (kai) functions adverbially, meaning 'also.' The verb is the aorist passive subjunctive of the compound συνδοξάζω (sundoxazo), meaning 'to be glorified together with,' 'to share in another's glory,' or 'to be fellow-glorified ones.'

The aorist tense is a culminating aorist. It views the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ in its entirety, regarding it from the standpoint of its existing results. The fact that Christ has been glorified means that the way is now open for any member of the royal family of God to share in His glory. The passive voice indicates that the believer receives the action of the verb — glorification is not achieved but received, imputed from the justice of God in eternity, above and beyond ultimate sanctification. The subjunctive mood is the potential subjunctive, indicating that the glorification depends on the believer's attainment of maturity adjustment to the justice of God in time.

The full arc is therefore: undeserved suffering in maturity in time → glorification with Christ in eternity. This is the pattern of Romans 8:18–30. The mature believer who endures undeserved suffering without succumbing to mental attitude sins — who remains relaxed, occupied with Christ, thinking clearly under maximum pressure — accumulates reward and blessing in eternity that exceeds what any form of earthly comfort or human recognition could provide. Undeserved suffering is not a problem to be solved; it is a privilege to be recognized and endured with capacity.

V. Structural Principles from the Transitional Clause

The following principles emerge from the exegesis of this transitional clause and govern the interpretation of the entire paragraph to follow.

First, the undeserved suffering of Christ was in the status of impeccability. The undeserved suffering of the born-again believer is in the status of maturity. These two statuses are structurally analogous but ontologically distinct. Christ was impeccable; the mature believer is not. The difference includes imputed sin, the old sin nature, the function of sin, human good, and evil. The undeserved suffering of the impeccable Lord Jesus Christ is unique in every respect.

Second, the mature believer's capacity for life has two sides: the capacity to receive and enjoy imputed blessing, and the capacity to endure and profit from imputed suffering. Both derive from the same source — maximum doctrine resident in the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Maturity adjustment to the justice of God is the prerequisite for both.

Third, undeserved suffering as a mature believer is itself a form of blessing. The justice of God does not impute what a believer cannot handle. The imputation of undeserved suffering is the justice of God's announcement in time that great reward is prepared in eternity. Romans 8:28 — 'all things work together for good' — is not a general comfort for all believers in any circumstance; it is a specific promise to the mature believer whose undeserved suffering is working toward an eternal outcome that no earthly measure can quantify.

Fourth, being a mature believer never implies cessation of sin. The mature believer continues to sin as long as he lives in the body. The believer who fails to use rebound — the naming of known sins to God in accordance with 1 John 1:9 — and remains in a state of sustained carnality is not functioning as a mature believer regardless of how much doctrine he has heard. Maturity requires both the accumulation of doctrine and the maintenance of fellowship through consistent rebound. The εἴπερ presupposes both.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ten

1. The transitional clause of Romans 8:17b sets the scope for 8:18–30. Both sentences of verse 17 summarize the preceding argument; the second sentence introduces the new paragraph on the arc from suffering to glorification. The entire paragraph addresses mature believers.

2. The word εἴπερ (eiper) presupposes maturity adjustment to the justice of God. It is not a simple conditional but an intensive particle assuming the condition as real. Two things are presupposed: maximum doctrine resident in the soul producing capacity for blessing, and the accompanying imputation of undeserved suffering from the justice of God.

3. The pronoun 'him' in standard translations is not in the Greek text. Neither Christos nor autos appears in this clause. The insertion of 'him' by translators implies a false parallelism between the believer's suffering and the atoning sufferings of Christ on the cross. The text warrants no such parallelism.

4. The compound verb συμπάσχω (sumpascho) denotes suffering in the status of maturity. Just as Christ suffered in the status of impeccability, the mature believer suffers in the status of maturity. The analogy is structural, not ontological. The believer does not participate in or extend the unique sufferings of the cross in any degree.

5. Undeserved suffering is an imputation from the justice of God, not a consequence of failure. It is categorically distinct from deserved suffering, which is divine discipline. Undeserved suffering is given because the mature believer has the capacity to endure it without mental attitude sins — with inner happiness, relaxed mental attitude, and undisturbed occupation with Christ.

6. Undeserved suffering is God's down payment on eternal reward. All undeserved suffering received by a mature believer is the justice of God's announcement in time of greater blessing and reward in eternity. The suffering is not incidental but structural — it is itself a category of blessing imputed to the believer's divine righteousness, the divinely prepared home for all divine imputation.

7. The compound verb συνδοξάζω (sundoxazo) denotes being glorified together with Christ. The aorist passive subjunctive is a culminating aorist viewing Christ's glorification from the standpoint of its existing results. The subjunctive mood is potential, depending on the believer's attainment of maturity in time. The passive voice confirms that glorification is received, not achieved.

8. Romans 8:28, 8:32, 8:36, and 8:38–39 are addressed to mature believers. These verses are not general promises available to any believer in any circumstance. They describe the specific inheritance of those who have cracked the maturity barrier and receive undeserved suffering as a blessing from the justice of God.

9. Maturity never means cessation of sin; it means the capacity to handle maximum pressure without mental attitude sins. The retroactive progressive present tense of sumpascho indicates that maturity is a sustained status, not a momentary attainment. The believer who maintains fellowship through rebound and continues daily doctrine intake remains in the status that qualifies him to receive the imputation of undeserved suffering as blessing.

10. The imputation of martyrdom is the highest expression of undeserved suffering in time. Romans 8:36 — 'we have been imputed as sheep for slaughter' — represents the culminating point of the paragraph. Martyrdom, properly defined as an imputation from the justice of God to a mature believer, is not a painful catastrophe but the most glorious transition from time to eternity, carrying with it the announcement of maximum eternal reward.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
eiper εἴπερ eiper — if indeed, if as is the case Compound conditional conjunction: ei (first-class condition with indicative) + per (intensive particle). Introduces a condition presupposed as real from the viewpoint of the speaker. Rendered "if indeed" or "if as is supposed."
sumpascho συμπάσχω sumpascho — to suffer together with, to suffer in the same status Compound verb: sun (with, together) + pascho (to suffer). Used by Plato to mean "to suffer at the same time" but not necessarily to the same degree or with the same content. In Romans 8:17, denotes suffering in the status of maturity, structurally analogous to Christ's suffering in the status of impeccability.
sundoxazo συνδοξάζω sundoxazo — to be glorified together with, to share in another's glory Compound verb: sun (with, together) + doxazo (to glorify). Aorist passive subjunctive in Romans 8:17. The aorist is culminating, viewing Christ's glorification from the standpoint of its existing results. The passive voice confirms glorification is received by imputation, not achieved by effort.
hina ἵνα hina — in order that, so that Conjunction introducing a final clause of purpose, aim, or objective. Takes the subjunctive mood. In Romans 8:17, introduces the purpose of undeserved suffering in maturity: glorification with Christ in eternity.
logizomai λογίζομαι logizomai — to reckon, to impute, to credit to one's account The standard New Testament term for imputation. In Romans 8:36 (quoting Psalm 44:22), rendered "regarded" or "accounted" in standard translations. The precise meaning is "we have been imputed as sheep for slaughter" — denoting the imputation of martyrdom from the justice of God to the mature believer.
Maturity adjustment maturity adjustment to the justice of God The progressive stage of adjustment to the justice of God achieved through daily intake of Bible doctrine over time, resulting in maximum doctrine resident in the soul and spirit. Produces capacity for blessing and capacity for undeserved suffering. Distinguished from salvation adjustment (instantaneous, at the moment of faith) and rebound adjustment (instantaneous, repeated as needed by 1 John 1:9).
Undeserved suffering undeserved suffering Suffering imputed by the justice of God to the mature believer as a category of blessing, not as divine discipline. It is given because the mature believer has the capacity to endure it without mental attitude sins. Distinguished from deserved suffering, which is divine discipline for sin and negative volition. Undeserved suffering is God's down payment on greater eternal reward.
Imputation of martyrdom imputation of martyrdom The highest category of undeserved suffering — the imputation from the justice of God to an ultra-supergrace believer of a death by martyrdom. Not a consequence of failure or of historical circumstance alone, but a direct imputation announcing maximum eternal reward. Distinguished from the sin unto death, which is the terminal divine discipline for sustained reversionism.

Chapter Three Hundred Eleven

Romans 8:18 — The Sufferings of the Present Time and the Glory to Come; Undeserved Suffering, Maturity Adjustment, and the Doctrine of Imputation

Romans 8:18 “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: For I conclude that the sufferings of the present period of time are not comparable to the glory which is destined to be revealed in us.

Romans 8:17 brought us to the threshold of a new paragraph with its transitional clause: "if indeed we suffer with maturity status, that also we might be glorified with Christ." Verse 18 opens the extended passage running through verse 30, in which the apostle Paul sets the undeserved suffering of the mature believer within the frame of the eternal glory that is destined to follow it. The paragraph surveys three categories of present suffering, described through three groans — the groan of nature (vv. 19–22), the groan of the mature believer (vv. 23–25), and the groan of the Holy Spirit (vv. 26–27) — and then concludes with the promise to the mature believer in verse 28 and the declaration of glory in verses 29–30. This chapter takes up the exegesis of verse 18 and establishes the doctrinal foundations required for the full passage.

I. Review of Principles from Romans 8:17

Before advancing to verse 18, the following principles drawn from the study of verse 17 require consolidation.

1. The undeserved suffering of Christ was in the status of impeccability. The undeserved suffering of the born-again believer is in the status of maturity. For Christ, impeccability made undeserved suffering the only possibility. For the mature believer, undeserved suffering is the distinctive mark of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

2. There is a vast difference between the impeccability of Christ and the maturity of the believer. That difference includes imputed sin, the old sin nature (OSN), the function of the OSN trends, personal sin, evil, and human good — none of which belonged to Christ.

3. The undeserved suffering of the impeccable Lord Jesus Christ was unique and unrepeatable. The undeserved suffering of the mature believer is designed to demonstrate that the same capacity produced by doctrine that provides capacity for blessing also provides capacity for suffering.

4. The undeserved suffering of the mature believer contributes to reward and blessing in phase three. In this connection, the highest honor afforded any believer in time is the imputation of martyrdom — a category that must be distinguished from the sin unto death, which is divine discipline terminating in physical death for sustained reversionism.

5. Just as the blessing imputed from the justice of God is the basis for blessing beyond all ultimate sanctification in eternity, so undeserved suffering from the justice of God to the mature believer is the basis for reward beyond all ultimate sanctification.

6. Maturity status in time is the result of the filling of the Holy Spirit plus maximum doctrine resident in the soul. It is the place of occupation with Christ, producing capacity for life.

7. Occupation with Christ in blessing means capacity for that blessing. Occupation with Christ in undeserved suffering means capacity for that suffering. Capacity for blessing and capacity for suffering are two faces of the same doctrinal coin.

8. Undeserved suffering of the mature believer anticipates the glorious inheritance of the future. Every instance of undeserved suffering is God's guarantee — a down payment and reminder — of the great blessing and reward that awaits the mature believer for all eternity.

II. The Exegesis of Romans 8:18

A. The Conjunctive Particle gar

Verse 18 opens with the explanatory use of the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ). This particle connects verse 18 to the transitional clause of verse 17 and introduces the doctrinal grounds for the comparison that follows. The genius of the apostle Paul is visible precisely in his use of connective and conjunctive particles. Paul possessed not only the capacity for superior theological thought but the ability to connect that thought to other superior thoughts, so that the entire structure of the Christian way of life becomes apparent through the architecture of his sentences. The use of these particles is an indispensable factor in the interpretation of the Pauline epistles.

B. The Verb logizomai

The particle is followed by the present middle indicative of the verb logizomai (λογίζομαι), which is one of the most frequently mistranslated verbs in the New Testament. The key to its correct translation lies in identifying the subject.

When God is the subject, logizomai means to impute — to credit or reckon to someone's account. When man is the subject, it means to conclude — to draw a reasoned conclusion from available facts. This distinction is not arbitrary. The verb traces to Attic and Classical Greek, where it denoted deliberation on the basis of facts followed by conclusions drawn from logic. It was the characteristic verb of non-emotional, rational thought — the deliberative mode of the great philosophers.

The verb therefore emphasizes a rational course of thought, free from emotion, and therefore able to utilize the facts as they are. When facts are tangled with emotion, erroneous conclusions follow inevitably. Emotions were not designed for the purpose of drawing conclusions. Emotions were designed to appreciate conclusions already reached by thought. Emotion does not originate thought; emotion can only respond to thought. The correct sequence is: thought first, then emotion as the appropriate response. When that order is reversed — when emotion precedes and drives thought — the result is paralysis of the reasoning process and the production of false conclusions.

When God is the subject, logizomai is rendered impute because God performed all thinking in eternity past from the vantage point of omniscience. God acts on the basis of facts — His own perfect knowledge — and therefore His reckoning is imputation. The great imputations that structure the doctrine of grace are the product of divine thinking: the imputation of life to the soul, the imputation of Adam's sin to the genetically formed old sin nature, the imputation of human sin to Christ on the cross, the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation, and the real imputations of blessing in time and in eternity.

Here in verse 18, Paul is the human author and the subject. The verb therefore means to conclude from reasoned thought. The present tense is a retroactive progressive present, denoting a conclusion begun in the past and continuing into the present. The middle voice is that of a deponent verb — middle in form but active in meaning — indicating that Paul as the human author produces the action through his cognizance of doctrine. The combination of natural genius and maximum doctrine resident in the soul is an unbeatable combination; both were present in the apostle Paul. The indicative mood is declarative, expressing a dogmatic conclusion drawn from doctrine.

C. The Content Clause — hoti

The conjunction hoti (ὅτι) follows, replacing the ecstatical infinitive in order to give the content of a conclusion drawn from a correct system of thought. It introduces the substance of what Paul concludes.

D. The Sufferings — pathemata

The subject of the content clause is the nominative plural of pathēma (πάθημα), meaning suffering, affliction, or passion. The nominative plural pathēmata (παθήματα) is translated the sufferings. The article is generic, representing a special category of suffering: undeserved suffering for the purpose of blessing, and specifically undeserved suffering that leads to glory. This is not suffering in general, and it is not the suffering of divine discipline. It is a distinct category belonging to the mature believer.

E. The Present Time — tou nun kairou

The phrase tou nun kairou (τοῦ νῦν καιροῦ) uses the genitive of time singular from the noun kairos (καιρός), which refers both to a point of time and to a period of time. Here it refers to a period of time — specifically, the period of maturity adjustment to the justice of God. This is the period that begins when the believer cracks the maturity barrier and terminates with dying grace. The adverb nun (νῦν) — now — places the believer in phase two and brings him face to face with all of the great imputations that constitute the outline of the passage and the skeleton of the Christian life.

Imputation is the skeleton of the Christian way of life. Once the imputations are properly understood, the entire story of grace becomes visible. The imputations are characterized by one consistent pattern: God gives something to God so that God is not compromised, and God gives something to God so that man cannot help God. God needs no assistance, and it is a form of theological confusion to suggest otherwise. Even the legitimate commands of the Christian life — prayer, witnessing, production — have no causal relationship to blessing. Production is the function of the believer's ambassadorship, not the source of divine blessing. Blessing flows exclusively through imputation, because God can only bless what has an affinity with His own perfect righteousness.

F. The Negative — ouk axios

Following the ellipsis that must supply the present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί, to be), we have the negative adverb ouk (οὐκ), which denies the reality of an alleged fact, and the predicate adjective axios (ἄξιος), meaning worthy of or comparable to. The correct translation is: are not comparable to, not the common rendering are not worth comparing with. The phrase to be compared does not appear in the original text; it was inserted by translators attempting to clarify an ellipsis.

G. Face to Face with the Glory — pros tēn doxan

The prepositional phrase pros tēn doxan (πρὸς τὴν δόξαν) uses pros with the accusative singular of doxa (δόξα), meaning glory. The preposition pros with the accusative indicates face-to-face relationship or direct comparison. The correct translation is therefore: face to face with the glory, rather than simply with the glory. The glory in view refers to the eternal blessings, rewards, and inheritance that belong to the mature believer — the content of phase three. These are the blessings above and beyond ultimate sanctification that belong exclusively to the mature believer and that no amount of human production, self-denial, or religious effort can procure.

H. Destined to Be Revealed — mellousēs apokalyphthēnai

The present active participle of mellō (μέλλω) expresses imminence or destiny: to be about to, to be destined. Used here as a futuristic present, it denotes an event not yet occurring but regarded as so certain in the mind of the speaker that it is contemplated as already occurring. The same construction appears later in chapter 8 with reference to present things and future things that are unable to separate the believer from the love of God. The active voice indicates that the glory itself — the rewards and blessings of eternity from the justice of God — produces the action. The participle is circumstantial.

This is followed by the aorist passive infinitive of apokalyptō (ἀποκαλύπτω), meaning to be revealed or to be uncovered. The aorist tense is gnomic — expressing an absolute certainty. The passive voice indicates that the mature believer receives the action of the verb: the reception of great blessing and reward in eternity. The infinitive is the infinitive of actual result.

The prepositional phrase eis hēmas (εἰς ἡμᾶς), using eis with the accusative plural of egō (ἐγώ), is translated in us or to us. Part of the plan of God for the mature believer is reward and blessing in eternity above and beyond all ultimate sanctification — that is, above and beyond the resurrection body itself. The resurrection body belongs to every believer. The rewards and blessings of eternity above and beyond the resurrection body belong only to the mature believer.

III. The Corrected Translation of Romans 8:18

For I conclude that the sufferings of the present period of time — that is, maturity adjustment to the justice of God — are not comparable to the glory which is destined to be revealed in us.

IV. The Analytical Outline of Romans 8:18–30

Verse 18 contains the outline of the entire paragraph, verses 18 through 30. Two controlling thoughts emerge from the verse:

First: The sufferings of the present time — developed in verses 19 through 27.

Second: The glory which is destined to be revealed in us — developed in verses 28 through 30.

The passage will be traced through the following outline:

A. The groan of nature (vv. 19–22)B. The groan of the mature believer (vv. 23–25)C. The groan of the Holy Spirit — an anthropopathism (vv. 26–27)D. The promise to the mature believer (v. 28)E. The glory destined to be revealed in us (vv. 29–30)

V. Three Foundational Principles for the Passage

Before proceeding verse by verse through the paragraph, three principles must be firmly in view.

First: There is no comparison between the sufferings of the mature believer and the rewards and blessings awaiting that believer in eternity. The two are beyond comparison. They share only one point of analogy: intensity. The suffering is intense. The blessing for all eternity is equally intense — but in a categorically different sphere of existence.

Second: No suffering in maturity is greater than the capacity produced by doctrine resident in the soul through the filling of the Holy Spirit. And no suffering in maturity is greater than the rewards and blessings of surpassing grace in eternity.

Third: Time is a drop in the bucket compared to eternity. Suffering in time cannot be compared to blessing in eternity. The undeserved suffering of the mature believer is God removing the normal human props — the usual supports that people lean on in times of disaster — so that the believer is left in a situation with no human solution, only doctrinal capacity. When that moment arrives, the believer is in the midst of some of his greatest blessings.

VI. The Doctrine of Suffering — Survey

The passage ahead requires careful groundwork in the doctrine of suffering. What follows is a systematic survey of the categories of suffering applicable to both believers and unbelievers, followed by the categories specific to Christian suffering.

A. General Causes of Suffering Common to All Persons

These categories of suffering are not unique to believers. Believers and unbelievers alike experience them.

1. Suffering from loss. This includes loss of health, wealth, property, money, loved ones, or anything of value to the one who suffers. Loss is the most universal category of human suffering.

2. Suffering from people. This suffering may be real or imagined — but whether it is real or imagined, it is genuine suffering for the one experiencing it. It includes gossip, ostracism, persecution, violence, crime, and on a broad scale, warfare.

3. Suffering from privation. Related to loss but distinct from it. Privation includes hunger, thirst, exposure to cold or heat, storm, earthquake, and other natural disasters, as well as accidents. The defining characteristic is deprivation of the normal conditions of life.

4. Suffering from the administration of law. Whether justly or unjustly applied, apprehension, trial, and sentencing constitute genuine suffering.

5. Social suffering. This is distinct from suffering caused by specific persons and from privation. It arises from loneliness, boredom, neglect, ostracism, and the absence of meaningful human contact or approval.

6. Mental suffering. Pressure applied to the mentality of the soul. This may arise from mental sins such as pride, arrogance, jealousy, hatred, bitterness, vindictiveness, implacability, or guilt complex. It may also arise from organic neurological conditions. Whatever its origin, mental suffering is one of the most pervasive categories of human affliction.

7. Suffering from rejection of authority. Failure in the sphere of authority relationships — marital, vocational, civic, and military — produces extensive suffering. Failure in adulthood because of the rejection of authority in childhood is a pattern with deep and well-documented consequences. This category includes suffering from failed marriage, loss of employment, dishonorable discharge, expulsion from institutions, and the removal of citizenship or standing.

8. Suffering from reversionism. This is the suffering that comes from reaping what one sows. Unbeliever reversionism is documented in the early chapters of Romans. Believer reversionism produces its own distinctive pattern of suffering, treated under the categories of divine discipline.

B. Basic Categories of Suffering by Time Frame

Suffering may be classified by its temporal location:

A. Suffering in time. Both believers and unbelievers suffer in time. The unbeliever suffers because of rejection of the laws of divine establishment or because of self-induced misery arising from reversionism under the influence of evil. The believer's suffering in time is treated under point four below.

B. Suffering in eternity. For the unbeliever, this means the lake of fire forever. For the believer, there is no suffering in eternity — Revelation 21:4 is explicit on this point. This includes the absence of regrets. The believer will carry no remorse into eternity for failures in time. All regrets belong to time. All eternity is blessing.

C. The Premise of Christian Suffering

Four foundational premises govern Christian suffering specifically:

1. All suffering for the believer is designed for blessing. This is the governing principle of Christian suffering — 1 Peter 1:7–8; 1 Peter 4:13.

2. The exception to that principle is divine discipline — Hebrews 12:6. Not all suffering is undeserved. Disciplinary suffering is real and must be distinguished from undeserved suffering.

3. The exception is removed under the principle of rebound — 1 Corinthians 11:31. When the believer names known sins to God (1 John 1:9), fellowship is restored and the divine discipline is lifted.

4. When rebound occurs, cursing is turned to blessing — Romans 8:28. Carnality is the failure of the believer to apply rebound. Carnality, sustained, eventuates in reversionism. Rebound recovery applies to the reversionist as well as to the carnal believer.

D. Categories of Christian Suffering: Deserved and Undeserved

Christian suffering divides into two basic categories: deserved suffering and undeserved suffering.

Deserved suffering — that is, suffering the believer has brought upon himself through his own failures — includes the following sub-categories:

1. Suffering from divine discipline for carnality — Hebrews 12:6; Psalm 38; the book of Ecclesiastes, which addresses reversionism specifically.

2. Suffering by association. When a believer has a sustained relationship with someone under divine discipline, that association carries the potential for sharing in the discipline. This is not undeserved suffering; it is a consequence of the association chosen. The remedy in most cases is disassociation. The one inescapable exception to disassociation is the marriage relationship — 1 Corinthians 12:26; Romans 14:7; 1 Samuel 21.

3. Suffering caused by wrong priorities. A disordered scale of values produces its own suffering. Solomon in Ecclesiastes and Song of Solomon is the classical illustration of the consequences of wrong priorities.

4. Suffering from a guilt complex. Auto-torture — inflicting suffering upon oneself through an unresolved guilt complex — is among the most destructive and unnecessary forms of suffering. It is unnecessary because the doctrine of rebound resolves the legitimate occasion for guilt immediately. Relevant passages include 1 Timothy 1:5–6, 19–20; 1 Timothy 3:9; 1 Timothy 4:1–2; Titus 1:15.

5. Suffering from national discipline. A nation under divine discipline imposes suffering on its citizens whether or not any individual citizen is personally guilty. This suffering is classified under deserved suffering because it involves not only association but potentially also the believer's own failures in citizenship and respect for legitimate governmental authority — Leviticus 26; Isaiah 33; Isaiah 59; the book of Hosea.

6. Suffering from rejection of the principle of right-man/right-woman — Ezekiel 16; Ezekiel 23; Jeremiah 12:7; Jeremiah 15:7–12, 17–18.

7. Suffering from failure to isolate sin. Many patterns of destructive behavior are built upon a sin that was never isolated and dealt with through rebound. Each subsequent sin is lit from the one before it — chain sin — Hebrews 12:15.

8. Suffering from temporary loss of grace orientation.

9. Suffering from war or revolution.

10. Suffering from reversionism — the first major category of deserved suffering, which includes the full harvest of what was sown in sustained carnality and departure from doctrine.

The second major category — undeserved suffering, or suffering for blessing — will be examined in detail as the exegesis of verses 19 through 27 proceeds.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eleven

1. Romans 8:18 is a transitional verse establishing the outline of vv. 18–30. It presents two controlling thoughts: the sufferings of the present period of time (vv. 19–27) and the glory destined to be revealed in us (vv. 28–30). The verse governs the entire paragraph.

2. The verb logizomai in verse 18 means to conclude from rational, non-emotional thought. When man is the subject, it denotes a reasoned conclusion drawn from facts. Emotion is not a tool of cognition; it is the appropriate response to conclusions already reached by thought. Doctrine must precede and govern all conclusions about suffering, glory, and the Christian way of life.

3. The present time (tou nun kairou) in verse 18 refers specifically to the period of maturity adjustment to the justice of God. It is not a reference to the Christian life in general. The comparison Paul draws applies to the mature believer's undeserved suffering, not to all suffering experienced by all believers at all stages of spiritual development.

4. The glory is destined to be revealed — it is certain beyond all contingency. The futuristic present participle of mellō indicates that the eternal rewards and blessings of phase three are so certain in the plan of God that they may be contemplated as already occurring. The aorist passive infinitive of apokalyptō confirms that the reception of this glory is an absolute certainty for every mature believer.

5. The phrase pros tēn doxan means face to face with the glory, not merely with the glory. The preposition pros with the accusative indicates direct, face-to-face relationship. The glory of phase three stands in direct confrontation with the sufferings of phase two, and the comparison is entirely in favor of the glory.

6. Imputation is the skeleton of the Christian way of life. The imputations — not production, sacrifice, religious activity, or moral effort — constitute the structure through which all divine blessing flows. God can only bless what has an affinity with His own perfect righteousness. Production is the function of the believer's royal ambassadorship; it is not the basis of blessing from God.

7. The doctrine of suffering must be mastered before verses 19–27 can be properly interpreted. The three groans of the passage — nature, the mature believer, and the Holy Spirit — each presuppose a thorough grasp of the distinction between deserved and undeserved suffering, and the further distinction between the tests of early spiritual growth and the sustained undeserved suffering that characterizes confirmed maturity.

8. The mature believer never loses blessing through undeserved suffering — the suffering enhances it. Adversity does not cancel the blessing of the mature believer. Doctrine resident in the soul provides capacity both for the prosperity of phase two blessing and for the most intense suffering that God can provide as a demonstration of His wisdom and grace in the angelic conflict.

9. There will be no regrets in eternity for any believer. Revelation 21:4 is absolute. Whatever failures occurred in time, the believer carries no remorse into eternity. All regrets belong to time. This truth is distorted whenever a speaker implies that believers will suffer in eternity because of sins committed or works omitted in time.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
logizomai λογίζομαι logizomai — to reckon, impute, conclude Present middle indicative in Romans 8:18. When God is the subject: to impute — to credit to an account on the basis of omniscient thinking. When man is the subject: to conclude — to draw a reasoned, non-emotional conclusion from available facts. Traces to Attic Greek usage for deliberative, logical thought.
gar γάρ gar — for, because (explanatory/causal conjunction) Post-positive conjunctive particle used here in its explanatory force. Connects verse 18 to the transitional clause of verse 17 and introduces the doctrinal grounds for Paul's comparison of present suffering to eternal glory.
pathēma πάθημα pathēma (pl. pathēmata) — suffering, affliction, passion Nominative plural pathēmata in Romans 8:18. The generic article marks a special category: undeserved suffering for the purpose of blessing and glory. Distinguished from suffering under divine discipline.
kairos καιρός kairos — a point of time; a period of time Genitive of time singular in Romans 8:18. Refers here to the period of maturity adjustment to the justice of God — beginning when the believer cracks the maturity barrier and terminating with dying grace.
axios ἄξιος axios — worthy, comparable, equivalent in weight Predicate adjective in Romans 8:18. With the negative ouk: not comparable to. The imagery derives from weighing on a balance — the sufferings of phase two do not balance, much less outweigh, the glory of phase three.
doxa δόξα doxa — glory, honor, splendor, radiance Accusative singular in the phrase pros tēn doxan in Romans 8:18. Denotes an event not yet occurring but so certain in divine purpose that it is contemplated as already occurring. Applied here to the glory that is destined to be revealed in the mature believer.
apokalyptō ἀποκαλύπτω apokalyptō — to reveal, to uncover, to disclose Aorist passive infinitive in Romans 8:18. The aorist is gnomic — expressing absolute certainty. The passive voice indicates that the mature believer receives the action: the revelation and reception of eternal rewards and blessings from the justice of God.
