klētois κλητοῖς klētois — the called ones Dative plural adjective from klētos. In Romans 8:28, introduces the doctrine of election: those called according to the pre-determined plan of God. Sets up the argument of Romans 8:29–30.
prothesis πρόθεσις prothesis — pre-determined plan, purpose Compound noun: pro (before) + thesis (placement, plan). In Romans 8:28, refers to the eternal divine decrees by which God predetermined the sequence of blessing for Church Age believers. The basis of the formula is not human performance but the pre-determined counsel of God.
parthenogenesis παρθενογένεσις parthenogenesis — virgin pregnancy Compound: parthenos (young woman, virgin) + genesis (origin, birth). The technical term for insemination without copulation. The controlling doctrine of the incarnation's biological foundation: God the Holy Spirit provided the twenty-three chromosomes that fertilized the ovum without male copulation, so that the resulting fetus carried no genetically formed old sin nature.
parthenos παρθένος parthenos — young woman; virgin The Greek term carries the primary meaning of 'young woman' and the secondary meaning of 'virgin.' The Hebrew equivalent almah likewise means 'young woman of marriageable age.' The emphasis in Isaiah 7:14 and its New Testament fulfillment falls on the mechanism of the pregnancy — insemination without copulation — rather than on the personal virginal status of the mother.
judicial imputation An imputation that takes place without natural affinity between the imputed attribute and its recipient. In the Y radical, judicial imputation number one is the imputation of personal sins to Christ at the cross; judicial imputation number two is the imputation of divine righteousness (+R) to the believer at salvation. Both operate against the grain of natural affinity and are therefore greater acts of the justice of God than real imputations.
real imputation An imputation that takes place to a natural home or target — an affinity. The imputation of human life to the soul at birth, the imputation of eternal life to regeneration at salvation, and the imputation of blessing in time to +R at maturity are all real imputations. The seventh imputation — eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ — is the culminating real imputation of the formula.
a fortiori a fortiori — from the greater to the less A form of logical argument: if the greater is true, the lesser necessarily follows. In Romans 8:28–30, Paul employs a fortiori with the unique addition of affinity as its antecedent: the greater judicial imputation of +R at salvation creates the affinity that makes the lesser real imputation of blessing in time at maturity both logically certain and structurally prepared.

Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Six

Romans 8:28–29 — The Predetermined Plan: God's Essence and the Five Steps to Glory

Romans 8:28–29 “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: We know in fact that to those who love God — that is, mature believers — that all things work together for the purpose of good, to those who are the called ones according to the predetermined plan. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.

We have arrived at Romans 8:28–29, resuming from the previous chapter's study. Verse 28 established the grand equation governing the believer's life in time and eternity: all things — across three radicals of divine imputation — work together for the purpose of good, which is ultimately the glory of God. Verses 29 and 30 now supply the mechanics: the five steps of the predetermined plan by which that good is achieved. Before examining those steps, the text requires us to understand the One who designed and executes the plan — the God whose essence makes every imputation possible.

I. Review of Romans 8:28 — The Equation of All Things

The corrected translation of Romans 8:28 reads: 'We know in fact that to those who love God — that is, mature believers — that all things work together for the purpose of good, to those who are the called ones according to the predetermined plan.' The 'good' of Romans 8:28 is the glory of God, achieved through a progression of three radicals.

The Three Radicals

The X radical: the imputation of human life to the soul at birth, plus the imputation of Adam's original sin to the old sin nature at birth. These two imputations constitute condemnation and establish the first potential — the potential of salvation. When that potential is joined with cognizance of the gospel, the first hope is produced. The first hope is the confident assurance of salvation. That hope is then replaced by the reality of salvation through the first plus: salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

The Y radical: judicial imputation number one — the imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross — plus judicial imputation number two — the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation. These together equal the second potential, which is the potential for blessing in time. Added to that potential is pertinent doctrine, which produces the second hope: the confident assurance of blessing in time. This hope is reached by the second plus: maturity adjustment to the justice of God, the point at which temporal blessings are imputed.

The Z radical: the imputation of eternal life at salvation, plus the imputation of blessing in time at maturity, equals the third potential — the potential for great reward at the judgment seat of Christ. Added to that potential are pertinent doctrine and the undeserved suffering treated in Romans 8:19–30, yielding the third hope: the confident assurance of great reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ, which is the seventh imputation. This seventh imputation is the 'good' of Romans 8:28 and simultaneously the glory of God.

II. Bridge to Romans 8:29 — The God Who Thinks

The first of the five steps to glory found in Romans 8:29–30 is the step called foreknowledge — literally, thinking. The believer was in the thoughts of God billions of years before birth. This forces a prior question: who and what is this God whose thoughts preceded all of history? Before the five steps can be traced, the nature of the One who designed them must be understood. The text therefore requires an examination of divine essence.

III. The Essence of God

The being of God is called essence. The Greek term is οὐσία (ousia), derived from the verb εἶναι (einai), to be. Ousia means being, inward nature, true substance. The corresponding Hebrew concept appears in the divine name rendered as the Tetragrammaton — the verb to be doubled: I am, I am — which conveys not merely being but absolute and eternal being. Essence designates the existence of God, the sum total of all His attributes and qualities.

God has always existed. There never was a time when God did not exist. He is the pre-existent, pre-eternal One who has never ceased to exist and who has not changed through the variations of history. Human beings came into existence at a point in time and are accustomed to thinking in terms of change. God is not subject to change. Approaching the study of divine essence requires setting aside all predetermined human conceptions of what a person must be.

A. God Is One — Uniqueness, Not Numerical Singularity

Scripture declares that God is one. The word 'one' in this context does not mean numerical singularity but absolute uniqueness. The Hebrew term אֱלֹהִים (Elohim) carries a plural suffix, indicating that three persons share the one divine essence. The claim that this plural is merely a 'plural of majesty' arose as a later attempt to avoid the implication of three persons in the Godhead. The text does not support that evasion.

God is one in the sense that the attributes of each person in the Trinity are co-equal and co-eternal — identical to the attributes of the others. God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit each possess the same sovereignty, the same love, the same integrity, the same eternal life, the same omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, immutability, and veracity. They have identical attributes without variation. The wonders and glory of God refer to His essence and character, all of which reside equally in each of the three persons.

The designations Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are nomenclature derived from how each person functions in relation to the human race within the plan of God, not ontological rankings. Each is a separate person with identical essence. This is documented in, among other passages, Isaiah 48:16; John 10:30 compared with Psalm 110:1; 2 Corinthians 13:14; and 1 Peter 1:2.

B. Divine Personality

Man's personality is grounded in the essence of the soul. The soul contains self-consciousness — awareness of one's own existence and the capacity to relate that existence to life and ultimately to God. It contains mentality, with initial processing of thought in the left lobe and transfer into the right lobe, where a frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary, categorical storage, and norms and standards are developed. It contains volition — the free will with its positive and negative poles — and it contains emotion, which responds to the norms and standards resident in the right lobe but has no independent thought content.

God also has personality, but at an absolute and infinite level. God recognizes Himself to be a person; He has self-consciousness and self-determination. He is never irrational. He does not have the anthropopathic characteristics ascribed to Him in Scripture — those are accommodations to man's frame of reference so that man can understand divine policy. What God has is not emotion but absolute perfection of thought, will, and action. Almost every page of Scripture asserts and teaches the personality of God: He designs and executes, He speaks in the first person singular, He thinks and decides.

C. The Two Categories of Divine Attributes

The attributes of God fall into two categories. The first category is the absolute attributes: those that are intrinsic, primary, and incommunicable — belonging to God entirely apart from any relationship to creation. The second category is the relative attributes: those that are secondary and communicable — understood in relation to creation, time, space, and moral beings.

IV. The Absolute Attributes of God

A. Spirituality — Life and Personality

God is immaterial. This is taught in John 4:24. In contrast to all living creatures, who are both material and immaterial, God is entirely immaterial. There is no body, no physical substance — God is spirit. Under the attribute of spirituality, two components are primary.

First, God is life. God does not merely possess life as creatures possess it — He lives absolutely and eternally. All life originates from Him, but the universe is not an extension of Him, as pantheism contends. God's life is eternal life: it always had existence and never began. It is this eternal life that God offers to mankind through the Y radical — specifically through judicial imputation number one, by which personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross, clearing the way for judicial imputation number two, the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation. Receiving divine righteousness establishes the grace pipeline through which all subsequent blessing flows. This is why the new birth is necessary: physical birth produces a soul bearing human life condemned by Adam's original sin; spiritual birth produces regeneration, a divinely prepared home for eternal life imputed by the justice of God.

Second, God has personality. Exodus 3:14 specifies that God is a person. Personality involves both self-consciousness and self-determination. God is self-conscious — He has always known Himself and His own existence. God has self-determination — He always acts consistently with His own essence and never makes an error with that self-determination, which distinguishes divine self-determination from human self-determination entirely.

B. Infinity — Self-Existence, Immutability, Unity

God is infinite. By infinity is meant that God is without boundary and without limitation of any kind. God cannot be tempted; He cannot sin; He cannot be compromised by ignorance or absurdity. His infinity is intensive rather than merely extensive — an infinite depth and energy of being, not simply an unlimited extension across space. God's holiness, integrity, love, veracity, and word are all characterized by His infinity.

The divine motive is God's own glory. This is not a form of arrogance; it is the sanity of deity. If God were to seek to glorify any creature, the entire system of blessing would collapse, because no creature's glory is perfect or immutable. God's glory consists in the sum total of His attributes, and that glory pre-existed any creature — angelic or human. God creates creatures in order to glorify Himself, not to acquire glory He lacked. His glory never changes through the failures of His creatures; creatures can only be blessed by relating to it and glorifying Him. This is the divine motive behind X plus Y plus Z equaling the good of Romans 8:28 and the glory of God.

Infinity has three characteristics.

Self-existence: God always existed, sustained by no source outside Himself. The Tetragrammaton means the eternally self-existing One. God is the cause of all existence outside Himself. He is the cause of creatures but not the cause of everything creatures do, because He has given rational creatures — angels and human beings — their own volition for self-determination, making them in His image in that one respect.

Immutability: God is unchanging, and it is impossible for Him to change. He cannot be better or worse. Anthropopathisms in Scripture — God repenting, God being angry, God relenting — represent divine policy explained in terms of man's frame of reference, not actual changes in God's character. When man changes, God's consistent policy produces different outcomes, and this appears to man as change in God. But God's essence remains absolutely constant. Salvation is not God's second best following the fall; it was always part of His eternal purpose. That man sinned, God knew eternally, and the plan of salvation was never reactive.

Unity: Deuteronomy 6:4 — 'Jehovah our God is one Jehovah' — asserts that there is one infinite, perfect, absolute spirit. Isaiah 44:6 and John 5:44 emphasize this. Unity is opposed to polytheism and tritheism. Unity means that all the attributes of God are consistent with each other and that no divine attribute is ever compromised by the exercise of another. This is why the grace pipeline functions as it does: when God blesses the believer, He imputes blessing in time to His own righteousness resident in the believer. The justice of God is the source of the blessing; the righteousness of God is the recipient. Since righteousness demands righteousness and justice can only execute what righteousness demands, the entire transaction is hermetically sealed within divine integrity. Sovereignty, eternal life, righteousness, justice, omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, immutability, veracity, and love are all simultaneously uncompromised in every imputation God makes. Unity is maintained whether God is judging, disciplining, or blessing.

C. Perfection — Truth, Love, Integrity

God's intellect, character, and affections are all perfect. Divine perfection involves three components: truth directed toward self, love, and integrity.

God is truth directed toward Himself. In John 14:6, Jesus declares: 'I am the truth.' God does not hold truth as something acquired; He is truth. He always was truth. There was never a time when God learned anything or lacked any form of knowledge. In God, every truth and every form of knowledge dwells in absolute form. This attribute guarantees the genuineness of divine revelation, and it is the basis on which the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) operates — doctrine taken in through the human spirit, processed into the right lobe, and built into the frame of reference and norms and standards.

God is love. Perfect love can only have a perfect object. God the Father loves God the Son, God the Son loves God the Holy Spirit, and each member of the Trinity loves the integrity of the others. This is why God cannot love a sinful creature directly. When God created the original angels and when He created Adam and the woman, they were perfect and therefore the objects of divine love. Through their own negative volition, they became imperfect, and divine love was then replaced by divine justice as man's point of contact with God. 'God so loved the world' in John 3:16 is an anthropopathism — it explains in human terms the policy of a God whose actual contact with sinful humanity runs through justice, not love as an attribute.

God's nature is to bestow Himself, and this is why the X-Y-Z equation exists. God cannot reach sinful man with direct divine love, so His justice must do it. The justice of God imputes divine righteousness at salvation; justice imputes logistical grace to sustain the believer through life; justice imputes blessing in time at maturity to the righteousness of God. Man never contacts God's love directly — he contacts God's justice, which then operates in relationship to His own righteousness. God's love remains absolutely perfect, uncompromised, and unchanging throughout all of human history.

God is holiness — or more precisely, integrity. Integrity is composed of righteousness and justice. God has absolute holiness from eternity past. This same holiness is required of man, which is why the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation is the indispensable foundation of the entire plan. Righteousness demands righteousness; justice executes what righteousness demands. When the believer has maximum doctrine resident in the soul — that is, capacity — the justice of God imputes the blessings in time for which that righteousness has been the standing prerequisite since salvation. The entire system of divine blessing is therefore absolutely secure. The believer did not earn it, does not work to maintain it, and cannot lose it, because it was imputed by justice to righteousness and operates entirely within divine integrity.

V. The Relative Attributes of God

A. Eternity and Immensity — Relation to Time and Space

God has attributes related to time and space. Eternity means He always existed, always will exist, and will never change. Time and space, though without substance of their own, are objects of His creation. God transcends His creation. He does not think chronologically as finite creatures must; He thinks logically, and through doctrine He superimposes the logical upon the chronological in the believer's experience.

Immensity means God is not subject to space. He is the cause of space but is not contained by it. In relation to space, He is both immanent and transcendent — omnipresent, above and beyond space simultaneously. These are descriptive categories, not limitations.

B. Omnipresence, Omniscience, Omnipotence — Relation to Creation

These three attributes are relative — understood in relation to creation. Omnipresence: God is everywhere simultaneously. Omniscience: God knows all things — actual and potential — simultaneously and eternally. Omnipotence: God has infinite power to execute His will. None of these attributes is ever compromised in the believer's experience, because all blessing flows through the grace pipeline, which encases every transaction within divine integrity.

C. Veracity and Faithfulness — Relation to Moral Beings

God's infinite perfection is truth and faithfulness toward moral beings. God honors doctrine resident in the soul of the believer with spiritual growth. This is the only means of spiritual advance. The GAP system — the Grace Apparatus for Perception — transfers doctrine through the human spirit provided at salvation into the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary, categorical storage, and norms and standards of the right lobe. Spiritual growth never occurs through production, good works, or obedience performed to earn blessing; production is the expression of the royal ambassadorship, not its source.

God's faithfulness provides logistical grace to sustain the believer from salvation to maturity. At salvation, the justice of God imputed divine righteousness to the believer. All potential for blessing in time resides in that imputed righteousness, not in any subsequent human performance. Between salvation and maturity, everything the believer has — food, shelter, clothing, transportation, spiritual communication, rebound — is logistical support, not blessing. Blessing in the technical sense begins only when the believer cracks the maturity barrier and the justice of God begins to impute temporal blessings to the righteousness already resident in the soul. Those blessings, once imputed, are as secure as the imputation of eternal life itself, because they were never earned and cannot be forfeited.

David provides the classical illustration. At the height of his maturity, David possessed wealth, military supremacy, and kingship — all imputed by the justice of God to his divine righteousness. When he subsequently entered into prolonged moral failure, he received extensive divine discipline, but he did not forfeit his wealth, his military preeminence, or his kingship, because none of those things had been earned by his performance. They had been imputed to plus-righteousness. The discipline was severe; the blessings were not withdrawn. This is the nature of imputed blessing: it is secured by divine justice operating on divine integrity.

D. Mercy and Goodness — Relation to Moral Beings

Mercy is grace in action — infinite love operating through the plan. Justice is the means of distributing whatever the plan provides. God is absolutely good in contrast to the policy of Satan, which is evil. Divine justice is always perfect: it provides discipline for the reversionist, logistical support for all believers in the Christian life, and imputed temporal blessing for the mature believer. All of these come from the same source — justice — and all are therefore permanent and unaffected by human performance.

E. Divine Freedom

God must be consistent with Himself. He cannot compromise His essence. The incarnation — the hypostatic union of full deity and true humanity in the one person of Jesus Christ — was the only way the free will of God could provide salvation for mankind without compromising any divine attribute. The anthropopathisms ascribed to God in Scripture — love in John 3:16 and Romans 5:8, hate in Romans 9:13, anger in Romans 1:18, scorn in Psalm 2:4, benevolence in Romans 8:32, compassion in Lamentations 3:33 — ascribe human characteristics to God so that man can understand divine policy. God does not actually possess these emotions; He is infinitely blessed in Himself, with absolute freedom from fear, anxiety, regret, annoyance, or any creaturely limitation. He has absolute authority over creatures, over nature, and over history.

VI. Divine Essence and the Predetermined Plan of Romans 8:29

The examination of divine essence is not a detour from Romans 8:29 — it is the necessary foundation for it. The five steps to glory beginning in verse 29 — foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, glorification — are steps designed and executed by a God whose essence makes every step immutable. His self-existence guarantees that the plan was formulated before creation. His immutability guarantees that no deviation from the plan has ever occurred. His unity guarantees that no attribute was compromised at any step. His omniscience guarantees that the believer was in His thoughts before the believer existed. His justice guarantees that every imputation in the plan is secure. Understanding who God is establishes why Romans 8:28 can be stated as an absolute fact: all things — X, Y, and Z — work together for the purpose of good, which is the glory of God, because the God who designed the plan is infinite, eternal, and unchangeable in all His attributes.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Six

1. The 'good' of Romans 8:28 is the glory of God. The three radicals — X, Y, and Z — represent the complete sequence of divine imputations from birth through eternity. All of them together equal not merely subjective benefit to the believer but the objective glory of God, which is the divine motive behind the entire plan.

2. The first step to glory is foreknowledge — God's eternal thinking. The believer existed in the thoughts of God before the universe was created. This demands an understanding of the God who thinks: His essence, His attributes, and the perfection of His self-knowledge. Foreknowledge is not merely chronological precedence; it is the eternal awareness of a God who has no beginning and no change.

3. God is one in essence but three in personality. The term 'one' applied to God denotes absolute uniqueness, not numerical singularity. The three persons of the Trinity — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — possess identical and co-eternal attributes. Each has the same sovereignty, love, integrity, eternal life, omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, immutability, and veracity without variation. God is one in essence, three in personality.

4. Divine essence consists of two categories of attributes: absolute and relative. The absolute attributes — spirituality, infinity, and perfection — belong to God entirely apart from creation and are incommunicable. The relative attributes — eternity, immensity, omnipresence, omniscience, omnipotence, veracity, faithfulness, mercy, goodness, and freedom — are understood in relationship to creation and to moral beings.

5. God is life — eternal, self-existent life — and offers that life to mankind. The eternal life resident in the divine nature is the very life imputed to the believer at regeneration. Physical birth imputes human life and Adam's original sin; spiritual birth imputes eternal life to the regenerate human spirit. The necessity of the new birth follows directly from the nature of God as life.

6. God's immutability means that salvation is not God's second best. The fall of Adam did not catch God unprepared or cause Him to devise an alternative plan. The plan of salvation was in place before the creation of man. God does not change when man changes; it is man who changes, and God's consistent character produces different outcomes relative to man's condition. Anthropopathisms in Scripture describe divine policy in human terms; they do not describe changes in divine essence.

7. The unity of God means no divine attribute is ever compromised in any transaction. The grace pipeline — from the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation through the imputation of temporal blessings at maturity — is designed so that sovereignty, righteousness, justice, eternal life, omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, immutability, veracity, and love are all simultaneously uncompromised. The justice of God is the source of blessing; the righteousness of God is the recipient. Since the believer possesses imputed divine righteousness, the justice of God can bless him without violating any other attribute.

8. Divine love requires a perfect object and therefore does not contact sinful man directly. God can love only that which is perfect. When creatures fall, divine love is replaced by divine justice as the operative contact point. 'God so loved the world' is an anthropopathism explaining divine policy in human terms. The believer's actual point of contact with God is always through the justice of God, which operates on the basis of imputed righteousness. God's love remains perfect and uncompromised, but it reaches sinful man only through the justice mechanism.

9. All blessing between salvation and maturity is logistical grace, not imputed blessing. The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation establishes the potential for blessing in time, but that blessing is not released until the believer cracks the maturity barrier through consistent doctrine intake. Everything provided between salvation and maturity — food, shelter, clothing, transportation, spiritual communication — is logistical support designed to keep the believer alive and progressing. It is not reward and must not be confused with the imputed blessings of maturity.

10. Imputed blessings are absolutely secure because they were never earned. The believer did not earn imputed blessings and cannot forfeit them by subsequent failure. The David illustration establishes this: his wealth, military preeminence, and kingship were imputed to his divine righteousness, not earned by performance. When he fell into prolonged moral failure he received severe discipline, but the blessings were not withdrawn. Security and capacity are the two operative principles of the Christian way of life: security because all blessing comes from justice to righteousness, and capacity because the justice of God imputes only what the believer has the doctrinal capacity to handle.

11. God's own glory is the divine motive, and this is the sanity of deity. If God were to seek the glory of any creature, the stability of the entire plan would collapse. God's glory consists in the sum total of His attributes and pre-existed any creature. He creates creatures in order to display that glory, and the X-Y-Z equation of Romans 8:28 is the mechanism by which the believer participates in — and thereby manifests — that glory. The divine motive for God's own glory is not arrogance; it is the only possible basis for a plan that never fails.

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
ousia οὐσία ousia — being, essence, substance Derived from the Greek verb einai (to be). The inward nature, true substance, and sum total of the attributes of a being. Applied to God, ousia denotes His eternal, self-existent being — all that He is in His intrinsic character.
Elohim אֱלֹהִים Elohim — God (plural form) Hebrew plural noun used as the primary designation for God in the Old Testament. The plural suffix indicates the three persons of the Godhead — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — each possessing identical divine essence. The unity implied by the term is not numerical singularity but absolute uniqueness of shared attributes.
Tetragrammaton יהוה YHWH — the self-existing, eternally existing One The four-consonant Hebrew divine name derived from the verb to be (hayah), meaning the eternally self-existing One. Conveys not merely existence but absolute and unalterable being. God existed before creation, sustains Himself by no external source, and will always exist without change.
einai εἶναι einai — to be Greek infinitive of the verb 'to be,' the root from which ousia (essence, being) is derived. The verbal root underlying the primary Greek term for divine being.
elpis ἐλπίς elpis — hope, confident assurance In the New Testament and in the context of the three hopes of Romans 8:28, elpis does not mean uncertainty ('I hope so') but confident assurance about the future. The first hope is the confident assurance of salvation; the second is the confident assurance of blessing in time; the third is the confident assurance of great reward at the judgment seat of Christ.
anthropopathism anthropopathismos — ascription of human emotion to God A figure of speech in which human emotional characteristics are attributed to God so that man can understand divine policy within a human frame of reference. Examples include God 'loving' in John 3:16, God 'hating' in Romans 9:13, God 'repenting' in various Old Testament passages, and God 'being angry' in Romans 1:18. These do not describe actual emotions in God but represent divine policy in human terms.
anthropomorphism anthropomorphismos — ascription of human physical form to God A figure of speech in which human physical characteristics are attributed to God — eyes, ears, hands — to make divine action comprehensible to man. God is immaterial and has no body; these are accommodations to human understanding, not literal descriptions.
hypostatic union The union of full deity and true humanity in the one person of Jesus Christ. In the incarnation, God the Son voluntarily restricted the independent use of His divine attributes (kenosis) while retaining all divine essence. The hypostatic union was the only means by which the free will of God could provide salvation for mankind without compromising any divine attribute.
logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the physical and spiritual existence of the believer between salvation and maturity. Includes food, shelter, clothing, transportation, spiritual communication, and rebound. Logistical grace is not imputed blessing; it is sustaining support that keeps the believer alive and progressing toward the maturity barrier. All logistical grace is imputed by the justice of God to the divine righteousness resident in the believer.
maturity adjustment The second of the three adjustments to the justice of God. Progressive rather than instantaneous; achieved through consistent daily intake of Bible doctrine via the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). When the believer cracks the maturity barrier, the justice of God begins to impute temporal blessings to the divine righteousness that has been resident since salvation. Maturity adjustment is the point at which the second hope — the confident assurance of blessing in time — is realized.
GAP Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled system by which Bible doctrine is received, processed, and stored in the right lobe of the soul. Doctrine enters through the human spirit provided at salvation, passes through the left lobe for initial processing, and is transferred into the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary, categorical storage, and norms and standards of the right lobe. GAP is the sole mechanism of spiritual growth; no amount of production, works, or obedience substitutes for it.

Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Seven

Romans 8:29 — Foreknowledge, Predestination, and the Divine Decrees: Steps One and Two of the Five Steps to Glory

Romans 8:29 “For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: For whom He foreknew, He also fore-ordained — conformed ones to the image of His Son.

Romans 8:28 established that all things work together for the purpose of God for those who are the called ones according to the predetermined plan. Verses 29 and 30 now provide the mechanical explanation of how all things work together for good, presenting what may be called the five steps to glory. Steps one and two are found in verse 29. This chapter examines both steps in detail, together with the doctrinal framework of omniscience, the divine decrees, and foreknowledge that underlies them.

I. The Connecting Conjunction and the Verb of Cognizance

Verse 29 opens with a conjunction that connects this verse directly to Romans 8:28. The conjunction is used after verbs of cognizance to express the content of that cognizance — it signals that what follows is the known doctrinal content of what was affirmed in the preceding verse. The conjunction therefore demands the repetition of the first-person plural perfect indicative verb from verse 28.

The verb repeated from verse 28 is oidamen (οἴδαμεν), the perfect active indicative of oida (οἶδα). The perfect functions as a present of existing state: we know. The conjunction following it is hoti (ὅτι), introducing the content of that knowledge. Corrected translation of the opening: We know that.

II. Step One — Reality in the Mind of God: Foreknowledge (Romans 8:29a)

A. The Relative Pronoun and Its Force

Following oidamen hoti comes the accusative masculine singular of the relative pronoun hos (ὅς), functioning as a direct object: whom. This pronoun establishes the object of the divine action that follows — the class of persons who are the beneficiaries of the mechanics of the divine plan.

B. Proginōskō — The Verb of Divine Foreknowledge

The verb is the aorist active indicative of proginōskō (προγινώσκω). The compound is formed from pro (before) + ginōskō (γινώσκω, to know), yielding: to know beforehand, to know in advance, to have foreknowledge of something. In the New Testament this verb is used exclusively with God as its subject.

The aorist is a constative aorist, gathering into one entirety the foreknowledge of God. The active voice indicates that the subject, God the Father as author of the divine plan, produces the action. The indicative mood is the declarative indicative, asserting the reality of the function of divine foreknowledge. Corrected translation to this point: We know that whom He foreknew.

C. The Doctrinal Content of Step One: Foreknowledge Distinguished from Omniscience

Step one in the five steps to glory is that reality is in the mind of God — foreknowledge. To understand foreknowledge correctly, it must be distinguished from omniscience, with which it is frequently confused. The two terms refer to distinct operations of the divine intellect, and their relationship to the divine decrees is the key to the distinction.

The relevant doctrinal points are as follows. The order is: omniscience → decrees → foreknowledge. This chronological sequence, though not the emphasis of Romans 8:29, is established elsewhere in Scripture, notably in Acts 2:23.

Point 1. Foreknowledge is more limited in its scope than the omniscience of God. Omniscience knows both the realities and all alternatives to those realities. Foreknowledge deals only with the realities — what actually occurs. Omniscience therefore precedes the decrees; foreknowledge follows the decrees.

Point 2. In omniscience, God knows perfectly and eternally all that is knowable, whether actual or possible — both the reality and every alternative to that reality.

Point 3. In foreknowledge, God deals with the reality only. Foreknowledge is the specific, restricted operation of divine cognition that acknowledges only what is contained in the divine decrees.

Point 4. Foreknowledge therefore refers only to those things which are adopted within the plan of God — only the reality, not the alternatives.

Point 5. In omniscience, God knows all that would have been adopted and knows an infinite number of alternatives to what occurred. Foreknowledge refers only to what God did in fact adopt and decree.

Point 6. Chronologically there is an order, but that chronological order is not in view in Romans 8:29. Romans 8:29 presents no chronological sequence; it presents instead the doctrinal reality that the foreknown, the predestined, and the elect are the same persons. The chronological order is in view in Acts 2:23.

Point 7. The important conclusion: election, foreknowledge, and predestination are coincidental with respect to their objects. There is no chronological sequence intended here. All three — foreknowledge, election, and predestination — are coincidental in respect to their objects, which in this age are the members of the royal family of God.

Point 8. Rather than a chronological order, Romans 8:29 expresses the doctrinal principle that the foreknown, the predestined, and the elect are the same persons. The believer is the beneficiary of all three simultaneously.

Point 9. Placing foreknowledge before the decrees chronologically would imply that another has caused what occurs, and that God is merely aware of what someone else has caused. That inference is blasphemous. The correct order is: omniscience, then the decrees, then foreknowledge.

Point 10. Omniscience knows both the reality and its alternatives. Only the reality is fed from omniscience into the decrees. Foreknowledge then acknowledges only what is in the decrees. Foreknowledge is not the totality of God's knowledge — it is that portion of divine cognition that corresponds to the decrees.

Point 11. The great principle: nothing can be foreknown until it is first decreed. Only the divine decrees establish reality.

Point 12. Only the divine decrees establish reality. All counterfactual or alternative history resides within omniscience alone.

Point 13. When it comes to chronology, omniscience and God's self-knowledge precede the decrees, while election and foreknowledge are actually the content of the decrees.

Point 14. Since the divine decrees establish certainty, nothing can be foreknown until it is first decreed. Hence the order: omniscience — then the decrees — then foreknowledge.

Point 15. Since foreknowledge deals only with what God decreed, it emphasizes that each believer was in the mind of God in eternity past. Every member of the royal family of God was personally known to God — by name, in detail — before time began.

Point 16. Divine thinking included every believer. No one is excluded from step one. God knows the full extent to which each believer will advance in the plan of God through the free exercise of volition. He knows which believers will reach maturity and which will not, which will die in dying grace and which will reach the sin unto death. All of these realities were in the decrees and therefore part of His foreknowledge.

Point 17. Divine thinking related to foreknowledge indicates that God has a plan for each believer's life.

Point 18. Everything was decreed simultaneously, not by stages. The mechanical breakdown of the five steps in this passage is designed to relate the believer to the plan of God, giving confidence and assurance, and setting forth a system of potentials and hopes as expressed in the X + Y + Z formula.

D. The Formula: X + Y + Z = The Glory of God

The five steps to glory, of which foreknowledge is step one, operate within the framework of seven divine imputations. The formula X + Y + Z = the glory of God (Romans 8:28) clarifies how foreknowledge and the decrees relate to the believer's advance through the plan of God.

X Radical: Human life imputed at birth + Adam's original sin imputed at birth = first potential (salvation). Plus the pertinent doctrine of the gospel = the first hope, confident assurance of salvation. The first plus: salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Y Radical: Judicial imputation one — all personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. Judicial imputation two — the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation. These two together = the second potential (blessing in time). Plus pertinent doctrine = the second hope, confident assurance of maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The second plus: the reality of maturity adjustment replacing the hope.

Z Radical: Imputation of eternal life at salvation + the real imputation of blessing in time at the point of maturity = the third potential. Plus pertinent doctrine + undeserved suffering = the third hope. The third hope is the confident assurance of the seventh imputation — real imputation of eternal blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. The equal sign: the glory of God.

God's foreknowledge extends across the full span of each believer's potential advance through this formula. A believer may stop at the first plus (salvation) and advance no further. God knew that billions of years ago. He also knew the alternatives — what would have been available had the believer continued. Omniscience contains those alternatives; the decrees and foreknowledge contain only the reality of how far each believer in fact advances.

III. The Doctrine of Divine Decrees

A. Definition

The decrees of God are the sum total of God's plan designed in eternity past. They deal with reality only — what actually happens, not the alternatives. God's purposes relating to all events of every kind constitute one single, all-comprehensive intention, perceiving from omniscience all the events that occur in history, all the decisions, all the persons, conceiving the free as free and the necessary as necessary, together with all their causes, conditions, relations, and successions as one indivisible system of things, every link being related to the essential integrity of the whole.

B. The Will of God and the Decrees

The decrees represent the complete and consummated exercise of the will and sovereignty of God, determining the certain futurity of all events. No event is directly caused by the decrees. Rather, the decree itself provides in every case that events shall be affected by causes acting in a manner consistent with the nature of the event in question.

In the case of every free-will act of a moral agent, the decree provides five things simultaneously: (1) that the agent will be a free agent, acting without divine coercion; (2) that the antecedents of the act shall be what they are, without divine interference; (3) that all present conditions of the act shall be what they are; (4) that the act shall be perfectly spontaneous and free on the part of the agent; and (5) that the act shall be certainly future.

This means God does not stamp His will upon the believer's volition. The will of God represents what God desires for each believer — maximum blessing through the full advance from X through Y and Z to the seventh imputation. The decrees contain what each believer actually does. God can only decree reality. If a believer advances only to the first plus of the X radical, that is what was decreed — not because God willed it in the sense of desiring it, but because God's omniscience knew that the free will of that believer would take him no further. The will of God and the content of the decrees are therefore distinct.

The crucifixion of Christ illustrates this principle in its sharpest form (Acts 2:23). It was the sum total of human evil and reversionism, yet God's purpose was executed through the spontaneous free choices of those involved. Under the principle of efficacious grace, God the Holy Spirit provides the information necessary for a volitional response; the individual's positive volition is the spontaneous act by which salvation adjustment is made. God knew that response billions of years before it occurred and decreed it accordingly.

C. Foreknowledge of God in the Decrees

God foreknows all events as certainly future because He has first decreed them. Omniscience knows what is certainly future and also knows all the alternatives. Only reality is inserted into the decrees. Foreknowledge comes after the decrees and deals only with that reality. God's decrees relate equally to all future events of every kind, to the free actions of moral agents and to the actions of secondary causes alike.

Since the divine decrees alone establish certainty, nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed. To place foreknowledge before the decrees would imply that God is responding to what another has caused — which is blasphemy. The members of the Trinity who foreknow, predestinate, and elect are the same persons of the Godhead, and no one is above or prior to them.

D. The Desires of God and the Decrees

The desires of God are aspects of the divine mind viewed separately, while the decrees of God are conceived as a whole. God is said to have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, yet the unbeliever's consignment to eternal judgment is part of His eternal purpose. Sin and death are displeasing to God; nevertheless they belong to His eternal decree, because God could only decree what He omnisciently knew the free will of each creature would produce. The will of God represents the ideal; the decrees represent the reality.

E. Characteristics of the Divine Decrees

A. All-comprehensive. Not the slightest uncertainty can exist regarding any event without introducing confusion into all events. Every decision, every act of volition, every consequence of every cause throughout all of history was known to God in eternity past. All events are interwoven and interdependent within one comprehensive system.

B. Eternal. God does not gain in knowledge. Whatever decisions are made in any given day, God knew them before time began. There never was a time when God did not know. We gain in knowledge; God does not. The decrees are not updated.

C. Perfect. God can only produce what is perfect. Like God Himself, His plans and works are perfect. The accuracy, the interwoven complexity, and the comprehensive cognizance of the decrees are all perfect.

D. Unchangeable and certain. Nothing can arise to necessitate change. Everything was decreed, known, and anticipated in eternity past.

E. Free choice of divine sovereignty. God is not bound to follow a necessary course. Having decreed, however, God is bound by His infinite faithfulness, His veracity, and His truth to complete what He has begun. This is the doctrinal foundation of the third hope — the confident assurance that what God has begun for the mature believer, He will complete at the judgment seat of Christ.

F. The Extent of the Divine Decrees

God has decreed ends as well as means, causes as well as effects, conditions and instrumentalities as well as the events that depend upon them. Some things God has decreed to accomplish directly through immediate divine action — creation is the primary instance. Other things God brings to pass through secondary causes acting under the law of necessity. Other things God decrees to permit free agents to do through the exercise of their own volition. In every case, the decree renders the event certainly future, regardless of the category of causation.

G. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God

The decrees unite in one all-inclusive and final objective: the satisfaction, manifestation, and glory of God. God's glory is what He is and what He thinks. Being the infinite One, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are uniquely worthy of glory. As the subject of the divine decrees, it is inevitable that God will be glorified in what He has decreed, since the manifestation of His declarative glory also secures the highest good for His creatures — namely, cracking the maturity barrier and receiving the imputed blessings of time, parlayed into the imputed blessings of eternity.

The decrees are those sovereign purposes of God which are efficacious, accomplished by God alone, apart from all creature ability, mentality, talent, counsel, or cooperation. Salvation, preservation, logistical grace, and the programming of the ages all glorify God. When the believer cracks the maturity barrier and receives the imputed blessings of time, God is pleased and God is glorified.

The following summary points synthesize the doctrine of divine decrees as it bears on the believer's advance through the plan of God:

1. The divine decrees are executed through imputation from the justice of God. There are seven imputations, all of which add up to the glory of God in the formula X + Y + Z.

2. The decree of God allows maximum blessing for any believer, but recognizes that human volition can fall short of that potential. Only the reality of how far a believer advances is in the decrees; the potential is in omniscience.

3. A positive response to doctrine can fulfill the maximum blessing God desires for the believer. To the extent every believer advances is the extent to which the decree of eternity past was recorded for that individual.

4. God has the good sense to know beforehand how far each believer will travel, and that advance — and only that advance — was what was decreed.

5. In too many cases the potential exceeds the reality. Only reality was decreed in eternity past. Nothing can be foreknown until it was first decreed. Omniscience knows all potentialities plus all realities; foreknowledge knows only the realities — the things which are decreed.

IV. Step Two — Reality in the Plan of God: Predestination (Romans 8:29b)

A. The Adjunctive Conjunction

The next phrase is introduced by the adjunctive use of the conjunction kai (καί), correctly translated also. Step two is added to step one: He also fore-ordained.

B. Prooorizō — The Verb of Predestination

The verb is the aorist active indicative of proorizō (προορίζω). The compound is pro (before) + horizō (ὁρίζω, to determine, to set a boundary, to decide). The meaning: to decide upon something beforehand, to predestinate someone as something, to pre-design, to fore-ordain. All of these renderings are interrelated and synonymous. This verb refers to the decrees or the plan of God in eternity past, specifically as they pertain to the church-age believer and the royal family of God.

The aorist is a culminative aorist, viewing the decrees of God for the church-age believer in their entirety but regarding the result from the viewpoint of what exists — i.e., the last three steps of the five steps to glory. The active voice indicates God the Father, as author of the divine plan, producing the action in eternity past. The decrees were brought into simultaneous existence in eternity past. The indicative mood is the declarative indicative, asserting the reality of the divine decrees and the church-age believer's relationship to them.

Corrected translation to this point: We know that whom He foreknew, He also fore-ordained.

C. The Doctrinal Content of Step Two

Step two states that reality is in the plan of God — the decrees. Step one placed reality in the mind of God (foreknowledge). Step two places reality in the plan of God (the decrees). Every believer was in God's thoughts in eternity past, and every believer was also in God's plan — not merely anticipated but specifically and individually decreed.

The purpose of the divine plan for each believer is to crack the maturity barrier in time, thereby parlaying the imputed blessings of time into the imputed blessings of eternity. God's decrees outline the most fabulous prosperity for the mature believer. The two judicial imputations of the Y radical — (1) all personal sins imputed to Christ and judged, and (2) divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation — constitute the basis for the real imputation of divine blessing in time, which is then parlayed into greater blessing in eternity.

D. Summorphous — Conformed Ones

The accusative masculine plural adjective summorphous (συμμόρφους) modifies the implied direct object. The word means conformed ones. He also predestinated us — conformed ones. The question of what the believer is conformed to is answered by the following phrase: to the image of His Son, which will be examined in the following chapter.

The term conformed ones refers to the royal family of God. This is a reference to the formation of the royal family at salvation through the baptism of the Holy Spirit, and therefore to current positional truth. It also carries the objective of phase two — maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Additionally, it takes cognizance of the third hope: the reality of blessing and reward in eternity at the judgment seat of Christ, including the resurrection body and the real imputation of eternal blessing.

The conformation in view moves through the entire formula. In the X radical, human life and Adam's original sin establish the first potential and the first hope, resolved by salvation adjustment. In the Y radical, the two judicial imputations establish the second potential and the second hope, with the point of conformation beginning at the cracking of the maturity barrier. In the Z radical, the imputation of eternal life plus the blessings of time at maturity establish the third potential, the third hope, and ultimately the seventh imputation at the judgment seat of Christ — the glory of God.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Seven

1. Foreknowledge and omniscience are distinct operations of the divine intellect. Omniscience knows both the reality of every event and every alternative to that reality. Foreknowledge deals only with the reality — what actually occurs. The two are separated by the divine decrees: omniscience precedes the decrees; foreknowledge follows them.

2. The chronological order is: omniscience → divine decrees → foreknowledge. This sequence, established in Acts 2:23, is not the emphasis of Romans 8:29, which presents foreknowledge, election, and predestination as coincidental with respect to their objects — the royal family of God. No chronological priority among these three is asserted in this passage.

3. Nothing can be foreknown until it is first decreed. Only the divine decrees establish certainty. To place foreknowledge before the decrees implies that another has caused what occurs and that God is merely a passive observer — an inference that is theologically untenable.

4. The decrees contain only reality, never the alternatives. All counterfactual and alternative history — what would have happened under different choices — resides within the omniscience of God alone. The decrees record what actually occurs, and foreknowledge acknowledges precisely what the decrees contain.

5. Every believer was individually in the mind and plan of God before time began. This is the personal comfort of step one (foreknowledge) and step two (predestination): God knew each believer by name, knew the full extent of his advance in the plan of God, and decreed accordingly, billions of years before that believer existed.

6. The will of God and the content of the decrees are distinct. God desires the maximum advance for every believer through the full X + Y + Z formula to the seventh imputation. The decrees contain only the reality of how far each believer actually advances. Where the potential exceeds the reality, the potential remains in omniscience; only the reality was decreed.

7. The divine decrees are all-comprehensive, eternal, perfect, unchangeable, and free. Every event of every kind throughout all of history was known to God and decreed simultaneously in eternity past. The decrees do not develop by stages; they are one indivisible system of things, every link related to the essential integrity of the whole.

8. The final objective of the divine decrees is the glory of God. The decrees unite in one all-inclusive purpose: the satisfaction, manifestation, and glory of God. This glory is realized in the believer's life through the seven imputations — culminating in the real imputation of eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ, which is the good of Romans 8:28.

9. Proginōskō (to foreknow) is used in the New Testament exclusively with God as subject. The aorist tense is constative, gathering the totality of divine foreknowledge into one act. The active voice indicates God the Father as the author of the divine plan.

10. Proorizō (to predestinate, to fore-ordain) refers specifically to the divine decrees for the church-age believer. The culminative aorist views those decrees in their entirety from the viewpoint of their existing results — the last three of the five steps to glory. The term summorphous (conformed ones) designates the royal family of God as the objects of this predestination.

Omniscience The divine attribute by which God knows perfectly and eternally all that is knowable, whether actual or possible — both the reality of every event and every alternative to that reality. Omniscience precedes the divine decrees and provides the basis from which the decrees are formed.
Divine Decrees The sum total of God's plan designed in eternity past, dealing with reality only. One single, all-comprehensive intention perceiving all events in omniscience, conceiving the free as free and the necessary as necessary, together with all causes, conditions, relations, and successions as one indivisible system of things. The decrees separate omniscience (which precedes them) from foreknowledge (which follows them).
