Step two of the five steps to glory (predestination) is designed to bring the believer to this point.
Seventh imputation The real imputation of eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body of the mature believer at the judgment seat of Christ. The final term in the formula X + Y + Z = the glory of God (Romans 8:28). The ultimate objective of the divine decrees for the church-age believer.

Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Eight

Romans 8:29–30 — Divine Thinking, Predestination, and the Five Steps to Glory

Romans 8:28–30 “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: We know, in fact, that to those who love God — mature believers — all things work together for the purpose of good, to those who are the called according to a predetermined plan. Because whom He foreknew, He also foreordained — predestinated — conformed ones to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brethren. And these same ones whom He foreordained, He also called.

Romans 8:28–30 presents the first two of five steps to glory — the mechanics by which all things work together for the purpose of the good. Verse 28 established the formula X + Y + Z = the glory of God through seven imputations spanning from physical birth to the resurrection body. Verse 29 introduces step one (divine thinking: omniscience, decrees, and foreknowledge) and step two (the divine purpose: predestination and conformity to the image of the Son). Verse 30 opens step three: entrance into the plan of God through election and calling. This chapter completes the exegesis of verse 29 and begins verse 30.

I. The Formula Reviewed: X + Y + Z = The Glory of God

The good of Romans 8:28 is the seventh and final imputation in God's plan for the Church Age believer — eternal blessings and rewards imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. This good is the product of three radicals, each containing two imputations and a hope.

The X Radical: Birth and the First Potential

Imputation 1: Human life is imputed to the soul at physical birth — the beginning of individual existence. Imputation 2: Adam's original sin is simultaneously imputed to the old sin nature, producing spiritual death and establishing the first potential: salvation. Because all members of the human race are condemned at birth, salvation becomes the universal first potential. When an individual at the point of God consciousness is positive toward God, pertinent doctrine — the gospel — is provided. No geographical isolation and no linguistic barrier can prevent this provision for the person who is positive at God consciousness (Romans 1). The first potential plus the gospel equals the first hope: confident assurance of salvation.

The Y Radical: Judicial Imputations and the Second Potential

The first hope is replaced by reality at the moment of faith in Christ — salvation adjustment to the justice of God. The Y radical then opens a new horizon. Judicial imputation 3: all personal sins of the world are imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. There is no antecedence — these sins were alien to the impeccable humanity of Christ. Judicial imputation 4: divine righteousness (

divine righteousness (+R) is imputed to the believer at salvation — again with no antecedence, no merit, no equivalence on the human side. This +R becomes the target and home — the system of antecedence — for blessing in time. The second potential is the potential of great blessing in time. When positive volition toward doctrine is sustained, the second hope forms: confident assurance that consistent doctrine intake will produce spiritual maturity and the real imputation of blessing in time.

The Z Radical: Eternal Life and the Third Potential

Imputation 5: eternal life is imputed to the regenerate human spirit at salvation. Imputation 6: blessing in time is imputed to the believer's

Imputation 6: blessing in time is imputed to the believer's +R at the point of maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The second hope is replaced by the reality of maturity; a third hope must therefore be established. The third potential is blessing and reward in eternity. This potential, combined with pertinent doctrine and undeserved suffering, produces the third hope: confident assurance of great blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. This is the hope operative at dying grace, expressed by Paul in 2 Timothy 4:7–8: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness."

The Seventh Imputation: The Good

Imputation 7: eternal blessings and rewards are imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. This is a real imputation and therefore has two factors: factor one is the content — the blessings and rewards themselves, which glorify the Lord forever; factor two is the home — the resurrection body, minus the old sin nature, as the system of antecedence and affinity. There is a perfect correspondence between the blessings imputed and the resurrection body that receives them.

The seven imputations in sequence: (1) human life imputed to the soul at birth; (2) Adam's original sin imputed to the old sin nature at birth; (3) all personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross; (4) divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation; (5) eternal life imputed to the regenerate human spirit at salvation; (6) blessing in time imputed to

(6) blessing in time imputed to +R at maturity; (7) eternal blessings and rewards imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ.

II. Step Two: The Divine Purpose — Conformed to the Image of His Son (Romans 8:29b)

Grammatical Analysis: 'To the Image of His Son'

The phrase rendered "to the image of his Son" involves a descriptive genitive singular from the noun eikōn (εἰκών), correctly translated image — a likeness or representation. With this descriptive genitive is a possessive genitive from huios (υἱός), referring to the Lord Jesus Christ, together with a possessive genitive from the intensive pronoun used as a personal pronoun: autos (αὐτός). In Greek, there is no third person personal pronoun. The first person is egō (ἐγώ); the second is su (σύ). For the third person, autos serves as both intensive pronoun and personal pronoun, supplying the referent "His" in the phrase "the image of His Son."

Theological Content: Conformed Ones

"Conformed ones" refers positionally to every Church Age believer, who is placed in union with Christ at salvation through the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Retroactive positional truth divorces the believer from the old sin nature — the former master — and current positional truth establishes the foundational reality of conformity to the image of the Son. This is the positional dimension.

The experiential dimension operates between salvation and the resurrection. Between union with Christ at salvation and the reception of the resurrection body in eternity, there is only one pathway of conformity: the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), producing maturity adjustment to the justice of God. No system of works, no ascetic discipline, no financial giving, no ordinance observance, no service organization, no form of human good can produce experiential conformity. Doctrine taken into the soul is the exclusive mechanism.

The ultimate dimension is the resurrection body itself — the conformity is completed at the rapture, when every Church Age believer receives a resurrection body exactly like that of the Son of God, minus the old sin nature, minus human good. Even the believer who was maximally negative toward doctrine in time receives this resurrection body, because it is given unconditionally at the rapture. It becomes, however, the basis for building: blessing in time — obtained only through GAP — is parlayed into the seventh imputation, eternal blessing and reward. The believer who was entirely negative toward doctrine has the resurrection body and nothing more. There will be no tears in eternity, but there will be great variation in the blessings and rewards imputed to the resurrection body.

The Three Stages of Sanctification

The phrase "conformed ones to the image of His Son" recapitulates the three stages of sanctification. Stage one is positional sanctification: union with Christ through the baptism of the Holy Spirit at salvation. Stage two is experiential sanctification: advancing toward maturity through the daily function of GAP. Stage three is ultimate sanctification: the resurrection body, received at the rapture. This is the Father's plan for the royal family of God.

"That He Might Be the Firstborn" — Grammatical and Theological Analysis

The purpose clause "that He might be" is expressed in Greek as a prepositional idiom: eis (εἰς) plus the accusative of the definite article, plus the present active infinitive of the verb eimi (εἶναι). The static present indicates a condition that perpetually exists. The active voice designates the Lord Jesus Christ — in resurrection body, in ascension and session — as the one producing the action. The infinitive of purpose is correctly translated "that He might be."

The referent "He" is derived not from the article but from the accusative singular of general reference from the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός), which in the accusative functions as the logical subject of the infinitive — describing the one connected with the action and properly translated as the third person singular pronoun.

The object of the infinitive is the accusative singular direct object from prōtotokos (πρωτότοκος), correctly translated firstborn. Full corrected translation: "that He might be the firstborn." Colossians 1:15 provides the parallel: "who keeps on being the exact image of the unseen God, the privileged firstborn with reference to all creatures."

Three Connotations of Firstborn

First, firstborn connotes rulership. Christ is the firstborn, which means He is the ruler — at present, of the Church, the royal family of God, and at the Second Advent, of the world.

Second, the firstborn is the family priest. Christ is ordained a royal priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 5–7).

Third, the firstborn possesses the double portion. Christ has two kingdoms of believers: Israel, over whom He rules as Son of David, and the Church, over whom He rules as King of Kings. The emphasis in Romans 8:29 is on His rulership of the royal family of God.

"Among Many Brethren" — The Royal Family

The phrase "among many brethren" involves en (ἐν) plus the dative plural of polus (πολύς) plus the noun adelphos (ἀδελφός). The "many brethren" are Church Age believers — the royal family of God. Corrected translation of the full verse: "We know that whom He foreknew, He also foreordained — predestinated — conformed ones to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brethren, the royal family of God, or Church Age believer."

The royal family of God was formed in eternity past. Christ is the firstborn of the royal family — its ruler, its high priest, and the holder of the double portion heritage. The many brethren — Church Age believers — constitute that royal family. All of this is designed to read the believer into the big picture: to understand how the divine decrees relate to the seven imputations, and to bring the believer to the objective in time — maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

III. Step Three: Entrance into the Plan of God — Election and Calling (Romans 8:30a)

Connective Particle and Demonstrative Pronoun

Verse 30 opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ) in a connective use, correctly translated and — linking verse 30 to verse 29 as a continuation of the same sequence of steps, rather than a contrast.

The subject is the accusative masculine plural from the relative pronoun hos (ὅς), "whom," followed by the aorist active indicative of proorizō (προορίζω) carried over from verse 29 — "whom He foreordained." The object "these same ones" is the accusative plural demonstrative pronoun houtos (οὗτος), the immediate demonstrative referring to what has immediately preceded. It cannot be translated merely as "them" — its force is these same ones, emphasizing continuity with the Church Age believers already in view.

The Verb Kaleō: Technical Sense — Election

The verb is the aorist active indicative of kaleō (καλέω), meaning to call, to name, to designate, to summon, to invite. Here it is used in the technical theological sense for the doctrine of election. The culminative aorist regards the doctrine of election for the royal family of God in its entirety, viewing it from the standpoint of existing results. The active voice designates God the Father as the author of the divine decrees and the divine plan. The declarative indicative mood states a dogmatic reality: all Church Age believers are elected. Every believer is in the plan of God.

Election Defined in Relation to the X Radical

Election is the point of the decision — specifically, the moment of faith in Jesus Christ. In the X radical: human life plus Adam's original sin equals the first potential; that potential plus the gospel equals the first hope; the first hope converted through faith in Christ is the point of election. Election emphasizes the fact that the believer is permanently in the plan of God. Second Timothy 1:9 states: "the One having saved us and having elected the royal family into a holy station of life, not according to our works, but according to His predetermined plan — even grace which has been given to us in Christ Jesus before human history, before the times of the dispensations."

The Relationship of Election, Foreknowledge, and Predestination

These three are simultaneous functions within the divine decrees, each with a distinct emphasis. Election is the point of the decision: the moment a given individual believes in Christ. Foreknowledge is the recognition of that decision: God's prior cognizance of the reality of what the individual's free will would do. Predestination is the function of the decisions: God's prior knowledge of what the believer will do at each subsequent point in time — the reality of all future decisions. All three face reality exclusively; none deal with alternatives. Omniscience encompasses both the reality and all alternatives. The decrees contain only reality. Foreknowledge, election, and predestination acknowledge only what is in the decrees.

Predestination does not coerce the free will. It is prior knowledge of what the free will will freely choose. The sum total of the decisions a person makes across a lifetime — every wise and every foolish decision, every advance and every retreat in the spiritual life — constitutes the reality placed in the decrees. What omniscience knows as alternatives (what would have happened had a different decision been made) is never in the decrees and is never the object of foreknowledge or predestination.

The order of logical sequence (as per Acts 2:23) is: first omniscience — which knows everything, including all alternatives; then the decrees — which contain only reality; then foreknowledge — which recognizes only what is in the decrees. The decrees of God for the Church Age cover the entirety of the royal family from Pentecost to the rapture: every person, every decision, every consequence.

Security and the Plan of God

There is no greater security than the recognition that before human history began, the believer's entrance into the plan of God was known in the omniscience of God, inserted into the decrees as reality, and guaranteed. The blessings of maturity adjustment were provided for the mature believer even before Adam existed. The decrees contain the most extraordinary and unique blessings for mature believers — blessings far exceeding anything available in the garden of Eden.

IV. Satan's Attack on the Seven Imputations

The formula X + Y + Z = the glory of God is the target of a comprehensive and systematic assault. At every node of the plan, a specific attack is mounted.

Against imputation 1 (human life at birth): the theory of evolution, which denies the direct creation of human life and the reality of individual existence as God's act.

Against imputation 2 (Adam's original sin): the assault on the dignity of man through denial of the fall and its consequences — spiritual death and condemnation at birth.

Against the first potential (salvation): the full range of philosophical systems that offer alternative explanations for human existence and destiny, foreclosing the gospel before it can be heard.

Against the first hope and the point of election (faith in Christ): the corruption of the gospel through addition or subtraction — faith plus baptism, faith plus church membership, faith plus emotional response, faith plus works of any kind.

Against judicial imputation 1 (sins imputed to Christ): the substitution of a physical theory of atonement — that Christ's physical blood, rather than the spiritual work of bearing the penalty of sin, is the basis of redemption.

Against judicial imputation 2 (divine righteousness imputed at salvation): widespread ignorance of this doctrine produces a failure to understand the basis for blessing in time.

Against the second potential (blessing in time): the attack of false austerity — the teaching that material prosperity is evidence of worldliness, that God blesses only those who divest themselves of all earthly goods, and that Christian credibility requires visible poverty.

Against the second hope and the maturity plus (maturity adjustment): the substitution of activity for doctrine — witnessing, prayer, church service, missionary work, discipleship programs, and Christian service organizations are presented as the path to spiritual maturity, displacing the daily function of GAP.

Against the Z radical and eternal security: the denial of the permanent nature of salvation, requiring repeated acts of repentance and faith after every failure.

Against blessing in time: the equation of prosperity with worldliness — so that the very blessings God designs for the mature believer become a source of guilt and accusation.

Against the third potential (blessing and reward in eternity): the claim that eternal rewards are tied exclusively to evangelistic activity or visible Christian service, bypassing the doctrine of the judgment seat of Christ and the seven imputations.

Against undeserved suffering: the inability to interpret it theologically, so that what God designs to maintain the third hope instead produces confusion, bitterness, or retreat. The result in every case is to redirect the believer from X + Y + Z = glory toward the devil's triangle: the old sin nature as the ruler of life, expressed through personal sin, human good, and evil.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Eight

1. The seven imputations span the entirety of the believer's existence. From physical birth (human life and Adam's original sin) through salvation (judicial imputations 3 and 4, plus eternal life) through maturity (blessing in time) to eternity (blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ) — the plan of God is a seamless, integrated sequence with affinity between what is imputed and the recipient at each stage.

2. The good of Romans 8:28 is the seventh imputation. It is a real imputation with two factors: factor one is the content — eternal blessings and rewards that glorify the Lord forever; factor two is the home — the resurrection body, minus the old sin nature, as the system of antecedence.

3. Being conformed to the image of the Son operates in three dimensions. Positionally, all Church Age believers are conformed ones now through union with Christ via the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Experientially, conformity advances between salvation and eternity only through the daily function of GAP leading to maturity adjustment. Ultimately, every Church Age believer will be conformed at the rapture through the reception of a resurrection body like that of the Son of God.

4. The worst believer who ever lived receives a resurrection body at the rapture. This is unconditional and guaranteed. It constitutes the basis for building — but without blessing in time through GAP, there is nothing above and beyond the resurrection body itself. The believer with zero doctrine has a resurrection body and nothing more at the judgment seat of Christ. There are no tears in eternity, but there is no equality either.

5. Election is the doctrine that relates the believer to the plan of God from eternity past. Election coincides with foreknowledge and predestination. Election emphasizes the fact of being permanently in the plan of God; foreknowledge is God's prior recognition of the decision of faith; predestination is God's prior knowledge of all subsequent decisions. All three deal exclusively with reality — what actually occurs — not with alternatives. Omniscience alone encompasses the alternatives.

6. The order of divine thinking is: omniscience → decrees → foreknowledge. Nothing can be foreknown until it is first decreed. The decrees establish reality. Omniscience is the broader term, encompassing everything that could happen and all alternatives. The decrees contain only what actually happens. Foreknowledge acknowledges only what is in the decrees. This sequence, established in Acts 2:23, is the foundation for understanding the plan of God.

7. Predestination does not coerce free will. It is prior knowledge of what the free will will freely do. The sum of a believer's actual decisions across a lifetime constitutes the reality placed in the decrees. The alternatives — what would have happened had different decisions been made — belong to omniscience, not to the decrees or foreknowledge.

8. There is no greater security than the eternal guarantee embedded in the divine decrees. Before human history began, the omniscience of God knew who would believe in Christ, inserted that reality into the decrees, and guaranteed the blessings of maturity adjustment. Those blessings were provided for the mature believer before Adam existed — blessings exceeding anything available in the garden of Eden.

9. Christ's designation as firstborn carries three connotations. Rulership — He is ruler of the Church now and of the world at the Second Advent. Priesthood — He is ordained a royal priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. Double portion — He rules both Israel as Son of David and the Church as King of Kings.

10. The only path of experiential conformity between salvation and eternity is GAP. Works, perfect conduct, charitable giving, ordinance observance, emotional experience, ascetic discipline — none of these produce experiential conformity to the image of the Son. Bible doctrine taken into the soul and metabolized through the Grace Apparatus for Perception is the exclusive mechanism. Without it, there is no maturity adjustment, no second hope, no blessing in time, and therefore no seventh imputation above the baseline of the resurrection body.

eikōn εἰκών eikōn — image, likeness Descriptive genitive singular noun used in Romans 8:29 in the phrase "to the image of His Son." Denotes a representation or exact likeness; used also in Colossians 1:15 of Christ as the image of the invisible God.

proorizō προορίζω proorizō — to foreordain, to predestinate Compound: pro (before) + horizō (to establish a boundary, to determine). To decide beforehand, to pre-design, to fore-ordain. In Romans 8:30, rendered "these same ones" to emphasize continuity with the Church Age believers already mentioned in verse 29. Distinct from the third person pronoun; carries a demonstrative force of identification and emphasis.

Maturity adjustment to the justice of God The second of three categories of adjustment to the justice of God. Real imputation An imputation in which there is antecedence and affinity between what is imputed and the recipient — the recipient possesses a quality or status that is the natural home for what is being imputed. Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Nine

Romans 8:30 — The Five Steps to Glory: Steps Four and Five; Justification and Glorification; Romans 8:31

Romans 8:30 “And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified.” (ESV)

Corrected translation: And whom he foreordained, these same ones he also called or elected; and whom he called or elected, these same ones he also justified; and whom he justified, these same ones he also glorified.

Romans 8:31 “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” (ESV)

Corrected translation: Therefore, face to face with these things, to what conclusion are we forced? If the God is for us — and he is — who is against us?

Romans 8:30 presents five sequential steps in the divine plan moving from eternity past through time and into eternity future. The first two steps were treated in verse 29 (foreknowledge and foreordination). The third step — election or calling — was completed in the preceding chapter. This chapter takes up steps four and five: justification and glorification. The chapter concludes with the opening of Romans 8:31, which introduces a new major paragraph running through verse 39: the new life and its challenges.

I. The Formula: All Things Working Together for Good

The governing formula of this entire section is Romans 8:28: all things work together for the purpose of good. The 'good' of that verse is the seventh divine imputation — blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. The formula is structured around three radicals.

X Radical

The imputation of human life at birth, plus the imputation of Adam's original sin to the genetically formed old sin nature, establishes the first potential: the possibility of salvation for every member of the human race. For those who are positive at God-consciousness, God provides the pertinent doctrine — the gospel — and this equals the first hope: the confident assurance that those who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ have everlasting life. This hope is replaced by reality at the salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ.

Y Radical

Y radical combines two judicial imputations. The first judicial imputation: all the sins of the human race were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. The second judicial imputation: divine righteousness is imputed to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ. Together these establish the second potential — justification, or qualification for blessing in time. For those positive toward doctrine, God provides the necessary instruction, and this equals the second hope: the confident assurance that sustained doctrine intake will result in maturity adjustment to the justice of God and the real imputation of blessing in time. That hope is replaced by reality at the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Z Radical

Z radical combines the imputation of eternal life at salvation with the imputation of blessing in time at maturity. This establishes the third potential, which — together with positive volition toward doctrine and undeserved suffering that maintains perspective — equals the third hope: the confident assurance of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. That hope is replaced by reality at the seventh imputation, which is the good of Romans 8:28 and the glorification of Romans 8:30.

II. Step Four — Justification (Romans 8:30b)

The corrected translation of the relevant clause reads: “And whom he called or elected, these same ones he also justified.”

Grammatical Analysis

The clause opens with the connective post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), translated 'and,' followed by the accusative plural of the relative pronoun hos (ούς), 'whom.' The aorist active indicative of kaleō (καλέω), 'to call, to elect,' is a dramatic aorist stating the present reality of election with the certitude of a past event in the divine decrees. God the Father, as the author of the divine plan, produces the action. The indicative mood is declarative, conveying a dogmatic statement of doctrine.

The demonstrative pronoun houtos (οὗτος), accusative plural, refers to what immediately precedes — 'these same ones.' The adjunctive kai (καί) adds 'also.' The main verb is the aorist active indicative of dikaiōō (δικαιόω), 'to declare righteous, to justify, to vindicate.' The constative aorist gathers into a single entirety the momentary act of imputing divine righteousness at the moment of faith in Christ. This is the second judicial imputation.

The Doctrine of Justification

A judicial imputation differs from a real imputation in that it lacks antecedence and affinity between what is imputed and the recipient. At salvation, divine righteousness is imputed to the believer without any merit or preparation on the believer's part. The imputation is made possible because all personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there. Having satisfied justice with respect to sin, God can impute His righteousness to the believer without compromising any divine attribute.

Justification has several sub-categories in the epistle. Justification at salvation is the judicial imputation of divine righteousness. Justification at maturity is the real imputation of blessing in time to that imputed righteousness. Justification at the judgment seat of Christ is the real imputation of eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body. And there is a justification or vindication of the believer's ambassadorship through production, as illustrated by the book of James.

The Grace Pipeline

The imputation of divine righteousness constructs a grace pipeline. On the giving end is the justice of God; on the receiving end is the righteousness of God imputed to the believer. This pipeline is completely encapsulated by the integrity of God — righteousness being the principle of divine integrity and justice being the function of divine integrity. Nothing external to this pipeline can introduce blessing from God. No human work, production, talent, personality change, system of morality, asceticism, or self-sacrifice can penetrate the encapsulation. All blessing from God is an imputation from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. This is why the pipeline is called the grace pipeline: grace is the policy of the justice of God in providing blessing for the mature believer.

A Fortiori Reasoning

A fortiori logic applies here. If the justice of God accomplished the greater at salvation — the judicial imputation of divine righteousness — it follows a fortiori that the justice of God can accomplish the less: the real imputation of blessing in time at the point of maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The greater occurs at salvation; the less occurs at maturity. The judicial imputation at salvation is the indispensable foundation for the real imputation at maturity.

Real Imputation and Its Two Factors

A real imputation requires two factors: (1) what is imputed, and (2) the home, affinity, target, and antecedence — the divinely prepared receiving point. Blessing in time is the content of imputation at maturity; the imputed righteousness of God is the divinely prepared home or target. There is a true affinity between blessing in time and the righteousness of God imputed at salvation, so that blessing can be imputed to that righteousness without compromising any attribute of God.

For comparison: at physical birth, human life is imputed to the soul — a real imputation requiring the divinely prepared target of the soul. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature — also a real imputation. At salvation, eternal life is imputed to regeneration — a real imputation requiring the divinely prepared target of the new birth. God must provide a birth before He can provide the life. This is the theological significance of regeneration: it is not merely a metaphor for spiritual experience but the divinely prepared home for eternal life.

Justification and the Second Hope

The judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation establishes the second potential in Y radical: qualification for blessing in time. This is justification in its primary Romans sense — vindication for blessing. Every believer in the Lord Jesus Christ has been vindicated for blessing. The potential is present. But potential does not become reality without the capacity that comes through sustained doctrine intake. The second hope — the confident assurance that maturity adjustment will result in blessing in time — follows from this judicial imputation. The righteousness of God demands blessing, and the justice of God executes that blessing, once the believer cracks the maturity barrier through maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

Principles from Step Four

1. Two judicial imputations are necessary for the real imputation of blessing at maturity. The first imputes all human sin to Christ on the cross; the second imputes divine righteousness to the believer at salvation.

2. Two real imputations at physical birth begin the structure of the divine plan. Human life is imputed to the soul; Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. Condemnation precedes salvation.

3. Condemnation at birth is by the imputation of Adam's original sin only. Personal sins are not the basis for condemnation. Adam's original sin condemns every member of the human race. All personal sins were frozen for judicial imputation to Christ on the cross.

4. Personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there. Therefore personal sin is not an issue at salvation; Christ is the issue. The remarks of our Lord in Gethsemane and on the cross — 'let this cup pass from me' and 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — confirm that personal sins were a real and definite issue for Him, though not for us in condemnation or salvation.

5. The righteousness of God is the guardian of the justice of God. The justice of God is the guardian of all divine attributes, protecting them from compromise. Righteousness demands what justice executes.

6. The justice of God executes divine blessing in six categories to the believer when the righteousness of God demands that blessing — i.e., when the believer cracks the maturity barrier.

7. There is no demand from the righteousness of God until the believer cracks the maturity barrier through the filling of the Spirit and the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

8. Justification relates the believer to the plan of God so that the attributes of God are never compromised by blessing imputed from the justice of God to the righteousness of God.

9. This defines grace: grace is the policy of the justice of God in blessing the believer.

10. Justification is the key to the divine plan for time. It qualifies the believer for blessing; the only requirement beyond justification is the capacity for blessing that comes through maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

III. Step Five — Glorification (Romans 8:30c)

The corrected translation of the final clause of verse 30 reads: “And whom he justified, these same ones he also glorified.”

Grammatical Analysis

The pattern repeats: connective de, accusative plural of hos, aorist active indicative of dikaiōō for justification; then the demonstrative houtos accusative plural with adjunctive kai. The new element is the aorist active indicative of doxazō (δοξάζω), meaning to praise, to honor, to glorify, to magnify, to promote — but here specifically to have a share in glory. The constative aorist gathers up into one entirety the real imputation of blessing in time at maturity and the real imputation of eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ.

The Meaning of Glorification

Every time the justice of God imputes blessing — whether at maturity in time or at the judgment seat of Christ in eternity — God is glorified. Those who receive the blessing share in His glory. The imputation of divine blessing is simultaneously the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ and the believer's participation in that glory. This is what the verb conveys: not merely that we are declared glorious, but that we share in God's own glory through imputation.

The 'also glorified' of verse 30 therefore encompasses two distinct elements: (1) the real imputation of blessing in time at the maturity adjustment to the justice of God — the sixth imputation; and (2) the hope of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ — which, when realized, becomes the seventh imputation, the 'good' of Romans 8:28.

A Fortiori Applied to Glorification

The constative aorist of the verb combines two a fortiori arguments from Romans 5. First: if the justice of God accomplished the greater through the judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation, it follows a fortiori that the justice of God will accomplish the less — the real imputation of blessing at the point of maturity. Second: if the justice of God accomplished the greater through the real imputation of divine blessing in time at maturity, it follows a fortiori that the justice of God can accomplish the less at the judgment seat of Christ — the real imputation of eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body.

Principles from Step Five

1. Blessing in time and blessing in eternity are both part of the divine decrees for the mature believer. It was decreed before human history that every believer who cracks the maturity barrier would receive blessing in time and blessing in eternity.

2. Divine blessing and glorification existed long before any believer existed. The blessings designed for the status of maturity adjustment to the justice of God were provided in the decrees before anyone actually achieved that status.

3. The omniscience of God regarding reality became the decree of God. Omniscience is primary; the decrees follow from omniscience; foreknowledge follows from the decrees. Nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed.

4. The divine decree alone establishes certainty. Since the divine decree alone establishes certainty, nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed (cf. Acts 2:23).

5. Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are coincident with respect to their objects. In verse 30 we do not have a strictly chronological sequence but the declaration that the same persons are the objects of all five steps.

6. The glorification of verse 30 is the 'good' of Romans 8:28. The seventh imputation — blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ — is the terminus of the entire x-plus-y-plus-z formula.

IV. The Corrected Translation of Romans 8:30

And whom he foreordained or predestinated, these same ones he also called or elected; and whom he called or elected, these same ones he also justified; and whom he justified, these same ones he also glorified — the real imputation of divine blessing at maturity plus the third hope of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ.

V. The New Life and Its Challenges — Romans 8:31

Beginning with Romans 8:31 and running through verse 39, a new major paragraph opens: the new life and its challenges. Five challenges are presented in this section. This chapter introduces the first two.

The First Challenge: Opposition

Paul opens with a characteristic debater's idiom: a rhetorical question that functions as a direct assertion. The construction begins with the neuter singular interrogative pronoun followed by the inferential post-positive conjunction and the future active indicative of the verb for speaking — here a deliberative future presenting a rhetorical question designed to force a correct conclusion.

The corrected idiomatic translation of the opening phrase is: 'Therefore, to what conclusion are we forced?' This refers specifically to Romans 8:28–30. The prepositional phrase that follows is pros (πρός) plus the accusative plural demonstrative houtos, translated 'face to face with these things' — a reference to the content of the preceding paragraph.

The rhetorical question that follows is elliptical — there is no verb in the original. Paul's excitement at this point in the argument produces a highly compressed syntax. The question reads literally: 'If the God for us, who against us?' — a first-class condition acknowledging the reality: God is indeed for the believer.

The subject is theos (θεός) with the definite article — the generic article identifying God the Father, who has been the subject throughout the preceding paragraph. The prepositional phrase is huper (ὑπέρ) plus the ablative of egō (ἐγώ), 'for us.' In context the plural applies specifically to mature believers, though God's provision extends to all believers. The opposing prepositional phrase is kata (κατά) plus the genitive plural of egō, 'against us.'

The corrected translation of Romans 8:31: “Therefore, face to face with these things, to what conclusion are we forced? If the God is for us — and he is — who is against us?”

The first-class condition recognizes that every believer is in the plan of God and that God has made provision for every believer — including for opposition, adversity, and every other difficulty. The plan of God is not threatened by its opponents. No one is God's equal. No one has more power or ability than God.

The two judicial imputations of Y radical are the ground for the assertion that God is for us. First: all personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged — God had to be for us to do that to His Son. Second: divine righteousness is imputed to the believer at the moment of salvation — God had to be for us to give His own righteousness to those who had no claim to it.

Romans 8:32 — to be treated in the following chapters — elaborates this verse. Its first half demonstrates that God is for us by means of the first judicial imputation (our sins to Christ on the cross). Its second half demonstrates that God will freely give us all things by means of the second judicial imputation: because the believer possesses a portion of divine integrity, God can impute blessing to that integrity without compromising His attributes.

The Second Challenge: The Incomprehensibility of Blessing as Glorification

The second challenge to mature believers is the absolute incomprehensibility — to underdeveloped believers — of the truth that God glorifies Himself by blessing the mature believer. The typical assumption in much of Christendom is that God is glorified by human effort, sacrifice, legalism, or austerity. The opposite is the case. Nothing we accomplish glorifies God. We can do nothing for our own salvation, and we can do nothing of ourselves to glorify the Lord Jesus Christ. Glorification occurs exclusively through the divine imputation of blessing to the righteousness of God resident in the mature believer. This challenge will be addressed in detail through the study of Romans 8:32.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Twenty-Nine

1. The five steps to glory in Romans 8:29–30 move from eternity past through time to eternity future: foreknowledge, foreordination, election, justification, and glorification. The same persons are the objects of all five acts.

2. Step four — justification — is the second judicial imputation: divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation. It is the indispensable foundation for the real imputation of blessing in time at maturity.

3. Justification means vindication for blessing. Every believer in the Lord Jesus Christ has been qualified for blessing. The potential is present from the moment of salvation; its realization awaits the development of capacity through doctrine.

4. The grace pipeline runs from the justice of God on the giving end to the righteousness of God on the receiving end. It is encapsulated by the integrity of God. Nothing external — no work, production, morality, sacrifice, or asceticism — can penetrate the encapsulation.

5. Step five — glorification — encompasses both the sixth and seventh imputations: the real imputation of blessing in time at maturity, and the real imputation of eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ.

6. The constative aorist of doxazō combines two a fortiori arguments: if justice accomplished the greater at salvation (judicial imputation of righteousness), it will accomplish the less at maturity (real imputation of blessing); if justice accomplished the greater at maturity (blessing in time), it will accomplish the less at the judgment seat of Christ (eternal reward).

7. The seventh imputation — blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ — is the 'good' of Romans 8:28 and the terminus of the entire formula x plus y plus z.

8. Divine blessing and glorification were established in the decrees before any believer existed. Omniscience is primary; the decrees follow from omniscience; foreknowledge follows from the decrees. Nothing could be foreknown until it was first decreed.

9. Romans 8:31 introduces the new major paragraph: the new life and its challenges (verses 31–39). The opening rhetorical question — 'to what conclusion are we forced? if the God is for us, who is against us?' — forces the conclusion that the plan of God is greater than any opposition.

10. The two judicial imputations of Y radical are the dual ground for the declaration that God is for us: He imputed our sins to His Son, and He imputed His righteousness to us. Both acts demonstrate that God has committed Himself to the blessing of the believer.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
doxazō δοξάζω doxazō — to glorify, to share in glory To praise, to honor, to glorify, to magnify. In Romans 8:30, the constative aorist gathers into one entirety the real imputation of blessing in time at maturity and the real imputation of eternal blessing and reward to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. The believer shares in the glory of God through imputation.
dikaiōō δικαιόω dikaiōō — to justify, to declare righteous, to vindicate To declare righteous, to justify, to vindicate. In Romans 8:30, the constative aorist refers to the momentary judicial imputation of divine righteousness at the moment of faith in Christ. Justification is the qualification for blessing: the believer is vindicated for the imputation of blessing in time at maturity.
kaleō καλέω kaleō — to call, to elect To call, to summon, to elect. In Romans 8:30, the dramatic aorist states the present reality of election with the certitude of a past event in the divine decrees. Election is the plan of God for the believer designed in eternity past, taking cognizance of what was decreed.
houtos οὗτος houtos — this one, these same ones Demonstrative pronoun used in Romans 8:30 to refer to what immediately precedes, emphasizing that the same persons are the objects of each successive divine act: foreordination, calling, justification, and glorification.
huper ὑπέρ huper — for, on behalf of Preposition with the ablative meaning 'for, on behalf of.' In Romans 8:31, 'God is for us' (huper plus ablative of ego) establishes the ground for the believer's confidence in the face of opposition.
kata κατά kata — against Preposition with the genitive meaning 'against.' In Romans 8:31, 'who is against us?' (kata plus genitive of ego) forms the counterpart to the assertion that God is for us, rhetorical in function.
judicial imputation An imputation that lacks antecedence and affinity between what is imputed and the recipient. The first judicial imputation: all sins of the human race imputed to Christ on the cross. The second judicial imputation: divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation. Contrasted with a real imputation, which requires a divinely prepared home or target with antecedence and affinity.
real imputation An imputation that requires two factors: (1) the content of what is imputed, and (2) a divinely prepared home or target with antecedence and affinity. Examples: human life to the soul at birth; Adam's original sin to the old sin nature at birth; eternal life to regeneration at salvation; blessing in time to imputed divine righteousness at maturity; eternal reward to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ.
maturity adjustment The second of the three adjustments to the justice of God. Progressive in nature; achieved through sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine resulting in maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Cracking the maturity barrier results in the righteousness of God demanding, and the justice of God executing, the real imputation of blessing in time.
a fortiori Latin: 'from the stronger.' A logical argument from the greater to the less: if God accomplished the greater (judicial imputation of righteousness at salvation), He will certainly accomplish the less (real imputation of blessing at maturity). Chapter Three Hundred Thirty

Romans 8:32 — The Second Challenge: Encouragement Through the A Fortiori Blessings and the Doctrine of Imputation

Romans 8:32 “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (ESV)

Corrected translation: The God who did not even spare His own Son, but on behalf of all of us delivered Him over to judgment — how shall He not also with Him in grace give to us the all things?

Romans 8:31 opened the first of a series of challenges, framing the question of opposition: if the God is for us, who is against us? The first half of that verse provides the outline for verse 32. In verse 32, the second challenge shifts from opposition to encouragement — the motivation for spiritual advance, the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the imputation of blessing in time. The verse establishes the two judicial imputations that constitute the greater degree of effort in the first a fortiori blessing, and then announces the less — the real imputation of all things to the mature believer.

I. The A Fortiori Framework Revisited

The Latin phrase a fortiori means 'with stronger reason.' It is a category of logic organized around the degree of effort involved in an action. Whenever the greater degree of effort has been fulfilled, the lesser follows logically and necessarily. The distinction between greater and lesser is not a matter of quality, but of the relative difficulty of the action from the standpoint of divine justice.

Two a fortiori blessings were introduced in Romans 5 and return to prominence in Romans 8.

The temporal a fortiori: if the justice of God provided the greater — salvation through the judicial imputation of divine righteousness — it follows a fortiori that the justice of God will accomplish the less, namely the real imputation of blessing in time at the point of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

The eternal a fortiori: if the justice of God provided the greater — maturity through the real imputation of divine blessing in time — it follows a fortiori that the justice of God will provide the less to the mature believer at the judgment seat of Christ through the real imputation of eternal blessing and reward (the seventh imputation).

Both a fortiori blessings are the means by which the believer shares in the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ, as established at the end of verse 30. They are administered through the grace policy of God for the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ.

II. Exegesis of Romans 8:32

A. The Subject: The God Who

The verse opens with the nominative singular of the relative pronoun hos (ὅς), which requires identification of its antecedent. The antecedent is houtos (οὗτος) from verse 31: 'the God.' Thus the subject of verse 32 is God the Father, and the translation begins: 'the God who.'

B. The Intensive Particle ge

An unusual intensive particle follows: ge (γε), meaning 'even.' It functions to heighten the force of what follows: 'the God who did not even.'

C. The Verb pheidomai — Did Not Spare

The verb is pheidomai (φείδομαι) with the negative ou (οὐ): to spare someone from something. 'The God who did not even spare.'

The aorist tense here is a dramatic aorist. The dramatic aorist states the present reality of the sacrifice of Christ on the cross with the certitude of a completed past event. It brings the first judicial imputation into sharp focus: the imputation of all personal sins of the human race to Christ on the cross. It is also a culminative aorist, viewing the judicial imputation of all personal sins to Christ in its entirety, and emphasizing the existing results — the entire complex of blessing in the Church Age that flows from that completed act.

The middle voice indicates a deponent verb: middle in form, active in meaning. God the Father produces the action of the verb by means of the first judicial imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross. The declarative indicative represents the verbal idea from the viewpoint of reality. Combined with the negative, it states a dogmatic fact: God the Father imputed our sins to Christ on the cross and judged them.

D. The Object: His Own Son

The object of the verb is the objective genitive singular of the adjective idios (ἴδιος), meaning 'unique in the group,' 'one's own.' This is the term from which the English word 'idiot' is derived, though in Greek it denotes distinctive ownership or relationship. It expresses the eternal relationship between the Father and the Son. Following this is the objective genitive singular of huios (υἱός): Son. The full phrase: 'His own Son,' referring to the Lord Jesus Christ in hypostatic union — undiminished deity and true humanity in one person forever.

This explains the cry of dereliction. Our Lord's utterance — 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' — is stated prophetically in Psalm 22:1 and historically in Matthew 27:46. When the personal sins of the human race were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged by the justice of God, the Father withdrew fellowship from the Son. This constituted the spiritual death of Christ, and it is to His spiritual death — not His physical death — that the saving work on the cross is assigned.

Salvation was completed before our Lord died physically. In John 19:30, when Jesus had received the wine, He said, 'It is finished,' and bowing His head, He dismissed His spirit. Physical death followed the completion of the work. The sins imputed to Christ were not inherently His own — there was no antecedence, no affinity. They were imputed for the purpose of judgment. This is a judicial imputation.

E. The Adversative Conjunction alla — But

The adversative conjunction alla (ἀλλά) sets up a contrast with what precedes and introduces the corresponding positive action.

F. The Verb paradidomi — Delivered Over to Judgment

The aorist active indicative of paradidomi (παραδίδωμι): to deliver over to judgment as the function of divine justice. This is the constative aorist, which contemplates the action of the judicial imputation of all personal sins to Christ in its entirety — every personal sin committed in all of human history imputed to the Lord Jesus Christ and judged at one time on the cross. The active voice identifies God the Father as the one who produces this action. The declarative indicative presents it as a dogmatic statement of doctrine.

The prepositional phrase huper (ὑπέρ) plus the genitive plural of pas (πᾶς) and the first person plural pronoun: 'on behalf of all of us.' This construction expresses substitutionary atonement.

The accusative singular of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός) functions as the third person personal pronoun: 'him.' Corrected translation to this point: 'The God who did not even spare His own Son, but on behalf of all of us delivered Him over to judgment.'

G. The Rhetorical Question: pos ouchi — How Shall He Not

The interrogative pronoun pos (πῶς) is used especially for rhetorical questions.

Combined with the interrogative negative ouchi (οὐχί), which expects an affirmative answer, the construction frames a question that functions as a declaration: 'How shall he not also?' The adjunctive conjunction kai (καί) is translated 'also.'

The prepositional phrase sun (σύν) plus the dative of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός) denotes accompaniment or association: 'with him.' Our association with the Lord Jesus Christ begins at salvation adjustment to the justice of God, marked by the second judicial imputation. The imputation of divine righteousness to the believer establishes the grace pipeline: all blessing flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. Righteousness is the principle of divine integrity; justice is the function of divine integrity. No human activity — witnessing, prayer, obedience — is the mechanism of blessing. All blessing is an imputation from the justice of God to the righteousness of God, received entirely apart from human merit.

H. The Verb charizomai — Graciously Give

The future middle indicative of charizomai (χαρίζομαι): to grace out, to graciously give, to give beneficially. The verb is derived from charis (χάρις), grace; the middle voice suffix is added to form the verb. The translation 'graciously give' is preferable to 'freely give' because it preserves the grace content of the word.

The future tense functions in two ways simultaneously, depending on the believer's position in the spiritual life. As a nomic future, it states a fact or performance that may be expected when the believer attains maturity adjustment to the justice of God — future from the standpoint of the believer who has not yet arrived. As a deliberative future, it replaces a direct assertion with a rhetorical question for the believer who has already cracked the maturity barrier, for whom this blessing is already a reality. The middle voice is deponent: active in meaning. God the Father produces the action of the verb at maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The interrogative indicative mood assumes an actual fact of doctrine that may be stated in answer to the question.

The direct object is the accusative neuter plural of pas (πᾶς) with the definite article, used generically to comprehend all six categories of blessing imputed to the believer: 'the all things.' This is not the same 'all things' as in Romans 8:28, where X + Y + Z together constitute the all things that work together for the good. Here the all things refers specifically to the blessings imputed at maturity — the content of the sixth imputation extrapolated from Z radical.

Corrected translation of the full verse: 'The God who did not even spare His own Son, but on behalf of all of us delivered Him over to judgment — how shall He not also with Him in grace give to us the all things?'

III. The Equation: X + Y + Z = The Glory of God

The exegesis of verse 32 is best understood within the seven-imputation equation developed through the epistle. The components are as follows.

A. X Radical — The Imputations at Birth

Human life is imputed at physical birth to its divinely prepared target, the soul. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. The result is that every member of the human race is born physically alive and at the same time spiritually dead. This constitutes the first potential: the potential of salvation. It is a potential for every person, because all personal sins of the human race were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. Adding pertinent doctrine — the gospel, provided to all who are positive at God consciousness — produces the first hope: confident assurance that faith in Jesus Christ results in instant salvation. When that hope is replaced by the reality of believing in Christ, salvation adjustment to the justice of God occurs.

B. Y Radical — The Two Judicial Imputations

Judicial imputation number one: the imputation of all personal sins of the human race to Christ on the cross. Judicial imputation number two: the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation. These two judicial imputations constitute the greater degree of effort in the first a fortiori. They cannot be separated. The sins of the world had to be settled at the cross before salvation was possible; the imputation of divine righteousness follows as the immediate result of faith in Christ. Together they produce the second potential: the potential of blessing in time at maturity. Adding pertinent doctrine produces the second hope: confident assurance that continued daily intake of Bible doctrine will result in cracking the maturity barrier and receiving blessing from God, which glorifies Him in time. When that hope is replaced by the reality of maturity adjustment to the justice of God, the sixth imputation occurs.

C. Z Radical — Eternal Life, Blessing in Time, and Eternal Reward

Eternal life, a real imputation to regeneration at salvation, combines with the imputation of blessing in time at maturity to produce the third potential: the potentiality of blessing and reward in eternity. Adding pertinent doctrine and the undeserved suffering of Romans 8:17–30 — which functions as a laser beam directed past the barriers of time toward the judgment seat of Christ — produces the third hope: absolute confident assurance of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. This is the hope that mature believers carry in the soul through every circumstance of life, including dying grace. It equals the good of Romans 8:28 and the glory of Romans 8:30. The seventh imputation — eternal blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ — is the culmination. X + Y + Z = the glory of God.

IV. The Doctrine of Imputation

A. Definition and Description

Imputation is the doctrine of attributing or ascribing something to someone — something they did not previously possess, which they now possess permanently. Before imputation, the recipient does not have what is imputed. After imputation, they have it, and since God is always the subject, they possess it irreversibly and eternally. God is always the subject of imputation. In this study, various categories of humanity are the beneficiaries or recipients.

B. The Source of All Imputation

The justice of God is the source of all imputation and the point of reference for mankind throughout history. Divine justice is perfectly fair: it never withholds anything from anyone on the basis of any factor in the recipient, and it never discriminates. God is the perfect judge. Justice is the function of the judge. Everything provided by the justice of God arrives at the right time, in the right place, in the right manner, with complete security. Imputation is therefore a function of the justice of God whereby either condemnation or blessing is attributed to mankind.

C. Two Categories of Imputation: Real and Judicial

There are two and only two categories of imputation: real imputations and judicial imputations. Of the seven total imputations in the equation, five are real and two are judicial.

A real imputation attributes to the recipient what is antecedently his own — that is, what has natural affinity with its target. A real imputation has two factors: (1) what is imputed, and (2) the target or home for that imputation. There is affinity and antecedence between the thing imputed and the target. Because God is always the subject, real imputations are permanent and irrevocable.

A judicial imputation ascribes to the recipient what is not antecedently his own. There is no affinity and no antecedence. A judicial imputation has only one factor: what is being imputed. Because there is no natural target, the source — the justice of God — is emphasized. There are only two judicial imputations.

D. The Seven Imputations in Order

The following are the seven imputations, their category, and the target or home where applicable.

# What Is Imputed Category Target / Home
1 Human life Real The soul
2 Adam's original sin Real The genetically formed old sin nature
3 All personal sins of the human race Judicial None (no affinity — imputed to Christ)
4 Divine righteousness (+R) Judicial None (no affinity — imputed to the believer)
5 Eternal life Real Regeneration (the new birth)
6 Blessing in time Real +R (divine righteousness as the target)
7 Blessing and reward in eternity Real The resurrection body

E. Real Imputation — Human Life and the Soul

Human life is the first real imputation. The soul is its divinely prepared target. The affinity is perfect and permanent: human life, once imputed to the soul, remains there forever. The soul may depart the body at physical death, but human life remains in the soul wherever the soul resides — whether in heaven, in resurrection, or in the eternal state. There is no cessation of human life. It cannot be extracted from the soul by any means. This permanence is the key to understanding all imputations: every imputation carries the same security factor. What God imputes is permanently possessed by the recipient.

Simultaneously with the imputation of human life, Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. The result is spiritual death at birth — physical life and spiritual death coexisting. This condemnation at the beginning of life is not arbitrary. It establishes the basis from which divine justice can then move to bless. The justice of God always condemns before it blesses. This principle governs the entire sequence from birth to eternity.

A direct consequence of this principle concerns those who die before reaching accountability. If an individual's mental capacity is such that no decision for or against God can ever be made, that person is automatically saved — condemned at birth, and therefore the basis for blessing is established, and no decision of negative volition is possible. Similarly, any child who dies before reaching the age of accountability is automatically saved, for the same reason: condemnation at birth has already satisfied the requirement of divine justice, providing leeway for salvation without a volitional decision. The justice of God is perfectly fair to every member of the human race.

F. Real Imputation — Eternal Life and Regeneration

Eternal life requires a target just as human life does. Since all life in the human race is provided at birth and only at birth — never in the womb, never afterward by any other means — eternal life must also be provided at a birth. The Holy Spirit therefore provides a new birth, creating the regenerate human spirit as the target for eternal life. Being born again is the act of the Holy Spirit in providing a home for eternal life that has both antecedence and affinity. Regeneration is the divinely prepared recipient of the fifth imputation.

G. Real Imputation — Blessing in Time and Divine Righteousness

The sixth imputation — blessing in time — must also have a target with affinity. It cannot be imputed to the believer directly, because the believer does not earn or deserve it. It is imputed to the divine righteousness (+R) already residing in the believer since salvation. The justice of God can only bless perfect righteousness. This is why the possession of +R at salvation is not itself the blessing, but the prerequisite for blessing. The believer carries +R from salvation forward. At the point of maturity adjustment to the justice of God, blessing is imputed to that righteousness. The entire grace pipeline runs from the justice of God to the righteousness of God — secured by and consistent with all the divine attributes.

H. Real Imputation — Blessing in Eternity and the Resurrection Body

The seventh imputation — blessing and reward in eternity — requires a permanent residence. The resurrection body, minus the old sin nature and minus the old man, is the divinely prepared target for eternal reward. The second a fortiori guarantees this imputation: if the justice of God provided the greater in time (blessing at maturity), it will certainly provide the less in eternity (reward at the judgment seat of Christ). There will be no equality of reward in eternity. Those who accumulated doctrine and cracked the maturity barrier will receive great blessing and reward; those who were negative toward doctrine will possess eternal life and a resurrection body but no reward — a foundation of +R with nothing built upon it. There will be no regret, no sorrow, and no tears in eternity, but there will be no equality of blessing.

I. Judicial Imputations — The Exchange at the Cross

The two judicial imputations are the hinge on which the entire system turns. In the third imputation, the personal sins of all humanity are imputed to Christ on the cross. These sins were not inherently His; there was no affinity and no antecedence. They were imputed for the specific purpose of judgment by divine justice. Every personal sin from the fall of Adam to the final sin of the Millennium was condemned at one moment on the cross. None of these sins were ever imputed to the individual members of the human race for judgment. Personal sin is not the issue in condemnation — Adam's original sin is the issue in condemnation. Personal sin is not the issue in salvation — Christ is the issue in salvation.

In the fourth imputation, the righteousness of God is imputed to the believer at salvation. There is likewise no affinity — the believer possesses nothing comparable to God's perfect righteousness. The imputation of divine righteousness therefore depends entirely on the prior judicial imputation of sin to Christ. The righteousness of God cannot be imputed until the sins of the world have been judged at the cross. This is why judicial imputation number one must precede judicial imputation number two, and why the saving work of Christ on the cross must precede the salvation of the believer in time.

These two judicial imputations form an exchange: our sins for His righteousness. They constitute the greater degree of effort in the first a fortiori. If the justice of God accomplished the greater — providing salvation through this exchange — it follows with absolute logical necessity that the justice of God will not withhold the less: the real imputation of blessing in time to the mature believer.

V. Prosperity as a Real Imputation from the Justice of God

The 'all things' of verse 32 refers to the categories of blessing imputed at maturity. This is the domain of prosperity as a theological category. Prosperity is a real imputation from the justice of God to the believer at the point of maturity and thereafter. It is not logistical grace, which supports every positive believer from salvation to death regardless of spiritual status. Logistical grace includes food, clothing, shelter, a right pastor, and the opportunity to hear Bible doctrine — all of it necessary but none of it constituting the blessing of maturity.

Prosperity as imputation is the objective of the plan of God for the believer's life after salvation. The content of that prosperity varies for each individual and is determined by the justice of God, not by the believer's preferences or production. Wealth, success, and recognition are only surface manifestations. The apostle Paul is the paradigm case: he died materially impoverished, yet was the most prosperous believer in the Church Age, having received the highest category of blessing available in time — the real imputation of martyrdom to his +R. Prosperity requires two accompanying factors: security and capacity. The justice of God provides both. The blessings imputed are secure because they are imputed from divine justice. Capacity must first be developed through doctrine, because blessing without capacity produces misery, not fulfillment.

All blessing, of whatever kind, arrives through the same mechanism: the grace pipeline from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. No commanded activity — prayer, witnessing, service, giving — is the means of receiving blessing. These functions belong to the ambassador and priest roles of the believer and have their own value, but they do not activate the imputation of blessing. Only the capacity produced by sustained doctrine intake, cracking the maturity barrier, triggers the sixth imputation.

Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Thirty

1. Romans 8:32 is the verse of the second challenge. Where verse 31 raised the challenge of opposition, verse 32 provides the corresponding encouragement: the two judicial imputations guarantee that the justice of God will not withhold the all things from the mature believer.

2. The dramatic and culminative aorist of pheidomai brings into focus the first judicial imputation. The imputation of all personal sins of the human race to Christ on the cross, judged by divine justice, is presented both as an ever-present reality and as an action complete in its entirety.

3. The saving work of Christ is assigned to His spiritual death, not His physical death. The judicial imputation and judgment of sin constituted His spiritual death. Physical death followed the completion of that work, as confirmed by John 19:30.

4. Personal sin is not the issue in either condemnation or salvation. Adam's original sin is the issue in condemnation. Christ is the issue in salvation. Personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross for judgment, never to individual members of the human race.

5. The two judicial imputations are inseparable and constitute the greater degree of effort in the first a fortiori. Judicial imputation number one (sins to Christ) plus judicial imputation number two (+R to the believer) equals the potential for blessing in time — the lesser that divine justice guarantees through the logic of a fortiori.

6. Imputation is the doctrine of attributing to someone what they did not possess, permanently and irrevocably. God is always the subject. Every imputation carries the security of its divine source. What is imputed is possessed forever, regardless of the recipient's subsequent behavior.

7. The two categories of imputation are real and judicial. Real imputations have affinity and antecedence between what is imputed and its target. Judicial imputations have no affinity or antecedence and have one factor only. Five of the seven imputations are real; two are judicial.

8. The five real imputations and their targets are fixed. Human life to the soul; Adam's original sin to the old sin nature; eternal life to regeneration; blessing in time to divine righteousness (+R); blessing and reward in eternity to the resurrection body.

9. The justice of God always condemns before it blesses. Condemnation at birth through Adam's original sin establishes the basis from which divine justice can move to bless through salvation and maturity. This principle ensures the fairness of God toward every human being, including infants and those who never reach accountability.

10. All blessing flows through the grace pipeline from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. No human activity constitutes the mechanism of blessing. Righteousness is the principle of divine integrity; justice is its function. The pipeline is sealed by the integrity of God, ensuring that blessing is both appropriate and secure.

11. Prosperity as an imputation requires both security and capacity. Security is guaranteed by the divine justice that provides the imputation. Capacity is developed through sustained doctrine intake, without which blessing cannot be received or enjoyed. Blessing without capacity produces misery.

12. The seventh imputation at the judgment seat of Christ will not be equal for all believers. Those who were negative toward doctrine will have eternal life and resurrection bodies but no reward. Those who cracked the maturity barrier and advanced to supergrace and ultra-supergrace will receive great blessing and reward in eternity. Equality of reward is not a principle of divine justice.

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition

When the greater degree of effort has been fulfilled, the lesser follows with logical necessity. In Romans 8, the two a fortiori blessings establish that if divine justice accomplished the greater (the two judicial imputations at salvation), it will certainly accomplish the less (blessing in time at maturity; blessing in eternity at the judgment seat of Christ).
pheidomai φείδομαι pheidomai — to spare, to refrain from harming Verb used with the negative in Romans 8:32: 'did not spare.' The dramatic aorist states the present reality of the judicial imputation of all sins to Christ with the certitude of a completed past event.
paradidomi παραδίδωμι paradidomi — to deliver over, to hand over to judgment Compound verb: para (over) + didomi (to give). Used in Romans 8:32 of God the Father delivering the Son over to judgment through the judicial imputation of all personal sins. The constative aorist gathers the entirety of this act — every personal sin of human history — into a single completed action.
huper ὑπέρ huper — on behalf of, in place of Preposition used with the genitive in Romans 8:32: 'on behalf of all of us.' In this construction it expresses substitutionary atonement — Christ delivered over to judgment in the place of, and for the benefit of, every member of the human race.
charizomai χαρίζομαι charizomai — to graciously give, to grace out Verb derived from charis (grace). Used in Romans 8:32 of the future real imputation of all things to the mature believer. The nomic future indicates a fact to be expected at maturity adjustment to the justice of God; the deliberative future frames it as a rhetorical declaration for the believer who has already arrived.
idios ἴδιος idios — one's own, unique to oneself Adjective expressing distinctive ownership or relationship. In Romans 8:32, used of the eternal relationship between God the Father and the Son: 'His own Son.' Denotes the absolute uniqueness of that relationship from eternity past.
real imputation An imputation in which there is both antecedence and affinity between what is imputed and its target or home. The thing imputed belongs in the target; it is antecedently the recipient's own. Five of the seven imputations are real. All real imputations are permanent and irrevocable.
judicial imputation An imputation in which there is no affinity and no antecedence between what is imputed and the recipient. The source — the justice of God — is therefore emphasized. There are only two judicial imputations: the imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross, and the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation.
